data: Start with a quickstart, then use the groups below.
data.configure#Configure: Resource classes: Define resource classes as Swarm services, size limits, choose replica counts, persistent classes, Rerun job with SSH, and the stack configuration reference. Images: Run the runner in stock Linux and Windows images with a read-only mount, and bring your own image. Docker builds: Build container images from jobs with an opt-in service that mounts the host Docker engine, and compare the rootless and daemonless alternatives. MicroVM jobs: Run each job in its own microVM with Kata Containers on labeled Linux nodes, set up the nodes, and learn what the add-on costs and what it does not cover.
data.contribute#Contribute: CI/CD: What the pipeline tests, how the docs site is built, and how releases are signed and published. Releasing: How a merge to main becomes a signed GitHub release, how maintainers enable publishing, and how to recover from a failed release. Contributing: How to report a bug, propose a change and open a pull request for machine runner swarm, a CircleCI Labs project.
data.get-started#Get started: Quickstart on Linux: Run a first job on a Docker Swarm node with CircleCI machine runner 3 in about a dozen commands, for a one-node trial or the start of a cluster. Quickstart on Windows Server: Run a first job on a Windows Server Docker Swarm node with CircleCI machine runner 3 in six steps, using the stock Server Core image. Concepts: How Swarm services map to resource classes, what the token proxy does, what a clean environment covers, and how the default and hardened classes differ.
data.install#Install: Linux: Deploy CircleCI machine runner 3 as a Docker Swarm stack on Ubuntu or RHEL, with one clean container for every job. Windows Server: Deploy CircleCI machine runner 3 as a Docker Swarm stack on Windows Server 2022 or 2025, with one clean container for every job. Multi-node clusters: Join Linux, Windows, and Arm nodes to one Docker Swarm, place resource classes with labels and constraints, and open the ports that the nodes need.
data.more#More: Security: Threat model, token storage on Linux and Windows, the token proxy, hardening defaults, CircleCI-side controls, egress hosts, and BitLocker. FAQ: Common questions about the Swarm runner stack: what to build, comparisons with official runners, scaling, unsupported jobs, and node loss.
data.operate#Operate: Operations: Status and logs, monitoring, capacity, backups, runner upgrades, token rotation, node drain, and uninstall for the Swarm runner stack. Troubleshooting: Symptoms, causes, and fixes for the Docker Swarm runner stack on Linux and Windows, with the error text to search for.
data.reference#Reference: Changelog: Release notes are on GitHub Releases. Read every release between yours and the one you install before you upgrade. Migrate from Docker Compose: Move from the old docker-compose.yml setup to the Docker Swarm stack, and map each Compose setting to its Swarm equivalent.

data: Resource classes: Define resource classes as Swarm services, size limits, choose replica counts, persistent classes, Rerun job with SSH, and the stack configuration reference. Images: Run the runner in stock Linux and Windows images with a read-only mount, and bring your own image. Docker builds: Build container images from jobs with an opt-in service that mounts the host Docker engine, and compare the rootless and daemonless alternatives. MicroVM jobs: Run each job in its own microVM with Kata Containers on labeled Linux nodes, set up the nodes, and learn what the add-on costs and what it does not cover.

By default, jobs on these runners cannot reach a Docker engine. Access to a Docker daemon is equivalent to root access to the machine, so this repository makes Docker builds opt-in, one dedicated class at a time.
This page describes pattern A, which is built and tested, and patterns B and C, which are documented alternatives. Pattern D, a Docker daemon in the microVM of the job, is part of the MicroVM add-on and needs nodes with KVM.
data.choose-a-pattern#Choose a pattern: Pattern Jobs get Root-equivalent on the node Status Platform A: host engine socket The full Docker API of the node Yes Built, with a stack file and an example Linux, and Windows images on Windows B: rootless BuildKit on the host Only a build API, through the socket of one BuildKit daemon No, but the daemon runs on the host Documented, not built Linux C: daemonless builder in the job Nothing from the host No Documented, not built Linux D: Docker daemon inside a microVM Its own daemon, in the VM of the job No, but the job has SYS_ADMIN inside a VM Built and tested with a fake API, in the microVM add-on Linux with KVM CircleCI lists Docker layer caching among the features that self-hosted runners do not support. Pattern A reuses the layer cache of the host engine, which every job on that node shares.
data.deploy-on-linux#Deploy on Linux:
Join a dedicated worker node. Refer to Multi-Node Clusters. Nothing is installed on it: the runner-distributor service also runs on a docker-build node and installs the runner there.
Label the node:
$ docker node update --label-add machine-runner-swarm.docker-build=true Create the resource class /linux-docker-build and the secret linux-docker-build-token. Refer to Resource Classes.
Deploy the add-on stack file with the main file. Pass the same list of files on every later deploy (why).
$ docker stack deploy -c linux/stack/runners.yaml -c linux/stack/docker-build.yaml runners The file linux/stack/docker-build.yaml defines linux-docker-build. It mounts the socket, and constrains the service to node.platform.os == linux, node.role == worker, and node.labels.machine-runner-swarm.docker-build == true. Every other service in the stack files carries node.labels.machine-runner-swarm.docker-build != true, so labeling a node moves the other classes off it. The class mounts the runner volume read-only, like every class, and the entrypoint adds the job user to the group of the socket, so jobs need no sudo to run docker. A job that controls the engine can also change the volume runner-bin of its node, which only this class uses there. The cimg/base image includes the Docker CLI.
Use the class in a job:
jobs: image: machine: true resource_class: /linux-docker-build steps: - checkout - run: docker build -t "app:${CIRCLE_SHA1:0:12}" . - run: name: Clean up, the engine outlives the job when: always command: docker image rm -f "app:${CIRCLE_SHA1:0:12}" || true The file examples/linux-docker-build.yml has the full job.
data.deploy-on-windows#Deploy on Windows:
The add-on stack file windows\stack\docker-build.yaml defines windows-docker-build. It mounts the named pipe \\.\pipe\docker_engine, which docker stack deploy supports, and the host directory C:\Program Files\Docker at C:\docker, read-only. It appends C:\docker to the PATH. Adjust the bind source if docker.exe lives elsewhere on your nodes. It runs on a worker node only (node.role == worker), as on Linux, so it needs a Windows worker that joined the Swarm (Multi-Node Clusters). The single-node Swarm of the Windows quickstart has only a manager, and the class stays Pending there.
Label the worker node: docker node update --label-add machine-runner-swarm.docker-build=true .
Create the resource class /windows-docker-build and the secret windows-docker-build-token.
Deploy the add-on stack file with the main file. Pass the same list of files on every later deploy (why).
docker stack deploy -c windows\stack\runners.yaml -c windows\stack\docker-build.yaml runners Jobs can build Windows images only, because the engine runs in Windows-container mode. Linux images cannot be built there. The file examples/windows-docker-build.yml has a job. Registry credentials for docker login and docker push belong in a restricted context.
data.pattern-a-the-host-docker-engine#Pattern:
A service of this class bind-mounts the engine endpoint of the node: /var/run/docker.sock on Linux, and the named pipe \\.\pipe\docker_engine on Windows.
Caution The engine endpoint is root-equivalent on its node, and administrator-equivalent on Windows. A job that can use it can start a privileged container, mount any host path, and read the data of other jobs and containers. Use pattern A only for trusted projects, on a dedicated node.
Four controls limit the damage:
Worker nodes only. The service runs only where node.role == worker. On a Swarm manager the socket also controls the Swarm, so a job can create a service that mounts any secret and read the token of every class. A single-node Swarm has only a manager, so do not use pattern A there. Labeled nodes only. The service runs only on nodes that carry machine-runner-swarm.docker-build=true. No neighbors. The engine shows every container on the node. Keep other classes off the node. Refer to Keep the docker-build node to itself. Trusted projects only. Restrict the class with a config policy, and keep production contexts away from it. Refer to CircleCI-side controls. State also persists. The images, containers, volumes, and build cache of the host engine outlive the job, so the environment is not clean. Remove what a job creates in a final step. Nothing else prunes this engine, so the disk of the node fills with layers and cache over time: schedule docker builder prune and docker image prune on it, as in Free disk space. Never run docker volume prune there: the node also holds the volume runner-bin.
data.pattern-b-rootless-buildkit-on-the-host#:
Run a rootless BuildKit daemon on the host under a dedicated unprivileged account, and mount only its socket into a runner service. Jobs send builds to that daemon with a BuildKit client. The daemon exposes only the BuildKit build API, not the Docker API, so a job cannot start arbitrary containers or mount host paths through it.
The risk shrinks, but it does not disappear. The daemon runs on the host and shares its kernel, and every job that uses it shares its build cache. This repository documents the pattern only. It has no stack file, helper, or test for it.
data.pattern-c-a-daemonless-builder-in-the-jo:
Run a daemonless builder inside the job container, such as a maintained fork of Kaniko or Buildah. The job needs no access to the host engine, and nothing of the host is exposed.
These builders have their own privilege needs. Rootless Buildah relies on user namespaces, and Kaniko expects to run as root inside its container. Swarm ignores security_opt and privileged in a stack file, so test your builder in a class that matches your policy before you rely on it. This repository documents the pattern only.
data.what-to-avoid#What to avoid: Mounting the Docker socket into any class that is not dedicated to builds. Starting a privileged Docker-in-Docker container from a job. Swarm ignores privileged, so it does not work in a stack, and it is root-equivalent where it does work. Running pattern A on a manager, or on a node that also runs production workloads.

data: This repository publishes no class images. (It publishes one image, the token proxy, which holds the class tokens and is no environment for a job: The token proxy image.) The stack files run stock images and mount the runner into them, so the image of a class is the environment that its jobs see. This page describes the stock Linux images, the stock Windows image, and how to bring your own image on each OS.
data.linux-bring-your-own-image#Linux: bring:
Build an image when jobs need tools that you do not want to install in every job. This is also the way to run a hardened class, because jobs there have no sudo.
The file linux/images/example/Dockerfile starts from a cimg image and adds postgresql-client. Copy it and replace the packages.
$ docker build -t registry.example.com/ci/linux-pg:1 linux/images/example $ docker push registry.example.com/ci/linux-pg:1 Then set the image of a service in your stack file:
image: registry.example.com/ci/linux-pg:1 Every node that runs the service must be able to pull the image. Refer to Registry needs. Rebuild the image when its base changes, for example once a month.
The Dockerfile has one target. It adds tools to a stock image and nothing of the runner, so the image needs no rebuild for a new runner version. It ends with USER circleci, which only affects a plain docker run of the image. The stack starts the container as root so that the entrypoint can create users.
data.linux-stock-images-with-the-mounted-runn:
The statically linked runner binary lives in the per-node volume runner-bin, which the runner-distributor service fills. In the volume, the link current points to the active version, versions//bin/circleci-runner. The stack mounts the volume read-only at /opt/machine-runner-swarm in every container. The entrypoint, circleci-runner-entrypoint, is a Swarm config that the stack mounts at /circleci-runner-entrypoint with the mode 0555. The service sets entrypoint: ["/circleci-runner-entrypoint"] and user: "0". The entrypoint starts as root, checks the runner against its SHA-256 record, prepares the users, and then runs the runner as circleci-runner.
The result is that the image contains none of the runner. You can use cimg/base or cimg/openjdk:21.0 unmodified, and a new runner version needs no image rebuild and no restart of a runner service. Refer to The runner distributor on Linux and Upgrade the runner on Linux.
The shipped file uses these images:
Service File Image linux-default runners.yaml cimg/base:2026.10 linux-java classes-extra.yaml cimg/openjdk:21.0 linux-hardened classes-extra.yaml cimg/base:2026.10
data.pin-the-image#Pin the image:
Tags such as 21.0 move when the publisher rebuilds the image. Pin production services by digest and update them on a schedule:
image: cimg/base:2026.10@sha256: $ docker buildx imagetools inspect cimg/base:2026.10
data.private-certificate-authorities#Private:
The runner, its task agent, and the steps of a job read the certificate store of the image of their class. To trust a private authority for them (an inspecting proxy, your CircleCI server, a private registry, or a package host), put the authority in an image of your own. The stack files need no change for that. This repository does not test it.
On Linux, add the certificate to the system store, in a Dockerfile on top of the image that you use:
FROM cimg/base:2026.10@sha256:
data.what-an-image-needs#What an image needs:
Requirement Why Linux, any C library The runner is statically linked. It runs unmodified in cimg/base, cimg/openjdk, Alpine, and UBI minimal sudo, or util-linux setpriv Steps each job down to the job user. The hardened class (MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO=false) needs util-linux setpriv with --no-new-privs, even when the image has sudo setpriv or su Starts the runner as circleci-runner useradd or adduser Creates circleci-runner, and the job user when the image has none sed, grep, stat, install, getent, id, cut, tr, chmod, env, sha256sum, readlink, sleep Used by the entrypoint. BusyBox and coreutils both provide them wget or curl, tar, awk, mktemp, mv, chown Only for a microVM class, whose entrypoint downloads the runner into the container. The cimg images have them The cimg images have everything. Alpine has only the BusyBox su, and UBI minimal has neither sudo nor setpriv. The tests run the entrypoint in cimg/base 2026.10, cimg/openjdk 21.0, Alpine 3 (with sudo and with setpriv), and UBI 9 minimal. Add the packages in a derived image:
Base Add Debian and Ubuntu apt-get install sudo Alpine apk add sudo setpriv UBI minimal microdnf install sudo util-linux. The util-linux-core package is not enough The entrypoint exits with code 80 and a message that names the packages when the tools are missing. The unit tests of the entrypoint cover the setpriv path, and the token test runs the hardened step-down against the real runner. The end-to-end CI jobs run real jobs through the sudo path in the default class and through the setpriv --no-new-privs path in the hardened class.
The job user is circleci by default. Set MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_USER to another existing account, such as the default account of a different image. If the account does not exist, the entrypoint creates it with uid 2001, and gives it passwordless sudo while MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO is true and the image has sudo. The image environment variables, such as PATH, JAVA_HOME, LANG, and proxy variables, reach the jobs. The runner token does not.
data.windows-bring-your-own-image#Windows: br:
Add tools in an image on top of stock Server Core. The image holds the tools only. The host still provides the runner and Git through the mounts, and the stack file still sets entrypoint and the full PATH, so add the directory of your tool to that PATH.
The file windows/images/example/Dockerfile is a generic example. It starts from stock Server Core and adds Node.js from the official zip, pinned by version and SHA-256. Copy it and swap the tool. Keep the pattern:
Start FROM the stock Server Core image of your host’s tag. Download a pinned release, and verify its SHA-256 checksum before you use it. Install the tool in a fixed directory, and add that directory to the PATH of the service in windows\stack\custom-image.yaml. Check that the tool runs. Leave USER alone: the runner needs ContainerAdministrator, which creates symbolic links for the task agent. Do not put PsExec64.exe on the PATH of the image or of the service. With it, the task agent switches to a desktop wrapper that containers cannot run. A PsExec64.exe on the PATH of the host does not matter, because the stack sets the PATH of the container in full.
Build the example from the root of the repository. The build context is the windows directory.
docker build -f windows/images/example/Dockerfile --build-arg WINDOWS_TAG=ltsc2022 -t machine-runner-swarm-windows-example:ltsc2022 windows Push the result to a registry that every Windows node can pull from, because Swarm does not share local images. Then set the image of the windows-custom service in windows\stack\custom-image.yaml, an add-on stack file, and create the resource class and the secret windows-custom-token for it. Deploy it with -c windows\stack\runners.yaml -c windows\stack\custom-image.yaml. The file examples/windows-custom-image.yml shows a job on that class. Rebuild the image when the base image or a tool changes.
A stop of a busy Windows container kills its job after about 5 seconds, with stock images and with your own. Refer to Stop a busy Windows container, which also shows an optional image that lifts the limit.
data.windows-stock-server-core-with-mounts#Wi:
The default Windows service runs the unmodified Microsoft Server Core image, for example mcr.microsoft.com/windows/servercore:ltsc2022. Two read-only mounts of the per-node volume runner-bin, which the service runner-distributor-windows fills, add what the runner needs:
Volume path (volume.subpath) Container path Content current C:\machine-runner-swarm bin\circleci-runner.exe, the record SHA256, and VERSION git\current C:\Program Files\Git Portable Git for Windows: git, bash, sh, tar, gzip, ssh current and git\current are relative directory symbolic links, to versions\ and to the pinned Git, which the distributor moves. Docker resolves a link when it creates a container, so a new runner version reaches the next container only, and a running job keeps its version. Docker refuses a junction or an absolute link in a subpath. Refer to Upgrade the runner on Windows.
The runner is the main process of the container. The service sets entrypoint to C:\machine-runner-swarm\bin\circleci-runner.exe machine --config C:\ProgramData\Docker\secrets\circleci_runner_config.yaml. The service also sets the full PATH, because a PATH in the service environment replaces the one of the image. Git for Windows appears after the Windows directories, so the Windows find, sort, and tar stay first. The runner passes its environment to the task agent, and the task agent passes it to every step, so jobs see this PATH.
The system Git configuration is in the read-only Git mount, so the service sets Git options through the environment: GIT_CONFIG_COUNT, GIT_CONFIG_KEY_0, and GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_0 enable core.longpaths. GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 and GCM_INTERACTIVE=never stop the prompts of the Git Credential Manager, which nothing in a container can answer.
Pin the image with a digest, and rebuild or redeploy when Microsoft republishes the tag. Microsoft updates the tags each Patch Tuesday.
$ docker buildx imagetools inspect mcr.microsoft.com/windows/servercore:ltsc2022 Nano Server is not supported. Windows images must match the host build. Refer to Image tags and host builds.

data:
A container shares the kernel of its node. A Kata Containers microVM does not: every container starts in a small virtual machine with its own Linux kernel, and a job that breaks out of its container reaches the guest, not the node. The add-on stack file linux/stack/microvm.yaml runs resource classes this way. It is optional, and the default classes do not change.
Use it when jobs need a boundary stronger than a container, or when a job needs privileges that are unsafe on a shared kernel. The second class, linux-microvm-docker, lets a job run its own Docker daemon inside its VM, so an image build needs no host Docker socket. It is a safer answer than the docker-build class for the same need. It builds images: docker run, Compose and service containers do not work in it (Run Docker inside the VM).
Warning Status: experimental. The classes ship and stay in the stack, and the maturity is this:
Tested by the CI (linux/tests/microvm.sh): placement, DNS, the claim through the token proxy, the runner download and its verification, the rolling update, and builds with the Docker daemon in the VM. On amd64, with Kata 4.2.0, Cloud Hypervisor and QEMU, in nested virtualization on AWS, against a fake CircleCI API. Not verified by this project: real CircleCI jobs, with checkout, caches, workspaces and artifacts through the task agent. The CI runs an empty task only. Run a real job on a node of your own before you depend on it. Not tested: arm64, AMD CPUs, other clouds, Firecracker, many VMs at once, out-of-memory behavior, and Kata upgrades under load. Refer to What is tested.
data.configure-docker#Configure Docker:
Add the runtimes to /etc/docker/daemon.json and make Kata the default. Merge these keys into the file if it exists. The runtime kata uses Cloud Hypervisor, the default virtual machine monitor. The runtime kata-qemu is the fallback. The test suite runs this exact block.
{ "default-runtime": "kata", "runtimes": { "kata": { "runtimeType": "io.containerd.kata.v2", "options": {"ConfigPath": "/opt/kata/share/defaults/kata-containers/runtime-rs/configuration-clh-runtime-rs.toml"} }, "kata-qemu": { "runtimeType": "io.containerd.kata.v2", "options": {"ConfigPath": "/opt/kata/share/defaults/kata-containers/runtime-rs/configuration-qemu-runtime-rs.toml"} } } } Restart Docker (sudo systemctl restart docker), then check that a container has its own kernel:
$ uname -r $ docker run --rm alpine uname -r The two kernels must differ. Containers that were running before the restart stay as they are.
QEMU as the fallback. Set "default-runtime": "kata-qemu" if Cloud Hypervisor does not work on your hardware. QEMU backs the memory of every VM with /dev/shm, so /dev/shm of the node must hold the memory of all VMs together. A tmpfs that is too small fails with kvm run failed Bad address and a vsock timeout. On a host, /dev/shm is half of the RAM by default. In a Docker-in-Docker container, which is how the tests run QEMU, start it with --shm-size=16g.
Label the node:
$ docker node update --label-add machine-runner-swarm.microvm=true Label the node before you deploy the stack, and always when Kata is its default runtime. A Kata node without the label still matches the forwarder microvm-dns, which cannot work in a VM, so a share of the DNS queries would fail. Labeling the node moves the forwarder off it.
data.deploy-the-classes#Deploy the classes:
Create the resource classes /linux-microvm and /linux-microvm-docker, and for each the secret linux-microvm-token and linux-microvm-docker-token, which holds the class token and goes to token-proxy only (Resource Classes). Delete a class from your copy of the stack file together with its secret and network if you do not want it.
Deploy the add-on stack file with the main file. Pass the same list of files on every later deploy (why).
$ docker stack deploy -c linux/stack/runners.yaml -c linux/stack/microvm.yaml runners The classes look like linux-default and run the same entrypoint. A VM has the CPUs of the class limit plus one, and the memory of the limit: a class with cpus: "2" and memory: 4G gets a VM that shows 3 CPUs and about 3.9 GB. A container without a limit gets 1 CPU and 2 GiB. Set limits and reservations for the VM you want (what it costs).
The file examples/linux-microvm.yml has a job for each class.
data.dns#DNS:
Docker’s embedded DNS server, 127.0.0.11, cannot be reached from inside a Kata VM, on an overlay or any other user-defined network. Kata has no fix for it yet. microvm.yaml works around it in two parts:
The forwarder. The service microvm-dns runs CoreDNS with forward . 127.0.0.11 on a node without the microvm label, where the embedded DNS works. It joins the networks of both classes, where token-proxy is too, so token-proxy and the service names such as linux-microvm and tasks.linux-microvm resolve. It is published on port 53, TCP and UDP, through the routing mesh, so every node answers on port 53. The node file. Each microVM node has a file that the stack mounts read-only at /etc/resolv.conf of every job. It names the gateway of docker_gwbridge, which is the node itself, and the routing mesh sends the query on to a forwarder. Write the node file, after the node joined the Swarm (the network docker_gwbridge exists from then on). The gateway is 172.18.0.1 by default and differs when that range was taken, so read it from Docker:
$ sudo install -d /etc/machine-runner-swarm $ gw=$(docker network inspect docker_gwbridge --format '{{(index .IPAM.Config 0).Gateway}}') $ printf 'nameserver %s\n' "$gw" | sudo tee /etc/machine-runner-swarm/microvm-resolv.conf Without this file the task does not start (the bind mount fails), so a node that skipped this step never runs a class with broken DNS.
Create the Corefile config once, on a manager:
$ printf '.:53 {\n errors\n forward . 127.0.0.11\n cache 30\n}\n' | docker config create microvm-corefile - Swarm configs are immutable. To change the Corefile, create a config under a new name and change microvm-corefile in your copy of the stack file.
Warning The routing mesh opens port 53 on every interface of every node, so the forwarder is an open resolver for anyone who can reach the node. Keep port 53 closed to the outside with your cloud firewall or security group, and open it only between the nodes. Docker also bypasses ufw and firewalld rules for published ports, so use the DOCKER-USER chain when you filter on the node itself. A node that runs its own DNS server on port 53 for other hosts loses it to the routing mesh.
A name that your own network serves, such as the host of an internal mirror of the runner download, resolves only if the node of the forwarder can resolve it: the forwarder asks the embedded DNS of its node, which uses the resolvers of that node. A mirror name that only the microVM nodes can resolve fails in the VM. Use a name that the runc node resolves, or an IP address in MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_DOWNLOAD_BASE_URL.
The forwarder needs a runc node. On a Swarm whose only node is a microVM node, replace forward . 127.0.0.11 with forward . 1.1.1.1 (or your resolver) and put microvm-dns on that node without the constraint. Public names then resolve, and service names do not.
data.how-it-works#How it works:
Swarm has no per-service container runtime: a service cannot ask for Kata. The Docker daemon of each node chooses the runtime, so the node decides. This add-on uses that:
A microVM node has Kata as the default-runtime of its Docker daemon and the label machine-runner-swarm.microvm=true. Every container on it is a microVM, including containers of other stacks. linux-microvm and linux-microvm-docker run only on nodes with that label. Every other class in the stack files carries node.labels.machine-runner-swarm.microvm != true, so labeling a node moves them off it. They would run in a VM without working DNS there. The classes set MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_REQUIRE_MICROVM=true. The entrypoint then exits with code 80 unless /proc/cmdline names kata-containers, so a node that falls back to runc by mistake, with the label but the wrong default runtime, never runs a class that has SYS_ADMIN. Docker’s embedded DNS (127.0.0.11) does not work inside a Kata VM. The service microvm-dns is a CoreDNS forwarder on a runc node, and each microVM node mounts a file that points /etc/resolv.conf at it. Refer to DNS. The classes claim through the token proxy, like the other single-task classes. A runner holds a placeholder config, and the class tokens are Swarm secrets of token-proxy alone, so a job in a VM never sees one, also in linux-microvm-docker. The runner finds token-proxy by name, and the forwarder resolves it, because it and the proxy are on the class networks. The proxy runs on a runc node, where Docker’s DNS works. The runner does not come from a shared volume. Each container downloads the pinned runner from CircleCI’s release bucket into itself, verifies its SHA-256, and runs it, so no state is shared between jobs, and a microVM node runs no runner-distributor and has no runner-bin volume. Refer to The runner in a VM. A Kata container that starts at the moment its overlay network leaves the node hangs, which is what a rolling update does. The global service microvm-netkeep runs one sleeping container on each microVM node, on both class networks, so the networks stay up. Refer to Rolling updates. linux-default linux-microvm linux-microvm-docker Kernel of the job The node kernel Its own guest kernel Its own guest kernel Runs on Nodes without the microvm and docker-build labels Nodes with microvm=true Nodes with microvm=true Job user circleci, with sudo circleci, with sudo circleci, with sudo Class token in the job No, the proxy holds it No No The runner The per-node volume, read-only Downloaded by the container, then verified Downloaded by the container, then verified Capabilities Docker’s defaults, minus NET_RAW and MKNOD The same Docker’s defaults, plus SYS_ADMIN (no NET_ADMIN, and NET_RAW stays) Replicas 2 2 1, and keep it at 1 (Security) Docker in the job No No Its own dockerd in the VM, on a tmpfs, for builds
data.nested-virtualization-in-the-cloud#Neste: Cloud Instances Notes AWS C8i, M8i, R8i (also the flex sizes), C7i, M7i, R7i (also the flex sizes), I7i, and every .metal size Intel only. Enable nested virtualization when you launch the instance. The tested node was an r8i-flex.2xlarge Google Cloud, Azure, and others Nested virtualization exists on some families Untested CircleCI’s own cloud executors do not offer nested virtualization, except the Android machine image. Refer to CI.
data.requirements#Requirements: KVM. The node needs /dev/kvm: bare metal, or a virtual machine with nested virtualization. A node without it cannot run Kata. Linux amd64. This add-on pins the amd64 build of Kata 4.2.0. Arm64 is untested. Docker Engine 24 or later, and a Swarm that follows Multi-Node Clusters. One runc node at least for microvm-dns and token-proxy, for example a manager. A single-node Swarm whose only node is a microVM node cannot run them. Refer to DNS. The base stack: runners.yaml with its placeholder secret (Install on Linux). The token proxy runs on a manager by default, and never on a microVM node. In a cluster, label the node of the proxy as Multi-Node Clusters says. Deploy microvm.yaml together with it. A node of its own. The default runtime applies to every container on the node, so a microVM node runs microVM classes only, and nothing else of your stacks. Egress to the release bucket. Each VM downloads the runner from circleci-binary-releases.s3.amazonaws.com, the host that its task agent comes from on every job already (Egress hosts).
data.rolling-updates#Rolling updates:
Docker removes an overlay network from a node when its last container leaves, and sets it up again for the next one. A Kata container that starts in that gap stays in the Created state for good, and Swarm tries again with a new task that hangs the same way. A restart after a finished job is safe, because Swarm waits delay: 10s first. A rolling update is not: update_config stops the old container and starts the new one at once (order: stop-first).
The service microvm-netkeep closes the gap. It is global, so one small VM sleeps on every microVM node, attached to both class networks, and the overlays never go away while the node runs. The test replaces a running container with a forced update, and a control without the keeper shows the hang. Keep the service in your copy of the stack file. Without it, drain a node before an update and use docker service update --force only when the service has a replica on another node.
data.run-docker-inside-the-vm#Run Docker insi:
A job on linux-microvm-docker starts its own Docker daemon in the VM and builds with it. No socket of the node is involved, so the job cannot reach other jobs or the node. The class has SYS_ADMIN and no NET_ADMIN, and a 6 GiB tmpfs at /var/lib/docker, because overlayfs cannot sit on the virtiofs root of the VM. Images and the build cache therefore live in the memory of the VM and vanish with the job.
Without NET_ADMIN a job cannot change the address of its container, which the token proxy trusts to tell runners apart. The price is the network of the daemon: start it with --bridge=none --iptables=false, because it cannot create a bridge or firewall rules, and build with --network=host, so the build steps use the network of the VM.
The VM mounts /sys, /sys/fs/cgroup, and /proc/sys read-only, and the job must remount them before dockerd can start containers:
$ sudo mount -o remount,rw /sys $ sudo mount -o remount,rw /sys/fs/cgroup $ sudo mount -o remount,rw /proc/sys $ sudo sh -c 'dockerd --bridge=none --iptables=false > /tmp/dockerd.log 2>&1 &' $ timeout 60 sh -c 'until sudo docker info > /dev/null 2>&1; do sleep 1; done' $ sudo docker build --network=host -t app . What works and what does not:
Builds work, and so do docker load, docker save, docker create with docker cp, and a push to a registry. Every RUN step needs --network=host. A Dockerfile cannot ask for it, so pass the flag to every build, also in docker buildx build. docker run, Compose and service containers do not work. Starting a container needs NET_ADMIN (failed to create default sandbox: operation not permitted, also with --network=host and --network=none). Use another class for jobs that start containers. If you need it here, add NET_ADMIN to cap_add in your copy of the stack file, and keep the class at one replica on its own overlay, for trusted projects only: a job with NET_ADMIN can take over the address of another container. The class keeps NET_RAW. BuildKit starts every RUN step with Docker’s default capabilities, and runc fails with unable to apply caps when the VM container has dropped one of them, such as NET_RAW or MKNOD, so the class drops none. Raw sockets stay possible, so a job can send packets with another source address into its overlay. Refer to Security for why one replica keeps that harmless. Rootless BuildKit does not work in the VM, because file capabilities do not survive virtiofs. A rootful dockerd or buildkitd does. The guest kernel has no seccomp profile around the job, so the VM, not the container, is the boundary.
data.security#Security: What the VM adds. A job that escapes its container, or abuses SYS_ADMIN, lands in a guest kernel and its own root filesystem. It does not reach the node, other jobs, or other classes’ tokens. The VM shares no writable state with other jobs: the runner is its own (above). What remains shared is the network. What it does not add. The VM does not filter egress, and replicas of a class still share an overlay network. The job holds no class token: its runner has the placeholder, and the proxy adds the token of the class to the claim of each container once. No dedicated nodes for the runner. No volume is shared between VMs, so a job with SYS_ADMIN has nothing writable of the node or of other jobs to reach, and the classes can share nodes. A bug in virtiofs, the VMM, or the guest kernel could still reach the node. If that residual risk matters to you, give linux-microvm-docker nodes of its own: label them machine-runner-swarm.class.linux-microvm-docker=true, as Multi-Node Clusters describes, add node.labels.machine-runner-swarm.class.linux-microvm-docker == true to the constraints of linux-microvm-docker in your copy of the stack file, and != true to those of linux-microvm. Tampering with the runner. A job that changes the runner in its VM changes its own copy, which dies with the VM (above). The entrypoint still checks the binary against its record at the start, as for every class. Why one replica. The token proxy accepts a claim from an address that Swarm lists for the class, once for each container. The classes of the stack files drop NET_RAW, so a job cannot send packets from another address. linux-microvm-docker cannot drop it (BuildKit needs it), and it has no NET_ADMIN either, so a job there can send raw packets but cannot take over an address. With one replica, no other runner of the class is on its overlay to impersonate, because each class has its own overlay. The stack-config test requires replicas: 1 and SYS_ADMIN as the only added capability. To run more builds at once, copy the service under another name (and resource class), with its own network, secret and proxy entries (Add a class), and do not raise replicas. The guard. linux-microvm-docker adds SYS_ADMIN. On runc that is a host escape. The label and the constraints keep the class on microVM nodes, and the entrypoint check keeps it off a node that has the label but not the runtime. The stack-config test requires MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_REQUIRE_MICROVM=true on every service that adds SYS_ADMIN, in every stack file. A bigger attack surface under it. The node now runs virtiofsd, a VMM, and the Kata shim for every job. Keep Kata and the node kernel current.
data.set-up-a-microvm-node#Set up a microVM n:
Run these steps on every microVM node, as root. The node joined the Swarm (Install on Linux). There is nothing to install for the runner: each VM downloads its own.
Check KVM and load the vhost modules. Kata uses vhost_vsock to reach the agent in the VM, and vhost_net for networking.
$ ls -l /dev/kvm $ sudo modprobe vhost_vsock vhost_net $ printf 'vhost_vsock\nvhost_net\n' | sudo tee /etc/modules-load.d/kata.conf $ ls -l /dev/vhost-vsock /dev/vhost-net Install Kata 4.2.0. The release tarball is about 1 GB and unpacks to /opt/kata, about 2.3 GB. It holds the runtime-rs shim, Cloud Hypervisor, QEMU, virtiofsd, a guest kernel, and a guest image. Check the SHA-256 before you unpack it.
$ curl -fLO https://github.com/kata-containers/kata-containers/releases/download/4.2.0/kata-static-4.2.0-amd64.tar.zst $ echo 'b828904fa3f1e49ddd7dc799c72cb1503cd1e772d354c3987c8d4189b2a623a8 kata-static-4.2.0-amd64.tar.zst' | sha256sum -c - $ sudo tar --zstd -xf kata-static-4.2.0-amd64.tar.zst -C / $ sudo ln -sf /opt/kata/runtime-rs/bin/containerd-shim-kata-v2 /usr/local/bin/containerd-shim-kata-v2 The tarball needs zstd. Upgrade by unpacking a new release the same way and restarting Docker. Existing VMs keep running on the old files until they stop. A site without a route to GitHub copies the tarball in from a host that has one and keeps the SHA-256 check.
data.the-runner-in-a-vm#The runner in a VM:
The other classes mount the per-node volume runner-bin read-only, which the runner-distributor service fills. A microVM class does not, because root with SYS_ADMIN inside a VM, which is what linux-microvm-docker gives a job, can remount a shared mount read-write, and the write would reach the volume of the node and the runner of every later job. There is no read-only mount to prevent it, because the distributor writes the same volume. So nothing writable is shared:
With MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_REQUIRE_MICROVM=true the entrypoint downloads the runner into the container itself, before it starts it. It runs the distributor script (/runner-distributor.sh, a Swarm config of the class) once, as sh /runner-distributor.sh --once, which resolves the version, downloads the tarball from CircleCI’s release bucket, checks its SHA-256 against the values that microvm.yaml carries for the pinned version (MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_SHA256: with manifest, against the manifest, which is weaker), checks that the binary reports the version, and writes the same record as on any node. The checks of the entrypoint follow as for every class. The source is the one that the task agent comes from on every job. The download is about 22 MB, and the VM does it for each job. A mirror of your own takes the load off the release bucket, and it needs to be reachable from the VM (see DNS). The settings are those of the distributor and have the same defaults: MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_VERSION (an exact pin by default, or 3.1, 3, current: the version policy), MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_MAJOR, MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_DOWNLOAD_BASE_URL (a mirror) and MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_SHA256 (the SHA-256 values of the pin for an exact version, or manifest when an exact pin has no list), set as variables of docker stack deploy. In these two classes they sit in the service, because no distributor serves them. The pin and its values are the same as in runners.yaml. A floating version is resolved in each VM when the job starts and ignores any list. A failed or mismatching download ends the container with exit code 80, and Swarm tries again after the restart delay of 10 seconds. What a job in linux-microvm-docker can do with the runner is limited to its own VM. It can rewrite the runner binary and its record in its own copy, and that copy goes away with the VM. The next job downloads a fresh one. The class tokens are not in the VM or in the runner, so a changed runner cannot read one. Because nothing is shared, no dedicated nodes are needed for this reason. The test microvm.sh rewrites the binary and the record in a VM and shows that the next VM runs a fresh one, that a download with a wrong SHA-256 is refused, and that no runner-bin volume exists on the node.
data.troubleshooting#Troubleshooting: Symptom Cause Fix A task is rejected with bind source path does not exist The node file /etc/machine-runner-swarm/microvm-resolv.conf is missing Write the node file The class exits with code 80 and not in a Kata microVM The node has the label, and Docker runs runc Check docker info --format '{{.DefaultRuntime}}' and Configure Docker, or remove the label The class stays Pending with no suitable node No node has machine-runner-swarm.microvm=true Label the node A job cannot resolve names, or only some queries succeed microvm-dns is not running, the config microvm-corefile is missing, a replica runs on a Kata node without the label, or another -c file overrides microvm-dns and the merge dropped its UDP port docker service ls must show *:53->53/tcp, *:53->53/udp for runners_microvm-dns, and docker service ps runners_microvm-dns the replicas on nodes without the label. Check the Corefile config. Change the service in your copy of microvm.yaml, not in another -c file A task stays Starting and its container stays Created after an update The overlay left the node while the task started Rolling updates. Check that microvm-netkeep runs on the node, then docker service update --force the class again A class exits 80 with “cannot download and verify the runner in this microVM” The VM could not download the runner, or its SHA-256 did not match docker service logs runners_linux-microvm shows the lines of the download above the error. Check DNS, egress to circleci-binary-releases.s3.amazonaws.com, MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_VERSION and MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_SHA256 A container does not start, with ETIMEDOUT on vsock vhost_vsock is not loaded, or QEMU lacks /dev/shm space Set up a microVM node step 1, and the QEMU note in Configure Docker dockerd in the VM fails with read-only file system The job skipped the remounts Run Docker inside the VM
data.what-is-not-tested#What is not tested: Real jobs: checkout, caches, workspaces, and artifacts over virtiofs with the real task agent. The real runner runs only an empty task in the suite. A real CircleCI job is a manual check. The behavior when a job runs out of memory against the cgroup limit. Other clouds, other CPUs (AMD), and arm64. Firecracker (it has no virtiofs), and the Go shim of Kata. A cluster with more than two nodes, and the load of many VMs at once. Kata upgrades under load. Windows: refer to the next section.
data.what-is-tested#What is tested:
linux/tests/microvm.sh runs two Docker-in-Docker nodes with KVM, the real stack files runners.yaml and microvm.yaml, the real entrypoint, a distributor on the runc node, a test mirror that serves the runner, the token proxy image built from proxy/, and the real runner against a fake API. It skips when /dev/kvm is missing. It checks:
The classes stay pending until a node has the label. The forwarder and the proxy run on the runc node, together with the distributor, and the Kata node runs no distributor and has no runner-bin volume. The guest kernel differs from the node kernel, /proc/cmdline names kata-containers, and /etc/resolv.conf is the node file and read-only. Public names, token-proxy, the service name, and tasks. resolve through the forwarder. A control service without the node file shows the failure that the forwarder fixes. The real runner claims through the real token proxy from inside a VM and runs a task as the job user. The class token is in no file, variable, or process of the VM. The runner of a VM: it is downloaded into the VM and verified, nothing is mounted at its path, a root shell that rewrites the binary and the record changes nothing for the next VM, a download with a wrong SHA-256 is refused (exit 80), and a floating version resolves in the VM. A forced rolling update of a class replaces its VM, because microvm-netkeep holds the overlay. A control without it shows the hang. dockerd starts in the VM with --bridge=none --iptables=false, uses overlay2 on the tmpfs, and builds an image with --network=host (its RUN step ran on the guest kernel). The class has SYS_ADMIN and no NET_ADMIN, and the stack-config test pins both and the replica count. The guard: the label on a runc node makes both classes exit 80. QEMU passes the same checks (SWARM_TEST_KATA_VMM=qemu).
data.what-it-costs#What it costs:
Measured on one r8i-flex.2xlarge (nested KVM), Docker 29.9, Kata 4.2.0, in a Docker-in-Docker container:
Measure runc Cloud Hypervisor Dragonball Container start 0.27 s 1.16 s 2.5 s Swarm deploy to the first output of the container 1.3 s 3.4 s not measured Memory. microvm-netkeep adds one small VM (256 MB limit) to every microVM node. An idle VM with 2 GiB takes about 160 MB of host memory, and the guest kernel and its page cache use more as the job runs. A VM has the memory of the class limit, and the tmpfs of linux-microvm-docker counts against it. CPU. Compute speed equals runc. A VM has the CPUs of the limit plus one, and the reservation of the class still covers only the limit. Disk. virtiofs makes fsync about twice as slow as on the node’s disk. Builds and test runs that write many small files with fsync feel it. A tmpfs avoids it. Start-up. A job in a new container waits about a second longer, which is small against the time the runner needs to claim a job. It also downloads the runner (about 22 MB) before it starts, which takes a few seconds on a normal link. Dragonball is the built-in VMM of runtime-rs and works with the same steps. It starts more slowly than Cloud Hypervisor, so the docs use Cloud Hypervisor.
data.windows-hyper-v-isolation#Windows: Hyper:
Windows containers have a counterpart: isolation: hyperv runs each container in a lightweight Hyper-V utility VM with its own kernel, instead of sharing the host kernel (isolation: process, the default in windows/stack/runners.yaml). This is untested. A stack file for it would be an add-on like this, with the host needing the Hyper-V role:
services: windows-hyperv: # ... the settings of windows-default in windows/stack/runners.yaml isolation: hyperv Hyper-V isolation does not need the image to match the host version, so a node label for the image tag matters less.
It needs nested virtualization, and CircleCI’s own Windows machines do not offer it: on them --isolation hyperv fails with “The request is not supported”, and installing the Hyper-V role fails with “processor does not have required virtualization capabilities”. Process isolation works there. On AWS, Windows runs on the instance families above (C7i, M7i, R7i, C8i, M8i, R8i, I7i with nested virtualization enabled, or .metal). Test it on your own hosts before you rely on it.

data: Each Swarm service in a stack file is one CircleCI resource class. This page describes how to define a class, size it, choose its replica count, run a persistent class, and enable Rerun job with SSH. It ends with a reference of every environment variable that the stack files and the entrypoint use.
data.choose-replica-counts#Choose replica cou:
deploy.replicas is the number of jobs that the class runs at the same time. Choose it as follows:
Estimate the peak number of parallel jobs for the class from your workflows. Check that nodes with enough room exist. A replica needs its full reservation on one node. Add headroom for short jobs. A replica needs about 10 seconds between jobs, so a class that receives many very short jobs benefits from one extra replica. Set the value in the stack file and deploy again. The file stays the source of truth. For a quick change, scale the service directly. The next docker stack deploy resets the count to the value in the file.
$ docker service scale runners_linux-default=4 Swarm has no autoscaling, and this stack adds none: capacity is fixed, and you pay for the peak. An idle replica holds its reservation, so a class with more replicas than demand wastes node capacity. Set replicas: 0 to switch a class off without deleting it, and know that jobs for a class with no runner wait without limit and hold concurrency (Capacity and concurrency). For elastic capacity, use the machine runner orchestrator or CircleCI cloud executors (FAQ).
data.define-a-class#Define a class:
The shipped linux/stack/runners.yaml has one class, linux-default. Every other class is yours to add, to your copy of the stack files (deploy/runners.yaml, as Install on Linux describes), and you deploy your copy. The file linux/stack/classes-extra.yaml is a worked example: it adds linux-java and linux-hardened the way this section describes.
To add a class:
Create the resource class and a token in CircleCI. The class name must equal the service name.
$ circleci runner resource-class create /linux-python --org --generate-token In your copy of the stack file, copy the service linux-default under another name and change the values in the table below.
Create the secret -token with the token. Refer to Create the secrets or Create the secrets on Windows. On Linux, a single-task class also needs two lines in the existing token-proxy service, as in the example below: its network and its secret. The proxy serves a class for every secret -token that it holds, and finds the runners of the class as tasks..
Deploy your copy again, with the same set of -c files as before. Swarm creates the new service and leaves unchanged services alone.
$ docker stack deploy -c deploy/runners.yaml runners Each service needs its own values for these keys:
Key Value for a class named linux-python Service name linux-python hostname and CIRCLECI_RUNNER_NAME (Linux) "{{.Node.Hostname}}-linux-python-{{.Task.Slot}}" CIRCLECI_RUNNER_NAME (Windows) "{{.Node.Hostname}}-windows--{{.Task.Slot}}". The Windows files set no hostname secrets.source (Windows, and Linux persistent classes) linux-python-token, declared under the top-level secrets: with external: true secrets.source (Linux, single-task) runner-placeholder-token (as the anchor *runner has it). The class token linux-python-token goes to the token-proxy service networks (Linux) [linux-python], declared under the top-level networks: with driver: overlay, and the same network under token-proxy The runner name must be unique across all runners of your organization. It has at most 64 characters and contains only letters, numbers, ., (, ), _, -, and spaces. A long hostname plus a long class name can exceed the limit, and the runner then exits with code 80.
A complete Linux example, in three parts of your copy of runners.yaml, where the anchors *runner, *env, *restart, *update and *placement of that file resolve. First, the service, next to linux-default under services::
services: linux-python: <<: *runner image: cimg/python:3.14 hostname: "{{.Node.Hostname}}-linux-python-{{.Task.Slot}}" environment: <<: *env CIRCLECI_RUNNER_NAME: "{{.Node.Hostname}}-linux-python-{{.Task.Slot}}" MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO: "true" networks: [linux-python] cap_drop: [NET_RAW, MKNOD] # keep NET_RAW dropped: the proxy tells runners apart by their source address deploy: replicas: 2 restart_policy: *restart update_config: *update resources: limits: {cpus: "2", memory: 4G, pids: 4096} reservations: {cpus: "2", memory: 4G} placement: *placement Second, the class goes into the proxy, which has the key token-proxy: once in the file. Add these lines to the keys that it has, and do not repeat the key:
token-proxy: secrets: # ... the secrets of the classes that are there - {source: linux-python-token, target: linux-python-token, uid: "65534", gid: "65534", mode: 0400} networks: [linux-default, linux-python] # every class network, the new one included Third, the network and the secret, at the top level:
networks: linux-python: {driver: overlay, driver_opts: {encrypted: "true"}} # as the other class networks: see Multi-Node Clusters secrets: linux-python-token: {external: true} The runner service inherits the placeholder secret and the proxy URL from *runner and *env. A deploy that adds the secret of a class changes the secrets of token-proxy, so Swarm replaces the proxy task, and the new proxy finds the class from its secret files when it starts. What the runners see during that restart is in Restart the proxy. A class that the proxy does not serve gets 403 on every claim, and the proxy log says not a runner of any class.
Use MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO: "false" with the capability settings of linux-hardened in linux/stack/classes-extra.yaml for a hardened class. Refer to Concepts.
To keep a class in a stack file of its own, as the add-on files do, write token-proxy there with only the additions (the secret and the network): Swarm merges the files by name. An anchor does not reach into another file, so repeat the settings of *runner, *env, *restart, *update and *placement in it, or copy the file classes-extra.yaml and change it. The anchor *runner brings the keys that a Linux class needs for the runner: user: "0", entrypoint: ["/circleci-runner-entrypoint"], the config entrypoint, the placeholder secret runner-placeholder-token (the token proxy holds the class token), and the volume runner-bin mounted read-only. A service written without the anchor repeats them:
services: linux-python: user: "0" entrypoint: ["/circleci-runner-entrypoint"] configs: - {source: entrypoint, target: /circleci-runner-entrypoint, mode: 0555} secrets: - {source: runner-placeholder-token, target: circleci_runner_config.yaml, uid: "2000", gid: "2000", mode: 0400} environment: CIRCLECI_RUNNER_API_URL: http://token-proxy:8080 volumes: - {type: volume, source: runner-bin, target: /opt/machine-runner-swarm, read_only: true} secrets: runner-placeholder-token: {external: true} configs: entrypoint: {name: machine-runner-swarm-entrypoint-<12 hex digits>, file: } volumes: runner-bin: {} The name of the config carries the first 12 hex digits of the SHA-256 of the file, because a Swarm config cannot change. Refer to Upgrade to a new release of this repository. The shipped add-on files repeat the top-level configs: and volumes:, so each of them also loads alone.
On Windows, copy a service such as windows-default in your copy of windows\stack\runners.yaml, with its two mounts of the volume runner-bin (subpath: current and subpath: 'git\current') and the top-level volumes: runner-bin. The secret has no uid, gid, or mode, and the file defines no networks. A single-task Windows class also needs the same lines in token-proxy-windows as the Linux example shows (its secret, with the target -token; there are no networks and no variable), and reads the placeholder secret runner-placeholder-token.
data.exit-codes#Exit codes: Code Source Meaning 0 Runner A normal exit after a job or after a runner drain. Swarm starts a new container 80 Entrypoint A prerequisite is missing: the link current does not exist after the wait, the runner does not match its SHA-256 record, the runner or a directory above it is not root-owned or is writable, the image has neither sudo nor setpriv (or, for a hardened class, no util-linux setpriv with --no-new-privs), MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO is invalid, or the entrypoint cannot remove every sudo right of the job user 80 Runner A configuration error: a missing or invalid name, an empty token, an unknown log level, or an invalid mode 1 Runner The config file is missing because the secret is not attached, the YAML does not parse, or a duration is malformed Swarm restarts a container that exits with any code after the restart delay of 10 seconds. It never gives up and never backs off, so a configuration error repeats until you fix it. Refer to Troubleshooting.
data.linux#Linux:
The file linux/stack/persistent.yaml defines linux-persistent. It sets CIRCLECI_RUNNER_MODE: continuous and sets no idle timeout. It mounts the named volume persistent-home at /home/circleci. Swarm copies the image content of that directory into the new volume on first use.
A volume lives on one node, so the service pins itself with the constraint node.hostname == CHANGE-ME. Edit that value in your copy of the file (deploy/persistent.yaml, from the copy of linux/stack that the install page makes) before you deploy.
The service keeps its class token in its own container and does not claim through the token proxy, because a continuous runner claims after every job and the proxy allows one claim for each container. A job that can use sudo can therefore read the token. The shipped file sets MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO: "false": jobs have no sudo (the step-down is setpriv --no-new-privs), so the job user cannot read the token file, and the tools that a job needs must be in the image (Images). Set it to "true" in your copy if its jobs need sudo, and accept that a job that uses it reads the token and can run a runner of its own on the class.
The service sets CIRCLECI_RUNNER_CLEANUP_WORK_DIR to "false". The runner user cannot remove files that the job user created, so the runner does not clean the working directory, and each job must clean up what an earlier job left. Refer to Working directory cleanup.
$ printf 'api:\n auth_token: %s\n' "$TOKEN" | docker secret create linux-persistent-token - $ docker stack deploy -c deploy/runners.yaml -c deploy/persistent.yaml runners Recycle the runner with a forced update. The runner drains first (a runner drain: it takes no new job and finishes the running one), so a running job finishes. The volume survives. The container keeps the runner version that it started with, so a forced update is also how the class moves to a new runner version.
$ docker service update --force runners_linux-persistent
data.persistent-mode#Persistent mode:
Status: experimental. CI runs the persistent class with a fake or idle runner only, and no real job runs on it in CI.
A persistent class runs the runner in continuous mode. One long-lived container claims job after job, and a named volume keeps data between jobs. Use it only for trusted projects that gain a lot from warm caches.
Warning Continuous mode removes the guarantee of a clean environment. A job can leave files, processes, or settings that later jobs see, and a job can change what later jobs run. CircleCI describes untrusted jobs on a runner that keeps its environment as the highest risk.
To limit the risk:
Create a separate resource class for it, and restrict the class to named projects with a config policy. Refer to CircleCI-side controls. Keep production contexts away from the class. Put cleanup steps at the start of its jobs. The runner does not clean the working directory on Linux. Recycle the runner on a schedule. On Linux, know that this class is weaker than the single-task classes: it does not use the token proxy, so the runner holds the real token. Refer to The persistent class.
data.rerun-job-with-ssh#Rerun job with SSH:
Status: experimental. CI checks that the files parse, merge and keep their contract (the host-mode port 54782, max_replicas_per_node: 1, the advertise address). The Swarm side was proven by hand on Linux with a real runner. No CI test logs in over SSH, and the Windows file is untested.
The add-on stack files linux/stack/ssh-rerun.yaml and windows\stack\ssh-rerun.yaml define the classes linux-default-ssh and windows-default-ssh. Their runners support Rerun job with SSH, which opens a shell in a running job so that a user can debug it. Deploy them only if you need this. The default classes publish no port and cannot serve SSH.
A runner turns the feature on when CIRCLECI_RUNNER_SSH_ADVERTISE_ADDR is set. The task agent then starts an SSH server on port 54782, which is fixed, and the Enable SSH and Wait for SSH steps show the advertised address. CircleCI only displays that address, so it can be any name or IP address that your users can reach. The add-on files set it to {{.Node.Hostname}}:54782, and Swarm fills in the node name for each task. If your DNS does not resolve the node hostnames, write a name or an address that it does, for example {{.Node.Hostname}}.example.com:54782.
The file publishes port 54782 in host mode, so it opens on the node that runs the task. The default ingress mode would send a connection to any replica of the class, which can be another user’s job. A node has one port 54782, so the service sets max_replicas_per_node: 1, and replicas beyond the number of eligible nodes stay pending.
A rerun uses the resource class of the original job. To debug a job, run it on the SSH class by setting its resource_class to /linux-default-ssh. To give an existing class SSH instead, copy three settings from the add-on file into that service in your copy of the stack file: the environment variable, the host-mode port, and max_replicas_per_node: 1. Every replica of that class then needs its own node.
$ printf 'api:\n auth_token: %s\n' "$TOKEN" | docker secret create linux-default-ssh-token - $ docker stack deploy -c deploy/runners.yaml -c deploy/ssh-rerun.yaml runners Before you use it:
Firewall. Open inbound TCP 54782 on the nodes that run the class, only from the networks where your users connect, such as a VPN. Runners need no other inbound port. Docker publishes the port with NAT rules that run before ufw and firewalld rules, so a rule in either does not restrict it: filter in the DOCKER-USER chain or with a cloud security group, for example sudo iptables -I DOCKER-USER ! -s -p tcp --dport 54782 -j DROP (an example that is not tested here). Refer to Listening ports on a node. SSH key. A user adds a public key in their CircleCI user settings, or, with a GitHub or Bitbucket organization, to their VCS account instead. Without a key, the Enable SSH step does not appear. CircleCI describes the steps in Debug jobs with SSH rerun. Concurrency. A rerun with SSH holds the runner for up to 2 hours after a user connects (1 hour on the Free plan), or 10 minutes if nobody does. The job counts against the concurrency limit of your organization, and the replica takes no other job. With one replica for each node, a forgotten session blocks the node, so size the class for it. Cancel. Cancel the rerun in the web app or with the CLI when you finish. The container then exits, and Swarm starts a new one. Security. The SSH user gets the privileges of the job user, and can reach what the job reached. Anyone who can start a job on the class can rerun it with SSH, and only the user who reruns gets their keys added. In linux-default-ssh the job user keeps sudo, as in linux-default, so the SSH user is root in the container, but it holds only the placeholder, because the class claims through the token proxy. Set MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO to "false" to take root away. Keep the class for named projects, and keep deploy contexts away from SSH reruns. Refer to CircleCI-side controls. On Windows, the SSH user must name the shell: ssh -p 54782 -- powershell.exe. Open the port in Windows Defender Firewall as well. The Windows file is not tested.
data.size-the-limits#Size the limits:
The stack sets the same values for limits and reservations. The limit caps what a runner can use. The reservation tells the scheduler how much room a replica needs.
This table lists what the shipped stack files ask of the nodes. A reservation is room that the scheduler holds for a replica whether or not it runs a job: you pay for the peak of the nodes that you run, and an idle replica costs the same as a busy one. A service with no reservation still has the limit shown.
Service File Replicas Reserved for each replica Limit, when it differs linux-default runners.yaml 2 2 CPUs, 4 GB token-proxy runners.yaml 1 0.1 CPU, 32 MB 0.5 CPU, 128 MB runner-distributor runners.yaml One for each Linux node Nothing 0.5 CPU, 256 MB linux-java classes-extra.yaml 1 4 CPUs, 8 GB linux-hardened classes-extra.yaml 1 2 CPUs, 4 GB linux-docker-build docker-build.yaml 1 4 CPUs, 8 GB linux-microvm microvm.yaml 2 2 CPUs, 4 GB The VM adds overhead of its own, which is not measured here linux-microvm-docker microvm.yaml 1 4 CPUs, 8 GB The same microvm-dns microvm.yaml 2 Nothing 0.5 CPU, 128 MB microvm-netkeep microvm.yaml One for each microVM node Nothing 0.2 CPU, 256 MB linux-persistent persistent.yaml 1 4 CPUs, 8 GB linux-default-ssh ssh-rerun.yaml 1 2 CPUs, 4 GB windows-default runners.yaml (Windows) 2 2 CPUs, 4 GB token-proxy-windows runners.yaml (Windows) 1 Nothing 1 CPU, 512 MB runner-distributor-windows runners.yaml (Windows) One for each Windows node Nothing 1 CPU, 1 GB windows-custom, windows-docker-build, windows-default-ssh The add-on files (Windows) 1 each 2 CPUs, 4 GB windows-persistent persistent.yaml (Windows) 1 4 CPUs, 8 GB The shipped runners.yaml therefore reserves 4.1 CPUs and a little over 8 GB on Linux, and 4 CPUs and 8 GB on Windows, before the operating system, Docker and the distributor.
What it costs. This project has no price of its own. The cost is the nodes that you run for the peak, your CircleCI plan, and the network and storage that jobs use. CircleCI says that runner compute does not use credits, that at least one credit is needed because storage and networking do, and that self-hosted runner concurrency is a separate limit of your plan (Run jobs on self-hosted runners). Disk is not measured here. Swarm cannot limit it, every finished container keeps its writable layer until Swarm prunes it, and a Windows node holds the servercore base image (about 2.2 GB compressed) as well.
Setting Linux Windows limits.cpus Caps CPU for the container Caps CPU. A value above the CPU count of the host is rejected limits.memory Caps memory. The kernel kills a job that exceeds it Caps memory limits.pids Caps processes. The files set 4096 Rejected by the Windows engine, so absent reservations Scheduler only. Equal to the limits, so extra replicas stay pending instead of overcommitting Scheduler only. The engine never receives it ulimits nofile 65536, core 0 Rejected by the Windows engine, so absent Size one runner for the largest job of the class, not for the average job. A job cannot choose a different size, because the resource class defines it. Create a second class for jobs that need more, for example linux-large.
Plan the node capacity from the reservations:
The sum of the reservations of all replicas on a node must fit in the node. Leave room for the operating system and Docker, for example one CPU and 2 GB of memory. The shipped Linux file reserves 4 CPUs and 8 GB of memory in total (two replicas of linux-default), and classes-extra.yaml adds 6 CPUs and 12 GB. A node with fewer resources runs fewer replicas, and the others stay Pending. The runner-distributor service reserves nothing, and its limit is 0.5 CPU and 256 MB. Swarm cannot limit disk for a container. Jobs share the Docker data disk of the node, so size it for the replicas plus the stopped containers that Swarm keeps. Refer to Start Swarm.
data.stack-keys-on-windows#Stack keys on Wind:
Not every key of a stack file reaches a Windows container. docker stack deploy and the Windows engine treat the keys as follows.
Effect Keys Used isolation, bind mounts of directories, npipe mounts, named volumes (with volume.subpath: Docker resolves a relative directory symbolic link in it when it creates the container, and refuses a junction or an absolute link), Swarm configs with an absolute target (a link to the config is created there; a relative target does not land there), secrets without uid, gid, and mode, stop_grace_period, logging, entrypoint, environment with Swarm placeholders, labels, deploy.mode: global, deploy.placement, deploy.restart_policy, deploy.update_config, deploy.endpoint_mode, and deploy.resources.limits for cpus and memory Scheduler only deploy.resources.reservations. The engine rejects a memory reservation, so Swarm never sends it Rejected by the Windows engine deploy.resources.limits.pids and ulimits, so the files do not set them. A limits.cpus above the CPU count of the host is rejected too No effect init, cap_drop, cap_add, read_only, tmpfs, and sysctls Ignored by docker stack deploy on every platform security_opt, privileged, userns_mode, restart, and build Three choices in the Windows files follow from this:
No hostname. A Windows computer name has at most 15 characters, and a templated hostname would give every container of a slot the same COMPUTERNAME. Without it, COMPUTERNAME is the container ID, which tells the containers apart. endpoint_mode: dnsrr. Nothing connects to a runner, so no virtual IP is needed. Settings repeated per service. YAML merge keys do not merge deeply. The idle timeout is set for each service, because the persistent class must not have one, and windows-docker-build repeats the PATH with C:\docker appended. The log driver is json-file with rotation. The local driver also works on Windows.
data.the-secret#The secret: Linux, token proxy Linux, runner (persistent class) and the placeholder Windows Name -token -token, and runner-placeholder-token for every proxied class -token Target -token circleci_runner_config.yaml circleci_runner_config.yaml Path in the container /run/secrets/-token, in the proxy /run/secrets/circleci_runner_config.yaml C:\ProgramData\Docker\secrets\circleci_runner_config.yaml Owner and mode uid 65534, gid 65534, 0400 uid 2000, gid 2000, 0400 Not supported. Administrators and SYSTEM only Content api: and auth_token: The same. The placeholder holds a made-up token The same The proxy accepts the file in this format or a bare token. The runner does not look for a config file on its own. The entrypoint arguments pass --config , and environment variables override the values in the file.
data.variables-in-the-stack-files#Variables i: Variable Value in the files Applies to Notes CIRCLECI_RUNNER_NAME "{{.Node.Hostname}}--{{.Task.Slot}}" Every service Required. Unique per replica CIRCLECI_RUNNER_MODE single-task, or continuous for persistent classes Every service single-task gives a new container for every job CIRCLECI_RUNNER_IDLE_TIMEOUT 1h Single-task services An idle replica exits and Swarm replaces it. Do not set it in continuous mode CIRCLECI_RUNNER_CLEANUP_WORK_DIR "false" on Linux, "true" on Windows Every service On Windows, the runner removes the working directory before and after each task. On Linux it stays off, because the runner user cannot remove files that the job user owns. Refer to Working directory cleanup CIRCLECI_RUNNER_LOGGING_FORMAT text Every service No color codes in logs CIRCLECI_RUNNER_MAX_RUN_TIME Commented out, default 5h Every service If you lower it, lower stop_grace_period to the same value plus 5 minutes HTTPS_PROXY, NO_PROXY Commented out Every service Jobs inherit variables that you set here MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO "true" or "false" Linux "false" makes the class hardened CIRCLECI_RUNNER_WORK_DIR C:\cci\w Windows The working directory of jobs. The task agent creates it CIRCLECI_RUNNER_TASK_AGENT_DIRECTORY C:\cci\agent Windows The task agent directory. The runner creates it MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_INSTANCE_ID {{.Task.ID}} Windows Lets a job tell which container it ran in GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT, GCM_INTERACTIVE, GIT_CONFIG_* 0, never, and core.longpaths=true Windows Stop Git prompts, and allow long paths. The system Git config is read-only PATH The full Server Core path, then Git Windows stock services Replaces the image PATH, so the file spells it out Refer to the machine runner 3 configuration reference for every other CIRCLECI_RUNNER_* variable. Environment variables override the config file.
data.variables-read-by-the-linux-entrypoint#V:
Variable Default Notes MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_WAIT 120 The seconds that the entrypoint waits for the link current of the runner distributor. Without it, the container exits with code 80 MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_USER circleci The account that runs jobs. The entrypoint creates it with uid 2001 when the image has none MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO true false removes every sudo right of the job user in that container and steps jobs down with setpriv --no-new-privs, which needs util-linux setpriv in the image (exit code 80 without it). Any other value exits with code 80 The runner user is circleci-runner with uid 2000. It owns the secret file and has no sudo rights.
The entrypoint sets these variables for the runner. It always sets the command prefix, and it keeps a value that you set for the other three:
Variable Value CIRCLECI_RUNNER_COMMAND_PREFIX ["sudo","-niHu","","--"], or a setpriv command when the image has no sudo, and always a setpriv --no-new-privs command in a hardened class CIRCLECI_RUNNER_CLEANUP_WORK_DIR false. Do not set it to true on Linux CIRCLECI_RUNNER_TASK_AGENT_DIRECTORY /var/lib/circleci-runner/agent, owned by the runner user CIRCLECI_RUNNER_WORK_DIR /var/opt/circleci/workdir, owned by the job user. Keep a custom directory under /var/opt/circleci Arguments that you pass to the entrypoint replace the default command, which is machine --config /run/secrets/circleci_runner_config.yaml.
data.variables-read-by-the-runner-distributor:
These are variables of docker stack deploy, and x-distributor-env in linux/stack/runners.yaml passes them to the runner-distributor service. They apply to that service only. Refer to Upgrade the runner on Linux.
Variable Default Effect MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_VERSION An exact version, the newest that CI tests An exact version pins it and never changes by itself. 3.1, 3 and current follow the manifest of CircleCI: the version policy MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_MAJOR 3 The major version that current may adopt MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_CHECK_INTERVAL 24h How often a floating version looks at the manifest again: seconds, or a number with s, m, h, or d MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_DOWNLOAD_BASE_URL https://circleci-binary-releases.s3.amazonaws.com/circleci-runner Where manifest.json and the tarballs are, for example a mirror. It must be https://, unless a SHA-256 list is set MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_SHA256 The tarball SHA-256 values of the pinned version A comma-separated list for an exact pin. manifest means no list: the hash of the manifest is trusted, which is weaker. A floating value ignores any list MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_ALLOW_HTTP Not set true accepts an http:// download base without a SHA-256 list, for a lab
data.windows#Windows:
The add-on stack file windows\stack\persistent.yaml defines windows-persistent. It sets CIRCLECI_RUNNER_MODE: continuous and sets no idle timeout. It declares and mounts the named volume windows-persistent-cache at C:\cache. Point NuGet, npm, and similar caches there with an environment variable in the job.
The service is pinned to the nodes that carry the label machine-runner-swarm.class.windows-persistent=true. Create the secret windows-persistent-token first, then label the node and deploy your copy of the file (in deploy\, from the copy of windows\stack that the install page makes) with your copy of the main file:
docker node update --label-add machine-runner-swarm.class.windows-persistent=true <node name> docker stack deploy -c deploy\runners.yaml -c deploy\persistent.yaml runners Swarm still replaces the container when the runner exits. Only the volume survives the replacement. On Windows, the runner and the jobs use the same account, so the runner cleans the working directory, and CIRCLECI_RUNNER_CLEANUP_WORK_DIR stays "true".

data: CI/CD: What the pipeline tests, how the docs site is built, and how releases are signed and published. Releasing: How a merge to main becomes a signed GitHub release, how maintainers enable publishing, and how to recover from a failed release. Contributing: How to report a bug, propose a change and open a pull request for machine runner swarm, a CircleCI Labs project.

The pipeline lints everything, tests the Linux and Windows Swarm stacks, and proves with real CircleCI jobs that every job runs in a fresh container, whether the runner is hosted by a Swarm service on Linux or on Windows. It publishes one image, the token proxy, from main only, and makes the signed releases (Releasing). Scan reports and logs are kept as job artifacts.
Setup config: .circleci/config.yml Pipeline: .circleci/continue.yml E2E helpers and their simulation: ci/ Lint settings: .hadolint.yaml, .yamllint.yaml, .shellcheckrc, PSScriptAnalyzerSettings.psd1, .trivyignore, lychee.toml (repository root)
data.a-pull-request-that-needs-a-checksum#A p:
Renovate cannot compute a SHA-256 value. For a tool that is pinned with one (Hugo, lychee, the CircleCI CLI, git-cliff, cosign, gh, Go, Kata, PortableGit, 7-Zip, Node.js), the pull request changes the version only, carries the label checksum and a note in its description, and its CI fails on the checksum. To finish it:
Take the new value from the checksums file of the release (the table in Pinned tools names the file), or download the asset and run sha256sum on it. Replace the old value next to the version, in the same branch, and push. For PortableGit, also set Version (X.Y.Z.N for the tag vX.Y.Z.windows.N) and run ci/config-names.sh --write: the distributor is a Swarm config. Update the version in the prose that names it (this table, Releasing, docs/microvm.md for Kata).
data.a-ruleset-for-main#A ruleset for main:
