The Windows tests, each printing CHECK lines and a RESULT line: Test-Injection.ps1 -Online, Test-Ephemerality.ps1, Test-Exit80.ps1, Test-Placement.ps1, Test-StopHandling.ps1 -Online (stock Server Core is killed 5 s after a stop, the control, an idle real runner drains on a stop, a Swarm secret is read), Test-Persistent.ps1, and Test-Distributor.ps1 (the distributor against a local mirror of fake releases). ci\Invoke-Test.ps1 runs each in a child PowerShell and keeps its complete output as an ASCII report under reports/ (artifacts). Tee-Object would write UTF-16 and would miss what a script writes with [Console]::Out. The bring-your-own-image example windows/images/example (stock Server Core plus Node.js, pinned with a SHA-256) is built in the same job and runs node, npm and git with the runner and Git mounted and the PATH of custom-image.yaml.
data.windows-tests-where-to-look-first#Window: Symptom Likely cause What to do Test-Install.ps1 fails at distributor The distributor could not download or unpack, or its post-install of Git warned The report prints the log of the service: look for cannot download, SHA-256 mismatch, 7zr.exe exited and Git post-install lines docker run fails creating a mount (invalid mount config or cannot access path) The engine refuses a subpath that is a junction or an absolute link, or the link current does not exist yet The links are relative directory symbolic links, which the distributor creates; for the Git destination under C:\Program Files, the task agent needs Git at exactly that path, so check the engine version toolchain fails: bash or git not found The stack’s PATH is wrong for this image The detail prints the container’s PATH; compare it with path-default, and fix the PATH string in runners.yaml and stack.e2e.yaml toolchain fails: no SeCreateSymbolicLinkPrivilege, or symlink_made=False The container user is not an administrator The stock Server Core default is ContainerAdministrator; check that no user: is set path-default lists lost entries The image’s own PATH has directories that the stack’s string lacks (for example on Server 2025) Add them to the PATH strings in runners.yaml and stack.e2e.yaml online hangs and times out The task-agent download failed (egress to circleci-binary-releases.s3.amazonaws.com), or the symlink was refused Container logs (printed): look for A required privilege is not held by the client stop-real-runner fails: not drained, exit not 0 The shutdown event does not reach the Go runtime The printed log tail of the container Test-Placement *-pending fails with state='Running' The label or OS constraint was not evaluated as expected docker node inspect self --format '{{json .Spec.Labels}}' swarm deploy fails creating a network HNS or overlay problems on a single-NIC VM docker network ls, delete a leftover transparent network, retry

data: Thank you for helping to improve the machine runner swarm. This repository is part of CircleCI Labs. Field engineering reviews issues and pull requests on a best-effort basis and does not provide an SLA. CircleCI support does not cover this repository.
data.commit-messages#Commit messages:
Use Conventional Commits: type(scope): summary. The release job reads these messages to choose the version and to write the release notes.
Type Use for feat A new capability, or a changed stack-file contract fix A bug fix docs Documentation only test Tests only ci The CircleCI pipeline chore Maintenance with no user-visible change refactor, perf Code changes that keep behavior, or improve speed Common scopes are linux, windows, docs, readme, and ci.
A breaking change appears first in the release notes. Mark it in the commit message, in one of two ways, and write what the user has to change:
Add ! after the type or scope: feat(linux)!: rename the persistent service.
Add a BREAKING CHANGE: footer:
feat(linux): rename the persistent service BREAKING CHANGE: the service is now linux-persistent. Rename it in your stack file. While the version is 0.x, a breaking change raises the minor number.
Keep each commit small and atomic.
data.development#Development:
Requirements: Docker with privileged containers for the Linux suite, bash, and PowerShell 7 for the Windows unit tests.
linux/tests/run-all.sh # the whole Linux suite, a Swarm inside Docker-in-Docker linux/tests/run-all.sh token drain # a subset linux/tests/stack-config.sh # stack file contract, no daemon needed pwsh -File windows/tests/Invoke-UnitTests.ps1 -InstallModules # PSScriptAnalyzer and Pester The Linux tests run a Swarm inside docker:dind containers, so your own Docker engine never enters Swarm mode. The Windows Swarm tests run on a Windows host, and the CI pipeline runs them on Windows Server 2022 and 2025. Refer to CI/CD for the pipeline and for every lint command.
Each Linux test prints RESULT lines and exits 0 when it passes. run-all.sh runs all of them against one shared pair of Docker-in-Docker containers.
Test What it checks stack-config.sh docker stack config for every combination of stack files, the settings of each service, and the names of the Swarm configs. Needs no daemon helper.sh setup.sh --swarm-init, --secret, and --deploy against a fresh Docker-in-Docker daemon ephemerality.sh A new container for every job and no residue. The negative control runs docker run --restart always exit80.sh The restart delay, no hot loop, and the exit codes 80 and 1 of the real runner token.sh What a job can read in the default class and in the hardened class task.sh The real runner runs tasks as the job user, against a fake API. Also the failure with CIRCLECI_RUNNER_CLEANUP_WORK_DIR=true, and a persistent runner placement.sh Placement on a manager and a worker, and docker-build.yaml distributor.sh The runner-distributor service: runners that wait for it and then exit 80, a node with no install, a joining node, an upgrade under three busy jobs, a rollback without a download, an exact pin that never changes by itself, 3.1, 3 and current that follow the manifest, the major-version guard, pruning to 3 versions, a tampered binary, a wrong SHA-256, and CircleCI’s real manifest. Needs network access persistent.sh Continuous mode and persistent.yaml microvm.sh The microVM add-on with Kata Containers: the node label, a guest kernel, DNS through the forwarder, a read-only node directory, dockerd in the VM, and the entrypoint guard. Skipped without /dev/kvm. Downloads Kata (about 1 GB) unless SWARM_TEST_KATA_DIR or SWARM_TEST_KATA_TARBALL points at a copy. Not part of run-all.sh drain.sh SIGTERM during a job: the job finishes limits.sh init, ulimits, pids, memory, CPU, reservations, and the capability sets take effect network.sh Network isolation between classes, and between the replicas of a class bats/run.sh The unit tests of the entrypoint on cimg/base, Alpine, and UBI minimal The suite needs no installed runner. The distributor of the shipped stack installs it, as it does for a user, from a small HTTP mirror in the harness: a manifest.json and the tarballs of the versions that a test publishes (publish_runner in lib.sh). ephemerality.sh, persistent.sh, limits.sh, network.sh, and drain.sh publish fake-runner.sh, a stand-in for circleci-runner that runs a fake job through the step-down and exits, as a single-task runner does. task.sh, token.sh, exit80.sh, placement.sh, distributor.sh, and the idle case of drain.sh publish the real runner binary, which the harness downloads once and checks against the SHA-256 of CircleCI’s manifest.
Three variables change the setup. SWARM_TEST_DIND_IMAGE sets the Docker-in-Docker image. SWARM_TEST_CACHE sets the directory that caches the real runner binary, ~/.cache/swarm-tests by default. SWARM_TEST_KEEP=1 keeps the Docker-in-Docker containers for debugging.
The Windows tests in windows/tests print CHECK PASS|FAIL lines and one RESULT line, and exit 0 only when every check passes. Invoke-UnitTests.ps1 runs the Pester tests on any system with PowerShell 7. The Test-*.ps1 scripts need a Windows host with Docker in Windows-container mode, and none of them needs a runner token.
Test What it checks Test-Injection.ps1 A stock Server Core image with the mounts of the volume runner-bin and the PATH of the stack: the toolchain, GNU tar as the task agent calls it, Git long paths, the exit codes of the runner, and the config file with environment overrides. -Online lets the real runner download its task agent. -Baked tests the baked image Test-Ephemerality.ps1 A new container for every job and no residue, with the restart-policy negative control Test-Exit80.ps1 Exit 80 without a hot loop Test-Placement.ps1 Placement constraints and node labels Test-StopHandling.ps1 What a stop does to a busy stock container (it kills the job, informational), and a Swarm secret as the runner config. -Online stops the real runner and expects a drain Test-Install.ps1 The distributor installs the runner and portable Git from CircleCI’s real manifest into the volume of the stack, and the stock mounts work and are read-only Test-Distributor.ps1 The distributor script against a local mirror: pin, current by SHA-256, the major-version guard, rollback, a wrong SHA-256, pruning, a changed binary, and a running container that keeps its version Test-Persistent.ps1 Continuous mode, and a named volume that outlives the container
data.documentation-checks#Documentation check:
Documentation follows the CircleCI docs style: sentence-case headings, active voice, no contractions, and short sentences. Every docs/*.md page has front matter with page-title, page-audience, and page-description.
CI checks the relative links and the Mermaid diagrams. To run the same checks locally:
docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/input" -w /input lycheeverse/lychee:0.24.2 --config lychee.toml './**/*.md' docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/workdir" davidanson/markdownlint-cli2:v0.18.1 '**/*.md'
data.license#License: By contributing, you agree that your contributions are licensed under the MIT license.
data.opening-a-pull-request#Opening a pull re:
Before you open a pull request:
Discuss large changes in an issue first. Run the tests for the platform you changed. Refer to Development. Update the documentation in docs/ when you change a variable, label, secret, port, or default. Write every commit message, and the pull request title, as a Conventional Commit. The release notes are generated from them, so there is no changelog entry to add. Refer to Commit messages. Check that the diff has no tokens, host names, or customer or vendor names. The repository is public. A pull request from a fork gets no CI. The project builds no forked pull request and passes no secret to one, because the code of a fork would otherwise run with this project’s settings (Secrets and public logs). A maintainer reads the change, and to run CI on it pushes its commits to a branch of this repository by hand. Never push or mirror an outside branch to main or to a branch named smr-swarm/*: those two names get the e2e runner tokens and, on main, the publishing contexts, and the configuration of a job comes from its own branch.
A pull request that changes only documentation (docs/, site/, Markdown files) runs the lint jobs and the docs site build, and skips the builds and the Swarm tests (Documentation-only changes).
Use the pull request template. Maintainers choose the merge method for each pull request. A squash merge turns the pull request title into the commit message on main, and a merge commit or a rebase keeps your commits. Refer to Merge method.
data.pinned-versions#Pinned versions:
Renovate opens a pull request every Monday for the pinned versions: the images and their digests, the tools that CI downloads, the Go toolchain and the docs theme. The configuration is renovate.json, and Pinned versions lists what it covers and what stays by hand. A pull request with the label checksum changes a version that is pinned with a SHA-256 value: Renovate cannot compute the value, so replace it in the same branch before you merge.
Pin images by tag and digest, and a new download by its version and checksum together, with a # renovate: comment above the version (see the page above). The runner version that the stack files install by default is pinned, in three places that must stay equal (linux/stack/runners.yaml, linux/stack/microvm.yaml and windows/stack/runners.yaml): the newest version that CI tests, bumped by each release (how). The alpine:3 image of the distributor is pinned by digest in linux/stack/runners.yaml. The pinned Git and 7-Zip versions and their SHA-256 values are in windows/stack/runner-distributor.ps1, and a change of the script needs ci/config-names.sh --write. Pin images by tag and digest.
data.releases#Releases:
Maintainers do not tag releases by hand, and nobody edits a changelog. Refer to Releasing for the details.
Versioning. The project follows Semantic Versioning and starts at 0.x. While the version is 0.x, a breaking change bumps the minor number. Version 1.0.0 is reserved for general availability or official adoption. Release job. A CircleCI job runs on main after every test job of that pipeline has passed. git-cliff reads the Conventional Commits since the last release tag and computes the next version, with the rules in cliff.toml. A fix is a patch. A feat is a minor. A breaking change is a minor in 0.x and a major from 1.0.0. A push that holds only docs, test, ci, chore, style, or refactor commits makes no release. Contents. Each release is a GitHub release with a tar.gz and a zip bundle of the user-facing files, a SHA256SUMS file, and a keyless cosign signature of that file, made with the CircleCI OIDC token. The release notes are generated from the commits, with breaking changes first. The job creates the tag through the GitHub API and never pushes a commit to main. Changelog. CHANGELOG.md is a short page. The release bundle contains a generated CHANGELOG.md with every release. Failures. If a release fails part way, a maintainer reruns the job in CircleCI. The job finishes the release at the same commit and never creates a second one. Refer to Verify a release to check a download.
data.reporting-a-bug#Reporting a bug:
Search the existing issues first, and check that you use the latest release. Then open a new issue with the bug template. Include:
The release or commit of this repository, and the runner version. On Linux, run docker run --rm -v runners_runner-bin:/v:ro alpine cat /v/current/VERSION on the node. On Windows, run docker service logs --tail 100 runners_runner-distributor-windows. The operating system of the node and the Docker Engine version. The output of docker service ps --no-trunc runners_ and docker service logs --tail 100 runners_. Remove tokens, runner config files, and internal host names from everything you paste.
data.requesting-a-feature#Requesting a featur: Open an issue with the feature request template. Describe the problem you want to solve, and name the platform and the files it affects. For problems in the CircleCI platform or the runner agent, contact CircleCI support instead.
data.security-disclosure#Security disclosure: Do not open a public issue for a security vulnerability. Email security@circleci.com and follow SECURITY.md.
data.swarm-config-names#Swarm config names: The entrypoint and the distributor scripts reach the nodes as Swarm configs. A Swarm config cannot change, and a service keeps the old file when the name stays, so the name of each config in the stack files carries the first 12 hex digits of the SHA-256 of its file. After you change linux/stack/circleci-runner-entrypoint, linux/stack/runner-distributor.sh, or windows/runner-distributor.ps1, run ci/config-names.sh --write and commit the new names with the change. lint-stack, linux/tests/stack-config.sh, and the release job run ci/config-names.sh and fail on a stale name. Nobody decides when to bump a number.
data.when-the-repository-moves-to-circleci-pu: Replace the Labs wording in these files: the banner and the Support section of README.md, SECURITY.md, the support paragraph at the top of this file, .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/config.yml, and .github/CODEOWNERS. Decide the license, because CircleCI runner repositories use Apache-2.0 and this one uses MIT.

data:
This page is for maintainers. A CircleCI job makes every release of this repository when a change is merged to main. Nobody tags a release by hand, edits a changelog, or pushes a commit to main for a release. The job creates the tag through the GitHub API.
Rules for the version and the notes: cliff.toml The job: release in the ci workflow of .circleci/continue.yml and ci/release.sh How users check a release: Verify a release
data.before-the-first-release#Before the firs:
Do these before the merge that makes v0.1.0, in this order. Each later release needs only the checks that it states.
Check the settings above, all of them, and note the date.
Rotate both e2e runner tokens. Until the ruleset of smr-swarm/** and the context restrictions were in place, anyone who could push a branch could have printed them, so treat every token that exists today as read. Create a new token for each class, store it in the context, run one pipeline on main and check that both e2e groups pass, and then delete the old token. circleci context secret set prompts for the value in a terminal, so the token is not in the shell history:
circleci runner token create cci-labs/scalable-machine-runner-e2e-linux --nickname ci-YYYYMM circleci context secret set scalable-machine-runner-e2e --org --name E2E_RUNNER_TOKEN_LINUX circleci runner token create cci-labs/scalable-machine-runner-e2e-windows --nickname ci-YYYYMM circleci context secret set scalable-machine-runner-e2e --org --name E2E_RUNNER_TOKEN_WINDOWS circleci runner token list --resource-class cci-labs/scalable-machine-runner-e2e-linux circleci runner token delete List the tokens of the Windows class and delete its old token the same way. Rotate them again whenever a token may have leaked, and when someone who could read them leaves the project.
Check the pin. The runner version and its SHA-256 values are the ones that CI tested (Bump the runner version).
Merge. The release job publishes, and the first release is its first real run (Not tested).
After the release, check the signature of the bundle and of the image as a user does (Verify a release), including the ref.
data.bump-the-runner-version#Bump the runner:
The stack files pin one exact runner version by default: MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_VERSION: ${MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_VERSION:-3.1.13} in the settings of the distributor of linux/stack/runners.yaml and windows/stack/runners.yaml, and in x-env of linux/stack/microvm.yaml. It is the newest runner version that CI tests, because the tests take their runner from the same line (STACK_RUNNER_PIN in linux/tests/lib.sh, so the real-runner tests and the end-to-end jobs run the pin), and a release carries the pin that CI tested.
Each release bumps it, in a commit before the release:
Pick the newest version in the manifest that has every platform (jq -r '.releases | keys[]' manifest.json, and check .releases[""] for linux amd64, arm64, ppc64le, s390x and windows amd64, arm64). Read the runner changelog for the version. In the same commit, change the default of MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_VERSION in all three stack files to that version, and change the default of MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_SHA256 to the tarball SHA-256 values of that version (from the release’s checksums.txt or from the manifest: linux amd64, arm64, ppc64le, s390x in linux/stack/runners.yaml and linux/stack/microvm.yaml, windows amd64 and arm64 in windows/stack/runners.yaml, comma-separated in that order). The version must stay equal in every file. linux/tests/stack-config.sh fails when they differ, and the release job (ci/release.sh, check_runner_pin) fails when the version is not in the manifest for every platform or when a default SHA-256 list does not match the manifest for the pin. Commit it as feat(runner): pin 3.1.14 by default for a new minor or patch of the runner that users should get, or fix(runner): ... for a fix, so that git-cliff makes a release with it. Let CI run: the pin is now the version that the Swarm tests and the end-to-end jobs run. Update the version in the examples of the docs only when you want them to move (docs/operations.md uses 3.1.12 and 3.1.13 as example values). A user then gets the new runner by deploying the new release: the pin is part of the release, and a deploy of the new stack files moves the distributor to it. A user who sets the variable keeps what they set.
The bundles come from git archive, so only tracked files ship. They leave out linux/tests/, windows/tests/, docs/ci.md, docs/releasing.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, ci/, .circleci/, proxy/ and site/: the pages about this repository’s own pipeline and release are for maintainers.
The pages that ship still link to some of those files. ci/bundle-links.py turns every relative link from a page of the bundle to a tracked file that the bundle leaves out into a link to that file on GitHub at the tag of the release (https://github.com///blob/vX.Y.Z/...), and the release job adds the rewritten pages in place of the originals. It stops the release when a link is dead in the repository too. ci/tests/bundle-links.sh tests it on a throwaway repository and on this one, in lint-circleci, so a new page that links to docs/ci.md does not need a special case.
data.check-the-settings#Check the settings:
Read the GitHub settings back with the API. The first command lists the rules that apply to main (it must include pull_request, non_fast_forward, deletion and required_status_checks), and the second shows the bypass list of a ruleset, which must be empty for main:
gh api repos/CircleCI-Labs/scalable-machine-runner/rules/branches/main --jq '.[].type' gh api repos/CircleCI-Labs/scalable-machine-runner/rulesets --jq '.[] | "\(.id) \(.name) \(.enforcement)"' gh api repos/CircleCI-Labs/scalable-machine-runner/rulesets/ --jq '{conditions, bypass_actors, rules: [.rules[].type]}' The ruleset of smr-swarm/** must show creation and update among its rules. The CLI cannot list the restrictions of a context, so read them from the API, once for each of the five contexts, and compare them with the table (a project restriction and an expression restriction each). The id of a context is in the output of circleci context list --org :
curl -s --header "circle-token: ${CIRCLECI_TOKEN}" https://circleci.com/api/v2/context//restrictions The project settings are in the web app (Project Settings, then Advanced), and the Docker Hub token scope in the security settings of the account. Keep the output with the release pull request, so that the next person sees what was set and when.
data.enable-publishing#Enable publishing:
Until you do this, the release job runs every step except the last one on a project that has no e2e tokens. It prints publishing skipped: GITHUB_TOKEN is not set in context scalable-machine-runner-release, keeps the version, the notes, the bundles, and the signature as job artifacts, and stays green. Nothing is published. On the production main (both e2e tokens present) the job fails with the same message instead, so a renamed or emptied token cannot go unnoticed.
Create a token. Use a fine-grained personal access token with the resource owner CircleCI-Labs, only this repository, and the repository permission Contents: Read and write. GitHub always adds read access to metadata. No other permission is needed, because gh release create makes the tag and the release. A fine-grained token expires, so note the date to rotate it. A GitHub App installation token with the same permission also works, but it expires after one hour, so it does not fit a context variable.
In the CircleCI organization settings, create the context scalable-machine-runner-release and add the variable GITHUB_TOKEN with the token.
Restrict the context to this project, and add an expression restriction so that only pipelines of main can use it, and neither an SSH rerun that could print the token nor a pipeline started through the API, which can name any branch and, where the organization allows it, bring its own config:
pipeline.git.branch == "main" and not job.ssh.enabled and not (pipeline.config_source starts-with "api") With the CLI, where is the organization slug and is 7bbdbb66-6ba8-4f6c-982e-d4fb401ec257:
circleci context restriction create scalable-machine-runner-release --org --type project --value circleci context restriction create scalable-machine-runner-release --org --type expression \ --value 'pipeline.git.branch == "main" and not job.ssh.enabled and not (pipeline.config_source starts-with "api")' In the organization’s advanced settings, leave pipelines with an unversioned config off.
In the project settings (Advanced), keep Build forked pull requests and Pass secrets to builds from forked pull requests off. The project uses the GitHub OAuth integration, and these settings are the ones that decide whether the code of a fork runs here.
Protect main on GitHub with the ruleset of A ruleset for main: a pull request required, no force push, no bypass, and the check ci. Whoever can change .circleci/ or ci/release.sh on main controls what runs with the token. What the release trust depends on lists every setting that the signature relies on.
The documentation site, its optional pull request comment and the weekly security scan have their own contexts and a schedule, and What a maintainer creates once lists them with the release context. Do not reuse this token for them: it can publish releases.
The next release run on main publishes. To check the setup before then, read the log of the release job for publishing skipped.
data.how-the-signature-works#How the signatur:
The job gets an OIDC token from CircleCI with circleci run oidc get --claims '{"aud":"sigstore"}' --root-issuer. The audience sigstore and the issuer https://oidc.circleci.com are the values that the public Sigstore certificate authority (Fulcio) accepts for CircleCI. cosign sign-blob swaps the token for a short-lived certificate, signs SHA256SUMS, and records the signature in the public Rekor log. The certificate expires within minutes, and the job keeps no key.
The certificate identity is https://circleci.com/api/v2/projects//pipeline-definitions/. The project and the definition IDs stay the same for every branch, and a job of any branch can get an OIDC token, with no context. The identity alone therefore does not prove that main signed. What does is the source repository ref of the certificate: the extension 1.3.6.1.4.1.57264.1.14, which Fulcio fills from the vcs-ref claim of the token, so it is refs/heads/main for a release and refs/heads/ for a job of any other branch. The certificate also records the repository, the workflow and the job.
cosign has flags for the GitHub extensions only, so ci/tools.sh reads the certificate itself (signed_only_on, tested by ci/tests/signature-ref.sh):
ci/release.sh checks the signature of SHA256SUMS with cosign verify-blob, and then that its certificate names refs/heads/main. The job stops if it does not. ci/proxy-image.sh does the same for every digest of the token proxy image, right after it signs it, and again in the release job before the image gets its release tags. It reads every signature of the digest (cosign download signature), not the first one: one signature of a feature branch next to a signature of main fails the check. To check the ref by hand, after cosign verify-blob printed Verified OK, look for the extension in the certificate of the bundle. The long hex string is the encoding of the OID 1.3.6.1.4.1.57264.1.14 followed by the value refs/heads/main, so the command matches the whole value and not a part of a longer ref:
jq -r '.verificationMaterial | (.certificate // .x509CertificateChain.certificates[0]).rawBytes' SHA256SUMS.sigstore.json | base64 -d \ | od -An -v -tx1 | tr -d ' \n' | grep -Eq '^([0-9a-f]{2})*2b0601040183bf30010e0411(0c|13)0f726566732f68656164732f6d61696e' \ && echo "signed for refs/heads/main" || echo "NOT signed for refs/heads/main: do not use this release" To see which ref a certificate has, print it with openssl asn1parse: base64 -d | openssl asn1parse -inform DER | grep -A1 57264.1.14 shows the value as hex digits after HEX DUMP]:, 0C0F and then the ASCII codes of the ref.
data.merge-method#Merge method:
The release notes come from the commits that land on main, so the merge method decides what the notes show.
Merge commit or rebase and merge. Every commit of the pull request lands on main and gets its own entry. Use this for pull requests whose commits are small, atomic Conventional Commits, as CONTRIBUTING.md asks. Entries link to their commits. The GitHub merge commit (“Merge pull request #12 …”) is not a Conventional Commit, so the notes ignore it. Squash and merge. The pull request becomes one commit with the title as the message, and one entry in the notes, so write the title as a Conventional Commit. GitHub adds the pull request number, so the entry links to it. If a pull request mixes a feat and a fix, the squash hides one of them. Mark a breaking change in a commit message, or in the title of a squashed pull request, with ! or a BREAKING CHANGE: footer.
data.pinned-tools#Pinned tools:
The job installs its tools in ci/release.sh install-tools. Each download is checked against a SHA-256 value in the script (cosign and crane, which the image jobs use too, are in ci/tools.sh), and the job image is pinned by digest. Each tool has its version and its SHA-256 value in two variables of the function, and a # renovate: comment above the version.
Tool Version Source of the SHA-256 value git-cliff 2.14.2 The .sha512 file of the release, and a local sha256sum cosign 3.1.3 cosign_checksums.txt of the release crane 0.22.1 checksums.txt of the release (the Linux x86_64 archive) gh 2.102.0 gh_2.102.0_checksums.txt of the release Go 1.27.2 The download page of go.dev, next to the archive cimg/base 2026.10 The digest in .circleci/continue.yml Renovate opens a pull request for a new version and changes the version only. The pull request has the label checksum and fails on the checksum until you replace the SHA-256 value in the same branch. To update a tool by hand, change its version and its SHA-256 value together in install_tools (cosign and crane: in ci/tools.sh), and then run the steps in Try it locally. To update the image, follow Pinned versions. A Renovate pull request for the Go toolchain also moves the golang and cimg/go images, so the proxy binaries of the release use the same Go as proxy-test.
data.release-notes#Release notes:
git-cliff writes the notes of the new version for the body of the GitHub release. Breaking changes come first. Then come features, bug fixes, performance changes, and reverts. Each entry shows the scope and the message. GitHub adds (#123) to the title of a squash merge, and the notes link that number to the pull request. An entry without a pull request number links to its commit instead.
CHANGELOG.md in the repository is not a list of changes: it points to GitHub Releases, where the notes of every release are. The release bundle holds a generated CHANGELOG.md with the notes of every release, from git cliff.
data.rerun-and-recovery#Rerun and recovery:
Rerunning is safe. Before it publishes, the job looks for a release tag at the commit that it checked out, and it never creates a second release.
Situation What to do A test job failed Fix it and use Rerun workflow from failed. The release job runs when all jobs have passed The release job failed before it published Rerun the job. It computes the same version The release exists but an asset is missing, for example after an upload error Rerun the job. It finds the tag at this commit and uploads all assets again with --clobber The job says that a tag exists at another commit Stop. Somebody created vX.Y.Z by hand, or an older release was moved. Compare git rev-parse vX.Y.Z with the commit of the pipeline. Delete the wrong tag and release with gh release delete vX.Y.Z --cleanup-tag, then rerun the job This commit is already part of vX.Y.Z A later commit was already released. The job ended green without doing anything The release job shows as skipped A newer pipeline is waiting for the release lock, and it will release this change too The Deploys view shows the release as FAILED The job failed after it planned the deploy. Read the failure reason there, fix the cause, and rerun the job: it records a new deploy of the same version, and the failed one stays in the history Nothing to release since vX.Y.Z The commits since the last release are only docs, test, ci, chore, style, refactor, or build. This is expected gh fails with 401 or 403 The token expired or lost its permission. Replace GITHUB_TOKEN in the context and rerun the job A release is wrong Prefer a new release that fixes it. If you delete a release and its tag, the next run makes the same version again Rerunning a pipeline from before a later release does not release again, because the commit is already part of a tag.
data.tag-pipelines#Tag pipelines:
The release creates the tag through the GitHub API, with no git push. GitHub then sends a push event for the new tag. The project uses the GitHub OAuth integration (project slug gh/CircleCI-Labs/scalable-machine-runner), not the GitHub App. An OAuth project has no trigger settings: CircleCI starts a pipeline for every push that GitHub reports, to a branch or to a tag, so the new tag starts a pipeline. In that pipeline pipeline.git.tag is the tag, and pipeline.git.branch and CIRCLE_BRANCH are empty.
That pipeline cannot release and runs no job. CircleCI does not run a job for a tag unless the job has a tag filter, and no job in .circleci/config.yml or .circleci/continue.yml has one. The setup phase also releases only when the branch is main. Look at the Pipelines page of the project after the first release: the pipeline of the new tag should show no job. To build for tags in the future, give a job a tag filter on purpose, and keep the release context out of that job.
data.the-signing-rehearsal#The signing rehear:
Signing runs for real on main only (the release job and the image jobs have the contexts), so the first merge would be its first real run, and a failure would leave sha-<12> tags with no release. The job signing-rehearsal runs the same code in every pipeline that is not documentation-only, on any branch, with no context and no secret (ci/proxy-image.sh rehearse):
It starts from a registry:2 container (the second container of the job, at localhost:5000) and pushes a throwaway image: one layer with one file that names the pipeline. It gets an OIDC token with circleci run oidc get --claims '{"aud":"sigstore"}' --root-issuer, signs the image with cosign sign against the real Fulcio and Rekor (a public service: a brief failure is tried again, three times), and verifies it with verify_signature, the function that main uses: the certificate identity, the issuer, and the ref, which here is refs/heads/. It checks that the same signature is refused for another ref (refs/heads/main on any other branch), so a check that has stopped looking at the ref turns the pipeline red. Each rehearsal adds an entry to the public Rekor log with the project, the branch and the commit, like every signature of a public repository. The release requires the job. The first pipeline after a change in CircleCI’s token claims or in Sigstore shows it, and the first merge does not.
CircleCI documents that OIDC tokens are issued to jobs that use at least one context. The release job always has one, the context with GITHUB_TOKEN. In a test on 2026-10-13, circleci run oidc get also worked in a job without a context, which is why the ref and not the identity decides, and which the rehearsal relies on.
data.the-token-proxy-image#The token proxy im:
The token proxy is a published image, ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy on Docker Hub, not a release asset. One tag is a manifest list that covers linux/amd64, arm64, ppc64le and s390x, and Windows Server 2022 and 2025 (windows/amd64). The pipeline builds and tests it in every run, and pushes it from main only:
Event Tags pushed A pull request or a branch None: the image is built and tested, never pushed A merge to main sha-<12 characters of the commit>, and nothing else, by proxy-image-publish The same merge, after linux-swarm and every e2e group have passed edge, by the last job of the pipeline, proxy-image-edge. It stays where it is when a newer commit is on main A release (ci/release.sh on main, the version vX.Y.Z that git-cliff computes) X.Y.Z (immutable), X.Y, X and latest, on the digest of that commit’s sha-<12> image: nothing is rebuilt The stack files of a checkout default to latest, so the only job that changes what a checkout deploys is the release job, and it runs after every test. edge is for people who want the newest tested commit, and sha-<12> is the image of one commit that nothing has tested yet: neither is the default of anything. Before the first release latest does not exist: deploy a checkout with MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_IMAGE set to a sha-<12> or edge tag, or use the release bundle once there is one.
X.Y.Z never moves: a release that finds X.Y.Z on another digest stops. X.Y, X and latest move only when the release is the newest of its minor line, its major line, and of all, so finishing an old release late moves nothing else. Three helper tags, sha-<12>-linux, sha-<12>-windows-ltsc2022 and sha-<12>-windows-ltsc2025, hold the parts that the jobs push first; pull the other tags.
How it is made, in the order of the pipeline (ci/proxy-image.sh, ci/Build-ProxyImage.ps1):
proxy-image-linux builds proxy/Dockerfile for the four Linux platforms with buildx and QEMU, and runs each image: it reports its version, runs as 65534 with a read-only root and no capabilities, takes a token file and a state volume, and becomes healthy. proxy-image-windows-ltsc2022 and -ltsc2025 build proxy/Dockerfile.windows from the windows/amd64 binary of proxy-test on the Windows machine executors and run it the same way. ci/tests/proxy-image.sh runs the publication against a registry of its own. Windows on Arm has no machine executor, so there is no windows/arm64 image (install-windows.md). On main (the pipeline parameter publish), the publish variants of those jobs run instead, with the context scalable-machine-runner-dockerhub: they push sha-<12>-linux, sha-<12>-windows-ltsc2022 and sha-<12>-windows-ltsc2025. Then proxy-image-publish joins the three with crane index append into one manifest list, tags it sha-<12> and nothing else, checks that every platform is in it, and signs every digest keyless with the CircleCI OIDC token, as ci/release.sh signs SHA256SUMS. It records a deploy of token-proxy-image in docker-hub with the version sha-<12> (Deploys). proxy-image-edge, the last job of the pipeline, runs after proxy-image-publish, linux-swarm and the e2e groups. It checks the signature of sha-<12> and tags it edge (not when a newer commit is on main: ci/proxy-image.sh edge). The release does not wait for it. The release job pins the digest of sha-<12> in the stack files of the bundle (MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_IMAGE:-ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy:@sha256:, in place of :latest), checks the signature, and adds the four release tags. The credentials. The context scalable-machine-runner-dockerhub holds DOCKERHUB_USERNAME and DOCKERHUB_TOKEN (an access token that can push to the repository), and is restricted to main and to this project (Docker Hub context). Without both values a pipeline that is not the production main builds, tests, prints NOT PUSHED with the reason, and passes. On the production main (the parameter strict, set when both e2e tokens are present) a missing credential fails the image jobs, proxy-image-publish, the release and the docs publication instead: Publishing fails closed on main.
A checkout keeps the default ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy:latest, which Renovate does not manage (it is a tag with no digest). A release bundle carries its own digest, and it is the documented way to install: users download it, verify its signature and run the image that it names. Users verify the image with cosign (Verify the token proxy image); the verification must also check that the certificate names refs/heads/main (How the signature works).
data.try-it-locally#Try it locally:
Everything except publishing and signing runs on a workstation. Install the tools, or run the script in the job image:
ci/release.sh install-tools # git-cliff, cosign, crane, gh into ~/.local/bin, and Go into ~/.local/go RELEASE_SKIP_SIGN=1 ci/release.sh # the files are in /tmp/release; nothing is signed or published To check that the release job requires every job of the workflow, as lint-circleci does, compile the config with every parameter on and read the release entry of workflows.ci.jobs:
circleci config process .circleci/continue.yml \ --pipeline-parameters '{full-suite: true, e2e-linux: true, e2e-windows: true, release: true, publish: true}'
data.versions#Versions:
The project follows Semantic Versioning and starts at 0.x. Tags are vX.Y.Z. git-cliff computes the next version from the Conventional Commits since the last tag. There are no tags yet, so the first release is v0.1.0: cliff.toml sets that as the initial tag.
Commits since the last release Next version while 0.x A breaking change: type!: or a BREAKING CHANGE: footer Minor, for example 0.2.3 to 0.3.0 feat Minor fix, perf, revert Patch Only docs, test, ci, chore, style, refactor, or build No release. The job ends green A message that is not a Conventional Commit, such as the first three commits of the repository or a GitHub “Merge pull request” commit Ignored A breaking change never raises the major number, so the job never makes 1.0.0 on its own. Version 1.0.0 is a decision for people. When the project is ready, merge a change to the [bump] section of cliff.toml (breaking_always_bump_major = true and features_always_bump_minor = false). The next breaking change then makes 1.0.0.
To see what the next release would be, run these commands in a clone with the tags:
git cliff --bumped-version # the next version, or the last tag when there is nothing to release git cliff --unreleased --tag "$(git cliff --bumped-version)" --strip header # its notes
data.what-a-release-contains#What a release c: Asset Content machine-runner-swarm-.tar.gz README.md, LICENSE, SECURITY.md, VERSION, the generated CHANGELOG.md, docs/, examples/, linux/ and windows/ machine-runner-swarm-.zip The same files, for Windows users SHA256SUMS The SHA-256 checksum of both bundles SHA256SUMS.sigstore.json The cosign bundle: signature, certificate, and transparency log entry
data.what-happens-on-merge#What happens on me:
A push to main starts a pipeline. The setup phase in .circleci/config.yml reads the branch. On main, with both e2e tokens present, it passes release: true to the pipeline, together with full-suite, the heavy suites (windows, proxy-image, microvm), e2e-linux and e2e-windows, and strict: true. The pipeline has one workflow, ci. With those parameters it runs all lint jobs, the Linux jobs, the Windows Server 2022 and 2025 jobs, linux-mixed-arch, and the e2e jobs on Linux and Windows. Expression filters on the parameters (filters: pipeline.parameters.release on the release job, and similar ones on the Windows, linux-microvm and e2e jobs) switch the jobs in and out, so no job runs twice. The release job requires every other job of the workflow, except the three optional ones that lint-circleci names (linux-mixed-arch, proxy-image-edge and docs-site-comment). If one required job fails, nothing is released. Fix the problem, then use Rerun workflow from failed. The release job runs once everything has passed. The release job runs in the serial group /release, so two quick merges cannot race for the same version. A newer pipeline whose release job waits in the group makes the release job of an older pipeline skip. The newer one releases both changes. ci/release.sh checks that every Swarm config of the stack files is named after the content of its file (ci/config-names.sh), and stops when a name is stale. Then it finds the next version, makes the notes, reads the digest of the token proxy image that the pipeline of the commit pushed and pins it in the stack files, builds the bundles, signs SHA256SUMS, verifies the signature, verifies the signature of the image and gives it its release tags, and creates the GitHub release. The release creates the tag at the commit of the pipeline. When the job will publish (GITHUB_TOKEN and the Docker Hub credentials are set, and the image of the commit is on Docker Hub), ci/release.sh also records the release in the Deploys view of CircleCI: component machine-runner-swarm, environment github-releases, version the tag; and the tags of the image: component token-proxy-image, environment docker-hub, version X.Y.Z. Each deploy ends as SUCCESS, or as FAILED when any step of the script fails (Deploys). A release needs the image of its commit. The job proxy-image-publish of the same pipeline pushes it (sha-<12 characters>) and the release requires that job. Without DOCKERHUB_USERNAME and DOCKERHUB_TOKEN in the context scalable-machine-runner-dockerhub, a pipeline that is not the production main stays green and publishes nothing: the image jobs say that nothing was pushed, and the release job builds the bundle, stores it as an artifact, and does not create the GitHub release, because a bundle that names an image tag that does not exist would be broken. On the production main the same gap fails the jobs (Publishing fails closed on main). Pipelines of other branches never release, and neither do tag pipelines.
A push to main that changes only documentation (docs/, site/, Markdown files) runs lint and the docs site build, and no e2e and no release job: the setup phase passes docs-only: true and turns release off (Documentation-only changes). That loses nothing, because cliff.toml makes no release for a docs commit. When a commit of the push would make a release, for example fix(docs): or a breaking change, the setup phase leaves docs-only off, so the whole pipeline runs and the release job with it. The docs site is published either way.
If an e2e token is missing on main, the setup phase passes release: false and says so in its log. The pipeline then runs the ci workflow without the release job (and without the e2e group whose token is missing), because a release must wait for every test.
Add a new job to requires of the release job. The release job lists every other job of the workflow in requires (in .circleci/continue.yml), and a comment at the job says so. The job lint-circleci compiles the workflow and fails when a job is missing from the list, so a pull request cannot add a test that the release does not wait for. The only exceptions are the optional jobs that lint-circleci names in its $optional list (today linux-mixed-arch, the emulated mixed-architecture cluster test, proxy-image-edge, which moves the edge tag after the tests, and docs-site-comment, which posts the preview address on a pull request).
data.what-the-release-trust-depends-on#What t:
A valid signature on a release says one thing: a job of this CircleCI project, from the pipeline definition of this repository, ran on refs/heads/main of this repository. The signing identity is the same for every branch, and a job of any branch can get an OIDC token, so the claim holds only as far as the settings below hold. They are settings of GitHub, CircleCI and Docker Hub, and not of the repository, so no file in it can enforce them or show them, and ci/release.sh does not check them. The maintainers have set all of them for v0.1.0. Check the settings says how to read them back.
Setting Where It must say Without it The ruleset of main GitHub repository Require a pull request. Block force pushes. Restrict deletions. No bypass list. Required status check: ci (A ruleset for main) A writer could push a change of .circleci/ or ci/release.sh to main, and the release job would sign it as main The ruleset of smr-swarm/** GitHub repository Restrict creations and updates, with the maintainers alone on the bypass list (The e2e context and smr-swarm/*) A writer could create smr-swarm/, change .circleci/ in it, and print the e2e runner tokens in a public log The context scalable-machine-runner-release CircleCI organization The restrictions project (this project) and expression: pipeline.git.branch == "main" and not job.ssh.enabled and not (pipeline.config_source starts-with "api") A job of another branch, an SSH rerun or an API pipeline could read the release token The context scalable-machine-runner-dockerhub CircleCI organization The same two restrictions as the release context (The Docker Hub context) A branch could push an image under the tag that the stack files name The context scalable-machine-runner-docs CircleCI organization project, and expression: pipeline.git.branch == "main" and not job.ssh.enabled and not (pipeline.config_source starts-with "api") A branch could read a token that writes to the repository The context scalable-machine-runner-e2e CircleCI organization project, and expression: (pipeline.git.branch == "main" or pipeline.git.branch starts-with "smr-swarm/") and not job.ssh.enabled and not (pipeline.config_source starts-with "api") A branch could read the e2e runner tokens The context scalable-machine-runner-pr-comments CircleCI organization project, and expression: not job.ssh.enabled and not (pipeline.config_source starts-with "api"). It cannot be limited to a branch: any branch pusher can read it, so the token has the least permission (Docs site previews) An SSH rerun or an API pipeline could read it The project settings CircleCI project and organization Build forked pull requests off. Pass secrets to builds from forked pull requests off. Auto-cancel redundant workflows off. SSH reruns off. Pipelines with an unversioned config off (Secrets and public logs) A fork could run its own .circleci/config.yml here, or an API pipeline could bring a config of its own The tokens GitHub, Docker Hub The release and docs tokens: fine-grained, this repository only, Contents: Read and write. The comment token: Issues: Read and write, of a bot account. The Docker Hub token: read and write on ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy and nothing else, from an account that has two-factor authentication (What each job can see) A leaked token would reach more than the job that needs it Two things are not covered, and you should not read the signature as covering them. The signature does not say that anyone reviewed the change: the ruleset sets the number of reviews, and .github/CODEOWNERS is a single line that asks the same people for every path. And it says nothing about main before the ruleset existed: a release signed from a commit that came in by another route is valid in the same way.

data.can-a-fork-pull-request-use-these-runner: No. CircleCI does not make self-hosted runners available to a public project that has Build forked pull requests enabled, because untrusted code on your machines is a significant risk. Keep that setting off for any project that uses these classes. For a private project, a collaborator’s branch runs your code on the node, so restrict each class to the projects that need it. Refer to CircleCI-side controls.
data.can-a-job-read-the-runner-token#Can a jo: Not from its own container in a single-task class, with or without sudo: the runner container holds only a made-up placeholder, and the token proxy holds the class token. On Windows, no test asserts this, and a hostile job on the same host as the proxy can reach the token, because process isolation is not a security boundary (Windows). In a persistent class the container holds the token: on Linux a job that uses sudo can read it (the shipped persistent class disables sudo by default), and every job can on Windows. Swarm also stores a Windows secret in clear text on the container disk, so use BitLocker and one token for each class and host. Refer to Token model on each OS and to the comparison with the official installs. A holder of a token can run a rogue runner on that class and claim its jobs, so rotate tokens (how).
data.can-i-run-a-long-lived-runner-with-warm-: Yes, with a persistent class. It gives up the clean environment, so use it only for trusted projects. The shipped Linux persistent class gives jobs no sudo by default. Refer to Persistent mode.
data.can-i-use-rerun-job-with-ssh#Can I use R: Yes, with the add-on stack file ssh-rerun.yaml. It defines the class linux-default-ssh (windows-default-ssh on Windows), which sets CIRCLECI_RUNNER_SSH_ADVERTISE_ADDR, publishes port 54782 in host mode, and runs at most one replica on each node. A rerun uses the class of the original job, so the job that you debug must run on that class. The Swarm side was proven by hand with a real runner. No CI test logs in over SSH, and the Windows file is untested. Refer to Rerun job with SSH.
data.do-i-need-to-open-inbound-ports#Do I nee: No. Runners connect outbound over HTTPS, and the shipped classes publish no ports. Only the optional SSH add-on publishes port 54782, for Rerun job with SSH. Multi-node clusters need the Swarm ports between the nodes. Refer to Inter-node ports.
data.do-proxies-and-custom-certificate-author:
The stack sets nothing for them, and this repository does not test them.
Proxy. Set HTTPS_PROXY, HTTP_PROXY, and NO_PROXY under environment of the service. The runner is a Go program that reads them, and jobs inherit them. Test a checkout through the proxy before you roll out a class. Refer to Egress hosts. On Linux, also set HTTPS_PROXY under environment of the token-proxy service, because it makes the call to runner.circleci.com for the runners, and add NO_PROXY: token-proxy to the runners, so that their calls to it stay on the overlay network. Certificate authority. Add your CA to a custom image and run update-ca-certificates, or mount a CA bundle read-only and point SSL_CERT_FILE at it. Windows images need the CA in the image too. On Linux, the token proxy needs the CA too when a proxy or your CircleCI server uses it: mount the bundle into token-proxy and set SSL_CERT_FILE there. Refer to Images.
data.does-circleci-support-it#Does CircleCI s: No. This repository is part of CircleCI Labs. Engineers at CircleCI created it, but CircleCI support does not cover it, and it is a pre-release 0.x project. Field engineering handles issues on a best-effort basis. The runner itself, the CircleCI platform, and your resource classes are covered by your normal CircleCI support. What is tested says how each claim of this documentation is checked, and which are not.
data.does-it-create-or-remove-nodes#Does it c: No. The nodes are yours. You install Docker, join the node to the Swarm, and label it from a manager (a node cannot label itself), and a Windows node needs its base image before the first task. A terminated instance leaves a Down node in the Swarm until you run docker node rm. This repository has no cloud integration, no machine image, and no example of user data. If you create nodes with user data, do not leave the Swarm join token readable in it (Cloud nodes: block the metadata address). Refer to Multi-Node Clusters.
data.does-it-scale-to-zero-and-what-does-idle: No. Capacity is fixed: the replicas are numbers in your stack file, and you pay for the peak. An idle replica keeps its reserved CPU and memory (reservations equal limits), on nodes that you run, so the cost of an idle class is the cost of its nodes. Scale to zero is a manual replicas: 0, and a class with no runner queues jobs without limit and holds concurrency (Capacity and concurrency). This documentation does not say which replica a scale-down removes, and a scale-down while jobs run is not tested: assume that it can remove a busy replica. On Windows it kills the job. If you need elastic capacity, use the machine runner orchestrator or CircleCI cloud executors. A script that reads the queue depth (below) and runs docker service scale is possible, and this repository does not ship one.
data.does-it-support-macos#Does it support ma: No. Docker has no macOS containers, so Swarm cannot schedule macOS jobs. Apple’s licence also limits macOS to Apple hardware, so running macOS in a container on other hardware is not an option. CircleCI documents how to run machine runner 3 directly on a Mac, and CircleCI offers hosted macOS executors.
data.does-it-work-on-hosts-without-internet-a: No, and it is not tested. A host without internet access is not supported by this release. Every runner needs outbound HTTPS to runner.circleci.com, and every new container downloads the task agent from circleci-binary-releases.s3.amazonaws.com. A host that reaches those names through an allow list or a proxy works. On Linux, the runner download of the distributor can come from a mirror of your own: set MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_DOWNLOAD_BASE_URL to an internal HTTP server that holds manifest.json and the tarballs. Refer to Run the downloads from a mirror. The mirror does not replace the task agent download. Pull the images, including alpine for the distributor, from a registry that the nodes can reach. Refer to Registry needs. What needs internet lists every download.
data.does-it-work-with-rootless-docker-user-n: Podman cannot run Swarm, so it cannot run this stack. Rootless Docker and userns-remap are not tested. The stack assumes a root daemon: the entrypoint checks that the runner volume belongs to root, and the secret belongs to uid 2000. Whether these checks hold under a remap is untested. Swarm also ignores userns_mode in stack files.
data.does-it-work-with-selinux-on-rhel#Does i: The RHEL steps are documented and not tested in CI. Keep SELinux enforcing. The runner is in a Docker volume and not in a host directory, so no directory needs a label for it.
data.how-do-i-report-a-bug-or-a-vulnerability: Open a GitHub issue for a bug. For a vulnerability, email security@circleci.com. Refer to SECURITY.md.
data.how-do-i-scale-up-or-down-and-see-how-ma:
Swarm has no autoscaling, so you choose the number of replicas.
Permanent change. Edit deploy.replicas in your stack file and deploy again with the same list of files. Refer to Choose replica counts. To add capacity beyond one node, add nodes. Refer to Multi-Node Clusters.
Quick change. docker service scale runners_linux-default=4. The next docker stack deploy resets the count to the value in the file. A scale-down stops containers: on Linux a running job finishes first, and on Windows it is killed (why).
Queue depth. The runner API reports the tasks that wait for a runner of a class. Use a personal API token, not a resource class token.
$ curl -s -H "Circle-Token: $CIRCLECI_API_TOKEN" \ "https://runner.circleci.com/api/v3/runner/tasks?resource-class=/linux-default" {"unclaimed_task_count": 3} $ curl -s -H "Circle-Token: $CIRCLECI_API_TOKEN" \ "https://runner.circleci.com/api/v3/runner/tasks/running?resource-class=/linux-default" {"running_runner_tasks": 2} Jobs wait while unclaimed_task_count stays above 0 and every replica is busy. Raise the replicas by that number, if the nodes have room. Refer to Monitor the cluster.
data.how-do-i-verify-a-release#How do I verif: Each release has a SHA256SUMS file and a keyless cosign signature that was made with the CircleCI OIDC token. Refer to Verify a release, or Verify a release on Windows. Those pages run the signature check, the ref check (refs/heads/main in the certificate), and the checksum check in one block that prints RELEASE VERIFIED only when all three pass. The runner binary is a separate download. On Linux, the distributor verifies its SHA-256 and the entrypoint checks it at every container start. Refer to Runner binary integrity on Linux.
data.how-does-the-runner-version-policy-compa: It follows them. Machine runner 3 on a host has no auto-update: you update the package. Container runner takes the image tag from the Helm values that you set, and publishes a floating tag for each major and minor version next to a fixed tag for each patch release. The orchestrator takes its pool image from the Helm chart, with a floating default tag and a dated tag that pins it. Here the version is a setting of the distributor service: an exact pin by default, and 3.1, 3 or current when you want the newest release of a line. Refer to How this compares.
data.is-docker-swarm-a-safe-bet#Is Docker Swa:
This project can state what it checks, and cannot promise the future of Swarm.
What it uses. Only core Swarm features: services, secrets, configs, overlay networks, placement constraints, and rolling updates. It uses no add-on, and no plugin. Which Docker versions. The CI of this repository runs Docker 29.4.2 on Linux and 29.4.0 on Windows. The documented minimum is 24 on Linux and 28.0 on Windows (Prerequisites, Windows). The way out. The resource class names are CircleCI objects, not Swarm objects. Jobs with machine: true keep their class when you move the class to the machine runner orchestrator or to a machine runner 3 on a host. Why Swarm and not container runner or another runner? says what to use instead. The support. This is a CircleCI Labs project, 0.x, with best-effort support and no commitment on how long it is maintained.
data.is-there-a-delay-between-jobs#Is there a: A replica needs about 10 seconds for the restart delay, plus the start-up time of the container and the download of the task agent, before it claims the next job. Other replicas of the class keep working during that time. Refer to Job lifecycle.
data.should-i-use-the-setup-helper-or-the-man:
Both give the same result. The helper is optional, and every step of it is on the install pages.
setup.sh or Setup.ps1 does It does not Linux Checks the node, creates a single-node Swarm on the loopback address, creates secrets from hidden prompts, and deploys the stack files you name Install Docker, install the runner (the runner-distributor service does that on every node), create resource classes or tokens, edit or copy the stack file, label or join nodes, or build images Windows Creates the Swarm, labels the node with the image tags it can run, creates secrets, and deploys Install Docker or Windows features, create classes or tokens, edit or copy the stack file, add the labels of the optional classes, join other nodes, or build images The steps run in a fixed order, and a rerun is safe. The helper installs no runner on either OS: the distributor service of the stack does. Refer to Optional: use the setup helper and the Windows helper.
data.what-do-sudo--nihu-and-setpriv-mean#What:
They are the two forms of the runner’s command_prefix, the setting that wraps the task agent so that a job runs as another user. CircleCI documents the setting in the machine runner 3 configuration reference. The entrypoint sets it in every Linux container, and a value in the service environment does not override it.
sudo -niHu circleci -- is the default class. The flags are -n (never prompt: fail instead), -i (run a login shell), -H (set HOME to the home directory of the target user), and -u circleci (the target user). -- ends the options, and the task agent follows. The file /etc/sudoers.d/90-circleci-runner allows only the runner user (uid 2000) to do this, and only to the job user. setpriv is the form without sudo. It comes from util-linux, switches to the job user, and clears every capability before it starts the task agent. The hardened class always uses it with --no-new-privs, which makes the job and everything it starts ignore the setuid bit, so sudo, su, or a vulnerable setuid binary cannot lift a job to root. An image that has no sudo uses setpriv too, whatever the setting. The setting MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO chooses between the default and the hardened class. It is not the prefix itself. Refer to Users and the runner token on Linux.
data.what-happens-to-a-job-when-a-node-dies#W: The job is lost. CircleCI reports it as failed because of an infrastructure problem, and self-hosted runners do not retry a job automatically, so rerun it. Swarm detects the lost node, and starts replacement runners on other nodes that match the constraints, which restores the capacity. A single manager that dies stops all replacements, and the quorum rules of Managers and quorum apply. Refer to Node death.
data.what-is-not-in-this-release#What is not: Autoscaling and creation of nodes. Metrics export. The stack exposes no metrics endpoint (Monitor the cluster). An external secrets manager, and a tested rotation of tokens. A hardened Windows class, and Hyper-V isolation. CircleCI server and hosts without internet access: neither is tested (What needs internet). A one-command verification script. A release is checked with the commands of Verify a release.
data.what-is-the-token-proxy-and-what-happens:
It is the service token-proxy in the Linux runners.yaml (token-proxy-windows in the Windows one). It holds the resource class tokens, so that the runner containers and their jobs never do. The runners hold a made-up placeholder and send their API calls to the proxy, which adds the real token to the task claim of a runner that Swarm lists in the DNS set of its class, once for each container. Refer to Concepts and Security.
When it is down, no runner can claim, and the jobs wait in CircleCI. Idle runners fail their claims and try again. They send nothing to CircleCI on their own, because they hold no token. Swarm restarts a failed proxy after 5 seconds. A claim whose outcome is unknown (the request reached CircleCI and the answer was lost, or the upstream sent no response headers within 60 seconds) is latched like a successful claim: that runner is refused until Swarm replaces it, so the proxy fails closed. A job that already runs keeps its container, but its API calls, such as step output, go through the proxy too, so keep outages to a restart. Refer to Monitor the token proxy, including what a restart does to idle runners. The proxy runs on a manager by default. On a single node it needs no label. In a cluster, label the node that runs it machine-runner-swarm.proxy=true: runner services never run on a node with that label. Refer to Where the proxy runs, and when it moves for what happens when it moves to another node. The proxy limits every client address to 50 requests a second (bursts of 200) and serves at most 512 requests at once, so one runner or job cannot use it up alone, and it logs a summary line a minute (The token proxy). The persistent classes do not use the proxy.
data.what-is-this-repository#What is this rep: It is a set of Docker Swarm stack files, a small Linux entrypoint, a Linux service that keeps the runner on every node (except the nodes of the microVM add-on, which have their own copy), optional setup helpers, and documentation. Together they run CircleCI machine runner 3 in containers, with one resource class for each Swarm service and a new container for every job. Refer to Concepts.
data.what-must-i-build#What must I build?:
Nothing, with one optional exception on Windows.
You build Optional Linux Nothing. The stack mounts the runner from a per-node volume, which its runner-distributor service fills, and the entrypoint from a Swarm config, into a stock image such as cimg/base. docker stack deploy is the whole install A custom image when jobs need tools, because the hardened class cannot install packages at run time. It needs util-linux setpriv. Refer to Images Windows Nothing. The service runner-distributor-windows of the stack installs the runner and portable Git into a volume that the stack mounts into the stock Server Core image A custom image for your tools, and a DIY image that lets a job finish after a stop. Refer to Windows images and the stop-timeout image You build no image. This repository publishes one, the token proxy (ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy on Docker Hub), which Swarm pulls when you deploy the stack, and the release bundle names the image of its release by digest. A Linux node needs a Docker engine and a Swarm join, and nothing else. A Windows node needs a Docker engine, the ltsc2022 base image, and a Swarm join, and nothing else.
data.where-are-the-tokens-kept-and-can-i-use-: Class tokens are Swarm secrets, and nothing else: the stack has no integration with an external secrets manager. Anyone in the docker group on a manager can read every token, and a Windows secret is stored in clear text on the disk of the container of the proxy (Token model on each OS). Rotation is a manual procedure that CI does not test (Rotate a runner token). If you need tokens in a secrets manager, that is outside this repository.
data.which-circleci-plans-and-platforms-work#:
The stack is tested against CircleCI cloud, on Linux and Windows. CircleCI server is not tested. CircleCI documents machine runner 3 for server 4.4 and later, and an install on server sets the runner API URL. This stack points the runners at the token proxy (CIRCLECI_RUNNER_API_URL: http://token-proxy:8080), so to try server you change the -upstream argument of the token-proxy service to the URL of your server, and keep the runner variable as it is. Nothing here shows that this works with your server version, and CircleCI server says what is known.
Self-hosted runners need at least one credit on your account, although runner compute does not use credits (Run jobs on self-hosted runners). Their concurrency is separate from the concurrency of hosted jobs and is shared by every class of the organization: CircleCI can tell you your limit, and the Runner tab of your organization shows it. Config policies, which restrict classes to projects, need the Scale plan on cloud or server 4.2 or later (Config policy management overview).
data.which-jobs-cannot-run-here#Which jobs ca:
The jobs run in unprivileged containers on a shared kernel, so some jobs belong on another runner.
Job needs Here Use instead A privileged container, /dev/kvm, or other host devices No. Swarm ignores privileged and devices. The microVM add-on gives a job its own kernel, not host devices The machine runner orchestrator, or a machine runner on a host Docker-in-Docker No, because it needs a privileged container The opt-in docker-build class, a daemonless builder, or a daemon inside the VM of the microVM add-on setup_remote_docker No. It belongs to the Docker executor The docker-build class, or a daemonless builder Docker commands in a job Only in the docker-build class, which is root-equivalent on its node Docker Builds A GPU Not supported or tested. The stack files declare no generic resources A machine runner on a GPU host Service containers (docker: secondary images) No. Jobs use machine: true Install the service in the image, or use container runner Desktop or UI automation on Windows No. Windows jobs are headless A machine runner on a host A docker: executor job No. Jobs use machine: true, and the image of the service is the environment of the job Container runner
data.which-operating-systems-does-it-support#: Platform Status Linux, Ubuntu LTS, amd64 Tested in CI, including real jobs Linux, Ubuntu LTS, arm64 Every pipeline tests that the distributor installs the runner and that the stack starts. On main and smr-swarm/* branches, three probe jobs also run on a real arm64 runner. Linux, ppc64le and s390x CircleCI publishes the runner for them, and the distributor and the token proxy are built for them. CI emulates them under QEMU: the distributor installs the runner of the right architecture, and the token proxy image runs on both. Nothing else runs there in CI Linux, RHEL 8 and later Steps documented, not tested in CI Windows Server 2025 and 2022 Tested in CI, on amd64 Windows on arm64 The distributor is built for it, and CI checks the file names. The token proxy has no windows/arm64 image (Windows). No Windows arm64 host runs the stack in CI Windows Server 2019 Supported by machine runner 3. Untested here, and the stack files have no label for it Windows Server 2016 and older Not compatible with machine runner 3 macOS Out of scope
data.which-runner-version-do-the-nodes-run#Wh:
The runner-distributor service of the stack decides, and the setup helper installs nothing. The default is an exact pin with the tarball SHA-256 values in the stack file: the newest runner version that the CI of this repository tests, which each release of this repository bumps. The nodes keep it until you change it. To float instead, set MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_VERSION to 3.1 (the newest 3.1.x), 3 (the newest 3.x.y) or current (CircleCI’s current release); the distributor then trusts the manifest’s hash (weaker), and looks again every 24 hours. Floating is supported and is the weaker choice: the manifest comes from the same bucket as the tarball, and a newer runner can change the protocol that the token proxy depends on (the claim and scale calls), in which case the proxy fails closed and jobs wait. Pin an exact version in production. No second setting is needed to float. To go back, pin an older version. Refer to The version policy.
On Windows, runner-distributor-windows decides in the same way, with the same variables. Refer to Upgrade the runner on Windows.
data.why-does-a-windows-job-end-when-i-update: Stopping a busy stock Server Core container from outside kills its job after about 5 seconds, whatever stop_grace_period says, and a finished job ends its container cleanly. Roll out changes while the class is idle, or rerun the interrupted jobs. Refer to Stop a busy Windows container.
data.why-not-plain-docker-compose#Why not pla:
The earlier version of this repository used Docker Compose. Compose is simple, but it has a flaw that matters for clean environments.
Plain Compose Docker Swarm Restart restart: unless-stopped restarts the same container restart_policy: any creates a new task and a new container Clean environment No. Files outside the working directory survive a restart Yes, for every job Token storage Environment file, visible in docker inspect Swarm secret, mounted as a file Hosts One host Many nodes, Linux and Windows, with placement Updates and drain Manual Rolling update, and each busy runner drains (finishes its job) first Setup Nothing to learn beyond Compose Swarm concepts, even on a single node The test linux/tests/ephemerality.sh includes a negative control that shows the flaw. Three jobs on docker run --restart always ran in one container, and two of them found files from an earlier job. A script can recreate containers in a Compose setup, but that is custom code that this repository avoids. If you use the old docker-compose.yml, refer to Migrate from Docker Compose.
data.why-swarm-and-not-container-runner-or-an:
Choose by what you already run and by the isolation that you need.
You have or need Use Why Elastic capacity, and nothing to host CircleCI cloud executors CircleCI runs and scales them. Choose them when your jobs do not need your own network, hardware, or data location Kubernetes, and jobs that fit a docker: executor Container runner CircleCI documents it, it scales pods, and it uses convenience images. Choose it when you have Kubernetes A boundary stronger than a container, privileged or KVM jobs, a full OS, or autoscaling Machine runner orchestrator A virtual machine for each job on Kubernetes with KubeVirt, and the token stays out of the VM. Refer to Compared with the official runner installs One host or a few, jobs that need the whole machine, or no containers at all Machine runner 3 on a host The simplest setup. Jobs share the host, and nothing separates one job from the next The same, but in a container Machine runner 3 on Docker It runs the runner with docker run. The container is reused for more jobs until you stop it, so the environment is not clean Docker hosts or Windows containers, no Kubernetes, and a clean container for every job This repository Swarm creates a new container for every job, and adds replicas, placement, secrets, and rolling updates. It has no support from CircleCI, no autoscaling, and no creation of nodes, and the containers share the host kernel Swarm mode is part of Docker Engine, and the stack files use only its core features: services, secrets, constraints, and rolling updates. To move to the orchestrator or to a plain machine runner later, keep the resource class names, and the jobs with machine: true stay as they are. Container runner needs the jobs to change to a docker: executor. CircleCI lists its own options in the runner overview.
The microVM add-on of this repository runs each job in a Kata Containers microVM on Swarm nodes that have KVM. It is experimental: CI runs the real runner against a fake CircleCI API on nested virtualization on AWS (amd64), and no real CircleCI job, other cloud, or arm64 is tested in CI. One real CircleCI job ran by hand on a Kata Cloud Hypervisor class. If you need a hardware boundary today, the orchestrator is the documented route.

data: Quickstart on Linux: Run a first job on a Docker Swarm node with CircleCI machine runner 3 in about a dozen commands, for a one-node trial or the start of a cluster. Quickstart on Windows Server: Run a first job on a Windows Server Docker Swarm node with CircleCI machine runner 3 in six steps, using the stock Server Core image. Concepts: How Swarm services map to resource classes, what the token proxy does, what a clean environment covers, and how the default and hardened classes differ.

This page explains the model behind the stack files in this repository. Read it before you change a stack file or choose between the default and the hardened class.
The stack runs CircleCI machine runner 3 as Docker Swarm services. Swarm handles replicas, restarts, secrets, and placement. This repository adds only a stack file for each operating system, a small entrypoint and a runner distributor service for Linux, and optional setup helpers.
data.add-on-stack-files-and-how-they-merge#Ad:
Each operating system has one main stack file, runners.yaml, that defines the default classes and deploys on its own. The optional classes live in add-on stack files next to it: persistent.yaml, docker-build.yaml, and ssh-rerun.yaml on both systems, custom-image.yaml on Windows, and microvm.yaml on Linux (MicroVM jobs). An add-on stack file is not a patch of the main file. It defines services of its own, and each service needs its own resource class and its own -token secret. The one exception on Linux is the token-proxy service: docker-build.yaml, ssh-rerun.yaml, and microvm.yaml also add their classes to it (a network, a secret, and a variable), so deploy them together with runners.yaml. persistent.yaml does not touch the proxy.
docker stack deploy -c runners.yaml -c persistent.yaml runners reads the files in the order given and merges them into one stack, as Docker Compose does for several -f files. A service, network, secret, or volume that only one file defines is added, and a key that several files set takes the value of the later file. The shipped add-on stack files only add services. YAML anchors work inside one file only, so each add-on stack file repeats the common service settings, and a change to one of them goes into every file that you use.
Pass the same list of files, in the same order, on every deploy. Swarm updates the services of the files you name. The services of a file you leave out stay as they are and stop following your edits, and --prune removes them. Check a merge without a Swarm with docker stack config -c runners.yaml -c persistent.yaml.
