data.glossary#Glossary: Term Meaning Stack file A Compose-format YAML file that docker stack deploy reads. Each OS has a main stack file (runners.yaml) and optional add-on stack files. This documentation never calls an add-on stack file an overlay, because an overlay network is a different thing Stack The services that one docker stack deploy creates. The documentation names it runners, so the service linux-default is runners_linux-default in Swarm commands Resource class, service A resource class is the CircleCI name, /, that a job selects with resource_class. A service is the Swarm object that runs it. One service serves one class, and the service name is the class name without the namespace Replica, container A replica is one runner of a service, and deploy.replicas says how many. Swarm runs each replica as a task, which is one container at a time. When a job ends, the container ends, and Swarm creates a new task and container for the same slot Node A host in the Swarm, a manager or a worker. Node labels and service constraints decide where a replica may run Single-task mode, continuous mode The two modes of machine runner 3. Single-task runs one job and exits, which gives a clean environment. Continuous keeps the runner up for many jobs. Refer to Single-task and continuous mode Persistent class A class that runs in continuous mode with a named volume, so jobs share state. It gives up the clean environment Default class, hardened class The Linux default classes (linux-default, and linux-java of classes-extra.yaml) keep passwordless sudo for jobs. The hardened class (linux-hardened of classes-extra.yaml) steps every job down with setpriv --no-new-privs, so sudo cannot raise the job user. Refer to Users and the runner token on Linux Token secret The Swarm secret -token. It is a runner config file that holds the token of the resource class. The token proxy mounts it, or, in a persistent class, the runner does Token proxy The service token-proxy of runners.yaml: it holds the class tokens of the Linux single-task classes and adds the token of a class to the claims of that class’s runners. Refer to The token proxy Placeholder secret The Swarm secret runner-placeholder-token: a runner config with a made-up token, which every proxied runner reads instead of a real token Entrypoint On Linux, the script circleci-runner-entrypoint, which a Swarm config delivers. It checks the runner, prepares the users, and then starts the runner. On Windows there is none: the runner is the main process Runner distributor On Linux, the global service runner-distributor; on Windows, runner-distributor-windows (it installs portable Git too). On every node it downloads, verifies, and installs the runner into runner-bin, moves current, and looks again every MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_CHECK_INTERVAL. Refer to The runner distributor on Linux runner-bin The named volume, one on every Linux node, that holds the runner versions. The distributor writes it, and the runner services mount it read-only at /opt/machine-runner-swarm current The link in runner-bin that points to the active versions/. A container resolves it once, when it starts. As a value of MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_VERSION, current is one of the floating values (with 3.1 and 3): it makes the distributor follow CircleCI’s current release Record The file versions//SHA256, which holds the SHA-256 of the binary in the format of sha256sum -c. The distributor writes it when it installs a version, and the entrypoint checks the binary against it at every container start Setup helper The optional scripts linux/setup.sh and windows\Setup.ps1, which run steps of the install pages with checks. On Linux the helper checks the node, starts Swarm, creates secrets, and deploys. It installs nothing, because the distributor installs the runner Stock image, custom image A stock image is a publisher’s image as it is, for example cimg/base or Windows Server Core. The stack mounts the runner into it, on Linux from the volume runner-bin and on Windows from the host. A custom image is one you derive from it, for example to add tools. Refer to Images Drain The word has two meanings. A runner drain happens when the runner gets SIGTERM: it takes no new job and finishes the running one. A node drain is docker node update --availability drain: Swarm stops the tasks of that node, which starts a runner drain in each, and starts replacements on other nodes. This documentation always says which one
data.job-lifecycle#Job lifecycle:
Swarm never reuses a container. Every exit, whether a finished job, an idle timeout, or a crash, leads to a new task and a new container because the restart policy is condition: any.
sequenceDiagram participant S as Swarm participant C as Container participant A as runner.circleci.com participant N as New container S->>C: start a task from the image C->>A: poll for a job (single-task mode) A-->>C: claim one job C->>C: run the job in a clean container C-->>S: runner exits, container stops Note over S: restart_policy any, delay 10s S->>N: create a NEW task and container N->>A: poll for the next jobThe steps in order:
Swarm starts a container from the service image. On Linux the entrypoint checks the runner, sets up the users, and starts the runner. On Windows the runner is the main process. The runner downloads its task agent, polls CircleCI, and claims one job. The runner steps the job down to the job user on Linux, runs it, and exits when the job ends. Swarm sees the exit, waits for the restart delay of 10 seconds, and starts a new container. Three timing facts follow from this design:
A replica needs about 10 seconds plus container start-up before it can claim the next job. The other replicas of the class keep claiming jobs in the meantime. Every new container downloads the task agent from circleci-binary-releases.s3.amazonaws.com. Allow this host in your egress rules. A single-task runner that finds no job exits after CIRCLECI_RUNNER_IDLE_TIMEOUT, which is 1h in the stack files. Swarm replaces it, so idle replicas pick up a rotated secret or a new image within an hour. Stopping a service sends SIGTERM to the runner. The runner drains (a runner drain), which means it accepts no new job and lets the running job finish. The stack sets stop_grace_period: 5h5m, which is the runner max_run_time of 5 hours plus 5 minutes.
On Windows, stop_grace_period does not hold a busy container: a stop from outside kills its job after about 5 seconds. A finished job ends its container by itself, so only an update, a scale-down, or a node drain is affected. Change a Windows service while its class is idle. Refer to Stop a busy Windows container.
data.placement#Placement: Services carry constraints and nodes advertise capabilities. The built-in properties are node.platform.os and node.platform.arch. This repository adds the node labels machine-runner-swarm.zone, machine-runner-swarm.docker-build, machine-runner-swarm.microvm, machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2022, machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2025, and machine-runner-swarm.class.. Refer to Multi-Node Clusters.
data.replicas-set-the-concurrency#Replicas se: deploy.replicas is the number of runners in the class, and so the number of jobs the class runs at the same time. A replica that cannot fit on any node stays in the Pending state until capacity is free. Refer to Resource Classes for sizing and for choosing the count.
data.services-are-resource-classes#Services a:
Each Swarm service is one CircleCI resource class. The service name is the short name of the class, so the service linux-default serves the resource class /linux-default. A job selects the class in its config:
jobs: build: machine: true resource_class: /linux-default Each service also has one Swarm secret named -token. The secret holds the token of that class. The single-task classes do not mount it in their runners: the token proxy holds it and adds it to the claims of the runners of that class, so a runner can only claim jobs for its own class. A runner holds a made-up placeholder. A persistent class mounts its token in the runner container itself.
flowchart TB nodes["Nodes: Linux amd64, Linux arm64, WindowsLabels decide where tasks may run"] subgraph services["Swarm services: one for each resource class"] direction LR s1["linux-defaultreplicas: 2"] s2["linux-pythonreplicas: 1"] s3["windows-defaultreplicas: 2"] end r1["container 1"] r2["container 2"] r3["container 1"] r4["container 1"] r5["container 2"] api["runner.circleci.comRunners connect outbound over HTTPS 443 only"] nodes --> services s1 --> r1 & r2 s2 --> r3 s3 --> r4 & r5 r1 & r2 & r3 & r4 & r5 --> apiThe runner containers poll CircleCI for work. Nothing connects to a runner, so the stack publishes no ports.
data.single-task-and-continuous-mode#Single-t:
Machine runner 3 has two modes. The stack files set the mode with the CIRCLECI_RUNNER_MODE environment variable.
Mode Value Behavior Environment Single-task single-task (default in every stack file) The runner claims one job, runs it, and exits. Swarm starts a new container for the next job. Clean for every job Continuous continuous (persistent classes only) The runner stays up and claims job after job in the same container. Shared by all jobs on that runner Use continuous mode only for trusted projects that need warm caches. The optional persistent classes are the only services that use it. Refer to Persistent mode.
data.the-runner-distributor-on-linux#The runn:
The Linux services use stock images such as cimg/base, and the image holds none of the runner. The service runner-distributor puts the runner on every Linux node that runs the classes of runners.yaml, so nothing is installed on a node by hand. docker stack deploy is the whole install, and it is the only upgrade path.
The service. runner-distributor is a global service, so it runs on every Linux node, on a Docker-build node too, and on a node that joins later, except a microVM node (machine-runner-swarm.microvm=true): the microVM classes download their own runner into each VM (MicroVM jobs). It runs the stock alpine:3 image, pinned by digest. Its script, linux/stack/runner-distributor.sh, is a Swarm config. The volume. The distributor writes to runner-bin, a named volume that exists once on every node. Each version has a directory versions/ with bin/circleci-runner, SHA256, VERSION, and TARBALL. The link current points to the active version and moves with one atomic rename. The file history lists the versions in the order they were active. The runner services. Every class mounts runner-bin read-only at /opt/machine-runner-swarm. The entrypoint is another Swarm config, mounted at /circleci-runner-entrypoint with the mode 0555, and it starts as root. A job cannot change either of them. Not the token proxy. The distributor installs the runner only. The token proxy is an image that Swarm pulls: refer to The token proxy. The wait. The entrypoint waits up to MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_WAIT seconds (default 120) until current exists, so a first deploy and a new node need no order. Then it resolves current once, when the container starts, and checks the binary against its record. Without a runner, or with a binary that differs, it exits with code 80, and Swarm tries again after the restart delay. Because a container resolves current once, a running job and its container keep their version. The next container, which is the next job, gets the new one. A persistent class runs one container for all jobs, so it picks up a new version when its container restarts. Refer to Recycle a class.
The runner services carry no version and no hash. Which version the nodes run is a setting of the distributor service only, so an upgrade, a pin, and a rollback change that one service, and the runner services never restart. An idle replica keeps the old binary until it recycles, which takes at most the idle timeout of 1 hour.
Setting Behavior MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_VERSION=3.1.13 (an exact version, the default: the newest that CI tests) The distributor pins that version, and checks the tarball against the SHA-256 values that the stack file carries for it, not against the manifest. It never changes by itself, it makes no request once the version is installed, and it switches to an installed version without any network, so a rollback needs no download. A release of this repository bumps the version and its SHA-256 values together MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_VERSION=3.1 or 3 A floating line: the newest 3.1.x, or the newest 3.x.y, of CircleCI’s manifest. The distributor looks again every 24 hours, ignores the default SHA-256 list of the pin, and trusts the hash of the manifest, which is weaker MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_VERSION=current A floating value: CircleCI’s current release, within major version 3. It looks again every 24 hours, ignores the default list, and trusts the hash of the manifest Like machine runner 3 and container runner, the runner version is chosen by the operator: an exact pin by default, a floating value on request. Refer to The version policy for the rules, and to how this compares with machine runner 3, container runner and the orchestrator.
The distributor verifies every download against a SHA-256 and records the SHA-256 of the binary next to it. Refer to Upgrade the runner on Linux for the settings and to Runner binary integrity on Linux for the checks.
data.the-runner-distributor-on-windows#The ru:
The Windows services use the stock Server Core image, and the image holds none of the runner and none of Git. The service runner-distributor-windows does what the Linux distributor does, with the same settings, the same version policy and the same rule that a runner service carries no version: docker stack deploy is the whole install, and the only upgrade path.
The service. A global service on the nodes with the label machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2022, from the stock servercore:ltsc2022 image with process isolation. Its PowerShell script, windows\stack\runner-distributor.ps1, is a Swarm config. The volume and the links. It writes to runner-bin: versions\ for the runner (with SHA256, TARBALL and VERSION), git\ for portable Git, and two relative directory symbolic links, current and git\current. Every class mounts the volume read-only twice, with volume.subpath: current at C:\machine-runner-swarm, and git\current at C:\Program Files\Git, where the task agent expects tar.exe. No entrypoint. circleci-runner.exe is the main process. A runner task that starts before the first flip fails and starts again after the restart delay, so a new node needs no order, and nothing checks the binary when a container starts. Refer to Runner binary integrity on Windows. Not the token proxy. It installs the runner and Git only. The service token-proxy-windows runs the Windows image of the token proxy, which Swarm pulls: refer to The token proxy. Locked files. Windows cannot replace or delete files that a running container uses. The distributor installs a version next to the others, flips the link, and removes an old version only when no container uses it. A running job keeps its version, and the runner services never restart, so no busy job is killed by an upgrade. Refer to Upgrade the runner on Windows for the settings.
data.the-token-proxy#The token proxy:
The service token-proxy of the Linux runners.yaml (on Windows token-proxy-windows of the Windows runners.yaml, which works the same way, with the differences in Windows: Windows has no NET_RAW drop, and nothing there is tested for a forged source address) keeps the class tokens away from the runners and their jobs. A runner sends its API calls to the proxy (CIRCLECI_RUNNER_API_URL: http://token-proxy:8080) and holds only a made-up placeholder token. The proxy adds the class token to one call, the task claim, and passes every other call on to CircleCI. The runner and its task agent use the task token from the claim response for the rest.
flowchart LR subgraph cls["Class overlay networks"] r1["linux-default runnersplaceholder token"] r2["linux-python runnersplaceholder token"] end p["token-proxyone replicaholds every class token"] api["runner.circleci.com"] r1 -- "claim, task calls" --> p r2 -- "claim, task calls" --> p p -- "HTTPS: the class token on the claim only" --> apiThe proxy decides who may claim from the network and not from what a runner says. It allows a claim only from an address that Swarm DNS lists now for tasks. of a class, once for each container, and gives it the token of that class. A container that is not a runner, or a runner that claims a second time, gets 403. A claim whose outcome is unknown (the request reached CircleCI and the answer was lost) counts as a claim, so the proxy fails closed. For this the proxy is attached to the overlay network of every class, runs with endpoint_mode: dnsrr so that it sees the real source address, and the runners drop NET_RAW so that they cannot forge one. Refer to The token proxy for what it protects and what it does not, and to Monitor the token proxy for what happens when it is down.
What this changes for you:
Secrets. You create the class secrets -token as before, and one more secret, runner-placeholder-token, with a made-up token. Only the proxy mounts the class secrets. Every runner mounts the placeholder. Classes. A new single-task class needs two lines in the proxy: its network (Linux) and its secret -token, which the proxy takes as a class named . Refer to Resource classes. The persistent classes do not use the proxy. The image. The proxy is a static Go binary in a published container image, ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy on Docker Hub (ccilabs is the Docker Hub organization of CircleCI Labs, and the signature is the trust root, not the name), on a minimal base: no shell, uid 65534 on Linux, a read-only root file system. One tag covers Linux amd64, arm64, ppc64le and s390x, and Windows Server 2022 and 2025 (amd64). The service token-proxy pulls it by itself, so no distributor installs it. A release bundle names the image of its release by tag and digest, and a checkout names latest, which only a release moves. Every digest is signed. Refer to The token proxy image and Verify the token proxy image. The state. The proxy keeps the addresses of the runners that have claimed in the small volume proxy-state, on the node that it runs on: a manager by default. A restart on that node refuses only the runners that claimed, and a runner that started before the proxy is never locked out. If the proxy moves to another node, the state stays behind: refer to Where the proxy runs, and when it moves. In a cluster, label the node that runs the proxy machine-runner-swarm.proxy=true: runner services never run on a node with that label, so jobs do not share a node with the proxy. On a single node, set no label. With several managers, the label and a placement variable pin the proxy to one.
data.users-and-the-runner-token-on-linux#User:
Inside each Linux container, two accounts exist:
The runner user circleci-runner (uid 2000) runs circleci-runner and owns the token file. It has no sudo rights and cannot write to /opt/machine-runner-swarm. The job user runs every job step. It is circleci in the cimg images, or the account you name with MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_USER. The runner steps each job down to the job user with command_prefix: sudo -niHu -- in the default class, or setpriv when the image has no sudo, and always setpriv --no-new-privs in the hardened class. The token is never in the job environment, and the config file that the runner reads is readable only by the runner user and root. In the single-task classes, that file holds the placeholder: the class token is in the token proxy, not in the container.
What happens next depends on one setting, MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO.
Class type Setting Jobs have sudo Can a job read the class token Default (linux-default, and linux-java of classes-extra.yaml) MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO: "true" Yes, passwordless, as in the Docker executor No, the container holds a placeholder. Only a job that escapes the container onto the node of the proxy can Hardened (linux-hardened of classes-extra.yaml) MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO: "false" No No, for the same reason Persistent (linux-persistent, no proxy) MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO: "false" (the shipped file; "true" is the opt-in) No (with "true": yes) No, as in the hardened class. With "true", yes if the job uses sudo. Refer to The persistent class The default class. Jobs keep the passwordless sudo that many orgs and orbs expect, for example sudo apt-get install. A job that uses sudo is root in its container: it can read the placeholder and the files of the runner, and become the runner user. It finds no class token. The test linux/tests/token.sh measures what the user of a job can read in the runner’s config file, and linux/tests/proxy.sh scans the containers as root and finds no class token.
The hardened class. The entrypoint steps every job down with util-linux setpriv --no-new-privs, even when the image has sudo, and edits no file of the image. Swarm ignores no-new-privileges, so setuid binaries such as sudo and su stay in the image, and the class keeps SETUID and SETGID for the step-down. The kernel flag that setpriv sets is inherited by the job and everything it starts and cannot be cleared, and it makes them ignore the setuid bit. The sudo of the image, with its rules intact, therefore cannot lift a job to root, and neither can any other setuid binary, even through a local-root bug. The job user then has no way to become root or the runner user, so the files and processes of the runner are out of reach of jobs. The container refuses to start if the image has no util-linux setpriv (exit code 80). The trade-off is that jobs cannot install system packages at run time, and that nothing in a job can gain privileges through setuid or file capabilities, for example ping or mount, so you build the tools into the image. CircleCI also recommends pre-installing dependencies as the most secure option. A kernel or container-runtime bug can still lift a job to root, because the containers share the host kernel.
Choose the hardened class for shared or regulated work. Choose the default class for a single trusted team that needs sudo. A stolen token lets its holder run a runner on that class and claim jobs, which exposes the code and secrets of those jobs, so the proxy matters more than the sudo setting. Refer to Security.
data.users-and-the-runner-token-on-windows#Us:
Windows containers have no step-down. The runner and the jobs run as ContainerAdministrator, because the runner needs the symbolic link privilege of that account to install the task agent. A job can therefore read the config file of its runner. In a single-task class that file holds only the placeholder, and the class token is in the service token-proxy-windows. In the persistent class it holds the real token. The token is not in the job environment. A hostile job on the same host as the proxy can still reach the token, because process isolation is not a security boundary: refer to Windows.
Treat each Windows resource class as a trust boundary: use one token for each class, restrict who can use the class, and rotate tokens. The Linux variables MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO and MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_USER do not exist on Windows, and Windows ignores them. Refer to Token model on each OS.
data.what-a-clean-environment-covers#What a c:
A clean environment means that a job starts in a container created from the image, with nothing left by an earlier job.
Covered Not covered Files and installed packages anywhere in the container filesystem Anything on a mounted volume: persistent classes keep a named volume by design The home directory, /tmp, and the working directory The Docker engine of the node when a class mounts its socket or named pipe: images, containers, and build cache persist Processes, environment variables, and shell history State outside the node, such as databases, registries, and shared storage Users, groups, and sudo rules created by an earlier job The kernel: all containers on a node share it On Windows, the registry, the user profile, %TEMP%, and C:\ProgramData Data of finished containers that Swarm has not yet pruned from the node disk The runner is mounted read-only, so a job cannot change what the next job runs. On Linux it comes from the per-node volume runner-bin, which a service of the stack fills. Refer to The runner distributor on Linux. On Windows it comes from the same volume, filled by the service runner-distributor-windows, through two links that Docker resolves when it creates a container. Refer to The runner distributor on Windows. A new runner version is a new directory and a moved link, so the next job runs the new version, and a job that runs now finishes on the old one. Refer to Upgrade the runner.
The working directory needs no cleanup in a single-task class, because the container is discarded. On Linux, the runner does not clean it at all. The runner user cannot remove files that the job user owns, so the stack sets CIRCLECI_RUNNER_CLEANUP_WORK_DIR to "false". Refer to Working directory cleanup.
Containers are not a virtual machine boundary. Read Security before you run untrusted code.
data.what-the-linux-entrypoint-does#What the:
The entrypoint circleci-runner-entrypoint starts as root, prepares the container, and then runs the runner as the runner user. It never reads the token or the placeholder. In order, it:
Waits for the runner distributor of the node, resolves the link current once, and checks the runner binary against its SHA-256 record. Then it checks that the runner and every directory above it, up to /opt/machine-runner-swarm, are owned by root and not writable by the group or others. Refer to The runner distributor on Linux. Looks for the tools it needs. sudo or util-linux setpriv steps jobs down, and setpriv or su starts the runner. With MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO=false, util-linux setpriv with --no-new-privs is required, whether or not the image has sudo. Without the tools it exits with code 80. Refer to What an image needs. Creates the users with useradd or adduser: circleci-runner with uid and gid 2000, and the job user when the image has none. It does not edit /etc/passwd by hand, because sudo refuses a user that has no passwd and no shadow entry. Sets CIRCLECI_RUNNER_COMMAND_PREFIX. A value in the service environment does not override it. With sudo, the prefix is ["sudo","-niHu","","--"]. The file /etc/sudoers.d/90-circleci-runner lets uid 2000 run commands as the job user only, keeps the PATH of the image, and keeps the environment variables of the image. Without sudo, or with MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO=false, the prefix is a setpriv command that gives the job no capabilities. In the hardened class it also carries --no-new-privs. It runs the job through env -u for every CIRCLECI_RUNNER_* and MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_* variable of the container (the runner name stays), so the settings of the runner and the stack do not reach the job, as with the reset environment of sudo. The runner holds CAP_SETUID and CAP_SETGID as ambient capabilities only to call it. Creates the directories: the task agent directory, owned by uid 2000, and the working directory with its parent /var/opt/circleci, owned by the job user. Adds the job user to the group of /var/run/docker.sock when the class mounts the socket and the group is not root. Refer to Docker Builds. Runs the runner with exec as uid 2000. The init process of the container (init: true) passes SIGTERM to it, which starts the runner drain. The entrypoint does not validate the runner name, the token, the mode, or the timeouts, and it has no guard against the reuse of a container. The runner checks its own settings and exits with code 80 for a bad one, and Swarm never reuses a container.
With sudo, a job gets the environment variables of the image, such as PATH, JAVA_HOME, and LANG, the variables you set in the service, such as a proxy, and CIRCLECI_RUNNER_NAME. It gets nothing else from the runner. The runner runs a few commands of its own, such as circleci-agent version, without the step-down, as the runner user.
data.why-swarm-and-not-plain-compose#Why Swar: A plain docker compose up restarts the same container, so the environment is not clean. Swarm creates a new container for every task. The FAQ lists the trade-offs.

data:
This page takes you from nothing to a first job on Linux with the shipped stack file and the setup helper, from a signed release. It sets up one class, linux-default. Nothing is installed on a node by hand: the stack has a service that installs the runner on every node. The page explains little. Install on Linux with Docker Swarm has every step by hand with the reasons, and Concepts explains the model.
Note This is a CircleCI Labs project. CircleCI support does not cover it. It is a 0.x release: a minor release can change your stack files, so read the release notes before you upgrade. It is tested against CircleCI cloud only. What is tested says how, and Security says what a job on a runner can reach.
Availability. One token proxy runs on a manager, and every runner API call goes through it. While the proxy or its manager is down, no new job starts, and Swarm restarts the proxy. Use three managers for a production cluster. This is not an autoscaling or high-availability product: the replicas are fixed, and the nodes are yours.
data.before-you-start#Before you start: A node with Ubuntu LTS, Docker Engine 24 or later, a clock on NTP, and outbound HTTPS. CI tests Ubuntu 26.04 on amd64 with real jobs, and the start of the stack on arm64, with probe jobs on a real arm64 runner on main. RHEL 8 or later is documented and not tested. ppc64le and s390x start under emulation only, and no job runs there. Prepare each node shows how to install Docker. Prerequisites has the details, and Sizing the CPU and memory. Outbound HTTPS from the node to runner.circleci.com, circleci-binary-releases.s3.amazonaws.com, circleci-tasks-prod.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com, your VCS host, github.com (the release download), and the registries for the images (Docker Hub). Egress hosts says what each is for, and What needs internet lists everything. A node without internet access does not work in this release. An organization admin who accepted the CircleCI Runner Terms, in the web app or by using the CLI for self-hosted runners, as CircleCI documents. The CircleCI CLI 1.4.0 or later on your workstation or on the node. Step 1 signs it in. cosign 3.1.3 or a later 3.x (CI signs and verifies with 3.1.3, and earlier versions are not tested), and jq and curl, on the node, to verify the release. A bash shell. Run the commands on the node with sudo, or as a user in the docker group. The docker group is equivalent to root, so limit it. Replace with your runner namespace, and with your organization slug such as gh/my-org, or its UUID.
data.next#Next: Install on Linux with Docker Swarm: the same steps by hand, RHEL, and the release verification. Resource Classes: add classes, and change sizes and replica counts. linux-java and linux-hardened are in linux/stack/classes-extra.yaml; deploy that file with an extra -c together with runners.yaml. A class is a service, its token secret -token and its network, and the secret and the network are also listed on token-proxy, which finds its classes in its secrets: there is no variable to set. Security: choose between the default and the hardened class before you give a class to a team, and read what a job on a cloud node can reach. Operations: pin or roll back the runner version, rotate tokens, and run the cluster.
data.sizing-and-pending-replicas#Sizing and P:
The shipped file reserves 4 CPUs and 8 GB of memory for the runners: two replicas of linux-default (2 CPUs, 4 GB each). The token proxy and the distributor reserve little. A replica needs its whole reservation free on one node. Leave about 1 CPU and 2 GB for the operating system and Docker. Size the limits has a table of every shipped class, with the CPU and memory of a replica, the default replicas, and what else it needs.
The cost of the project is your own hardware, plus the runner concurrency of your CircleCI plan: the replicas of all classes and the jobs that wait share the concurrency limit of your organization. Disk is not limited per container. Each finished job leaves a stopped container until Swarm prunes its task (the setup in step 4 keeps the last 2 for each slot), and the images take space too. This repository has no measurement of the disk that a job needs, so watch a node during a trial.
A replica that does not fit stays Pending. That is not an error: Swarm waits for room, the other replicas work, and docker service ps --no-trunc runners_ shows insufficient resources on 1 node. To fit a small node, lower deploy.replicas in your copy and deploy it again with the same command. The smallest useful test is replicas: 1 for linux-default, which needs 2 CPUs and 4 GB. Refer to A task stays pending for the other causes.
data.steps#Steps:
Sign in, and check that your organization has a namespace. Each organization has one namespace, which orbs and runners share, and only CircleCI support can change it. If your organization publishes orbs, it has one. circleci namespace get looks up a name that you know. If your organization has none, create it.
circleci auth login circleci namespace create --org # only when the organization has no namespace yet Create a resource class and a token for it. The command prints the token once, so keep it for step 5. Without --org, the CLI takes the organization of the git remote of the current directory.
circleci runner resource-class create /linux-default --org --generate-token On the node, download a release, verify it, and unpack it. A release is the install path: its stack file names the token proxy image of that release by tag and digest, and the CircleCI job that made it signed the checksums with a keyless cosign signature. A git clone of a branch or a tag gets the stack files with the default image latest, which is not pinned. The token proxy image is ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy: ccilabs is the Docker Hub organization of CircleCI Labs, and the signature check, not the name, is the trust root (Verify the token proxy image).
Set version once, to the number of the latest release without the v, and read its notes. The line below is a placeholder: with it unchanged, the download fails and nothing runs.
version=X.Y.Z Then paste this block. It runs in a subshell with set -euo pipefail, so the first failing check ends it. The three checks are the signature, the ref in the certificate, and the checksum, and only a bundle that passes all three is unpacked.
( set -euo pipefail base="https://github.com/CircleCI-Labs/scalable-machine-runner/releases/download/v${version}" curl -fsSLO "${base}/machine-runner-swarm-${version}.tar.gz" -O "${base}/SHA256SUMS" -O "${base}/SHA256SUMS.sigstore.json" # 1. the signature: the CircleCI project and pipeline definition of this repository signed SHA256SUMS cosign verify-blob SHA256SUMS --bundle SHA256SUMS.sigstore.json \ --certificate-identity "https://circleci.com/api/v2/projects/7bbdbb66-6ba8-4f6c-982e-d4fb401ec257/pipeline-definitions/8b2a66db-3f28-5c80-88e4-03f4694b5b60" \ --certificate-oidc-issuer "https://oidc.circleci.com" # 2. the ref: a job of any branch can sign with that identity, so the certificate must also say that the job ran for refs/heads/main # (the long string is the OID 1.3.6.1.4.1.57264.1.14 followed by the value refs/heads/main) hex=$(jq -r '.verificationMaterial | (.certificate // .x509CertificateChain.certificates[0]).rawBytes' SHA256SUMS.sigstore.json | base64 -d \ | od -An -v -tx1 | tr -d ' \n') grep -Eq '^([0-9a-f]{2})*2b0601040183bf30010e0411(0c|13)0f726566732f68656164732f6d61696e' <<< "${hex}" \ && echo "signed for refs/heads/main" || { echo "NOT signed for refs/heads/main: stop"; exit 1; } # 3. the file: its checksum is in the signed list sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS --ignore-missing # only a verified bundle is unpacked tar -xzf "machine-runner-swarm-${version}.tar.gz" echo "RELEASE VERIFIED" ) Continue only when the last line is RELEASE VERIFIED. Anything else, an error message or no output at all, means that the release is not verified: delete the downloaded files and start again, or ask in an issue. The ref check exists because the signing identity is the same for every branch, so the block looks in the certificate for the extension 1.3.6.1.4.1.57264.1.14 (the OID in the long string) with the value refs/heads/main, and fails when a job of another branch signed the file. Verify a release explains the identity and what a valid signature does not prove, and How the signature works explains the ref check.
Change into the unpacked bundle. The paths below are relative to it.
cd "machine-runner-swarm-${version}" Check the node and create the Swarm. Choose one of two forks. A Swarm that listens on the loopback address cannot accept other nodes, so a trial cannot grow into a cluster without a new swarm init and new secrets. Decide now.
Trial, one node. The Swarm listens on the loopback address, so nothing is exposed and no other node can join. The runners and the token proxy share the node, so a job that escaped its container could read the class tokens: use it for a trial.
sudo linux/setup.sh --check --swarm-init Cluster. Check every node, create the Swarm on the first one with an address that the others can reach, join the rest, and label the manager that runs the token proxy. Open the inter-node ports first. The shipped Linux class overlays are encrypted, so a multi-node cluster also needs IP protocol 50 (ESP) between nodes (Encrypted class networks). A first cluster of one manager and two workers is enough to try it. A node needs nothing else: the stack installs the runner on each node that joins.
sudo linux/setup.sh --check # on every node sudo docker swarm init --advertise-addr # on the manager sudo docker swarm update --task-history-limit 2 # on the manager sudo docker swarm join-token worker # prints the join command: run it on each worker sudo docker node ls # on the manager: every node is Ready sudo docker node update --label-add machine-runner-swarm.proxy=true # on the manager The label marks the node that runs the proxy, which holds every class token. Runner services never run on a node with this label, so jobs do not share a node with the tokens. With no worker, the runner replicas stay Pending. With one manager, the proxy runs there by default. With several managers, pin the proxy to the labelled one when you deploy in step 6: Where the proxy runs, and when it moves shows the variable. Keep one manager that you do not drain, because the proxy needs it.
Run steps 5 to 7 on the manager. Refer to Multi-Node Clusters for labels, zones, quorum, and encrypted overlays.
Create the Swarm secret for the token. The helper asks for it with hidden input and never prints it. The token goes to the token proxy only. Then create the placeholder that the runners read instead of a token: any value works.
sudo linux/setup.sh --secret linux-default printf %s machine-runner-swarm-placeholder | sudo linux/setup.sh --secret runner-placeholder Copy the stack directory, and deploy your copy. For a first run, change nothing in it. You review it later, and from here on you deploy your copy and never the shipped files. The directory holds the stack files and the two scripts that they ship as Swarm configs, which the stack files name next to themselves. A new release changes the shipped files, so an upgrade is a merge of your copy with the new files: Upgrade shows how.
cp -r linux/stack deploy sudo linux/setup.sh --deploy --stack-file deploy/runners.yaml This is the whole install. The service runner-distributor starts on every Linux node (a node that you label for the microVM add-on is the exception: it has its own copy), downloads the runner of CircleCI, checks its SHA-256, and makes it available to the runner services. A runner container that starts first waits up to 2 minutes for it. In a release bundle, the token proxy image is pinned by digest. The helper warns when MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_IMAGE is not pinned by digest.
Check that the runners are up and connected. docker stack deploy does not wait, so the replicas need a minute to start.
sudo docker stack services runners sudo docker service logs --tail 20 runners_runner-distributor sudo docker service logs --tail 20 runners_linux-default circleci runner instance list --org --resource-class /linux-default The runners are healthy when REPLICAS shows 2/2 for runners_linux-default (or fewer for Pending replicas) and 1/1 for runners_token-proxy, the distributor shows one task for each node and logs a line such as [ ok ] current -> versions/3.1.13, the log of the runners has no 401 or error lines, and the CLI lists an instance with the status online. The same list is in the web app under Runners.
Run a job. Save the following as .circleci/config.yml in a project of your organization, replace my-namespace, commit, and push. The same file is examples/linux-hello.yml.
version: 2.1 jobs: hello: machine: true resource_class: my-namespace/linux-default steps: - run: name: Show where this job runs command: | echo "runner: $CIRCLECI_RUNNER_NAME" echo "user: $(id -un)" if [ -e /tmp/hello-marker ]; then echo "the container was reused"; exit 1; fi touch /tmp/hello-marker echo "clean container: no marker from an earlier job" workflows: hello: jobs: - hello Run the workflow twice. Both runs pass, because Swarm starts a new container for each job.
data.what-you-did-not-do#What you did not do: The helper checks the node, starts Swarm, creates the secrets, and deploys the stack. It does not install Docker, create classes or tokens, edit the stack file, label or join nodes, or build images. It does not install the runner either: the runner-distributor service of the stack does that on every Linux node. Optional: use the setup helper lists each step.

data:
This page takes you from nothing to a first job on one Windows Server node with the shipped stack file and the setup helper, from a signed release. It explains little. Install on Windows Server with Docker Swarm has every step by hand with the reasons, and Concepts explains the model. Nothing is built and nothing is installed on the host: the service uses the stock Server Core image, and the distributor service of the stack installs the runner and Git.
Note This is a CircleCI Labs project. CircleCI support does not cover it. It is a 0.x release: a minor release can change your stack files, so read the release notes before you upgrade. It is tested against CircleCI cloud only. What is tested says how, and Security says what a job on a runner can reach.
Availability. One token proxy (token-proxy-windows) runs on a manager, and every runner API call goes through it. While the proxy or its manager is down, no new job starts, and Swarm restarts the proxy. This page sets up one host, which runs the proxy and the jobs together: use it for a trial. This is not an autoscaling or high-availability product: the replicas are fixed, and the nodes are yours.
data.before-you-start#Before you start: A Windows Server 2022 or 2025 host that is not a domain controller, amd64, with a clock on NTP and outbound HTTPS. CI tests both versions with real jobs. Windows Server 2019 is not tested. Docker Engine and CLI 28.0 or later in Windows-container mode (the stack files mount a subpath of a volume; .\windows\Setup.ps1 checks the version), and the Windows Containers feature, which needs a reboot. The Install-DockerCE script in the helpful_tools directory of the Microsoft Windows Containers repository installs both (Prerequisites has the details). The first pull of the servercore base image is about 2.2 GB and takes minutes to tens of minutes, depending on the network (about 10 minutes on the CI machines). Refer to Sizing for the CPU and memory. Outbound HTTPS from the host to runner.circleci.com, circleci-binary-releases.s3.amazonaws.com, circleci-tasks-prod.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com, your VCS host, github.com and release-assets.githubusercontent.com (the release, Git, and 7-Zip), mcr.microsoft.com, and Docker Hub. Egress hosts says what each is for, and What needs internet lists everything. A host without internet access does not work in this release. An organization admin who accepted the CircleCI Runner Terms, in the web app or by using the CLI for self-hosted runners, as CircleCI documents. The CircleCI CLI 1.4.0 or later. It can run on your workstation. Step 1 signs it in. cosign 3.1.3 or a later 3.x on the host, to verify the release (CI signs and verifies with 3.1.3, and earlier versions are not tested). Install cosign shows how. An elevated Windows PowerShell 5.1 session on the host for the steps that start with docker or .\windows. Replace with your runner namespace, and with your organization slug such as gh/my-org, or its UUID.
data.next#Next: Install on Windows Server with Docker Swarm: the same steps by hand, with the release verification. Images: add your own tools on top of Server Core. Security: the token model and BitLocker. Operations: upgrade, rotate tokens, and run the cluster.
data.sizing-and-pending-replicas#Sizing and P:
The shipped file runs two replicas of windows-default, and each reserves 2 CPUs and 4 GB of memory, so the service needs 4 CPUs and 8 GB. The distributor and the token proxy set limits and reserve nothing (1 CPU and 1 GB, and 1 CPU and 512 MB), so leave room for them and for the operating system. The Windows engine rejects a CPU limit above the CPU count of the host. A replica needs its whole reservation free on one node. Size the limits has a table of every shipped class. The cost of the project is your own hardware, plus the runner concurrency of your CircleCI plan, and the disk is not measured here: the base image alone is about 2.2 GB, and every finished container keeps its layer until Swarm prunes it.
A replica that does not fit, or that no node is allowed to run, stays Pending. That is not an error: Swarm waits, and the other replica works. docker service ps --no-trunc runners_windows-default shows the reason, such as insufficient resources or scheduling constraints not satisfied. For a small host, lower deploy.replicas in your copy and deploy it again. Refer to A task stays pending for the other causes.
data.steps#Steps:
Sign in, and check that your organization has a namespace. Each organization has one namespace, which orbs and runners share, and only CircleCI support can change it. If your organization publishes orbs, it has one. circleci namespace get looks up a name that you know. If your organization has none, create it.
circleci auth login circleci namespace create <namespace> --org <org> # only when the organization has no namespace yet Create the resource class and its token. The command prints the token once, so keep it for step 6.
circleci runner resource-class create <namespace>/windows-default --org <org> --generate-token On the host, download a release, verify it, and unpack it. A release is the install path: its stack file names the token proxy image of that release by tag and digest, and the CircleCI job that made it signed the checksums with a keyless cosign signature. A git clone of a branch or a tag gets the stack files with the default image latest, which is not pinned. The token proxy image is ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy: ccilabs is the Docker Hub organization of CircleCI Labs, and the signature check, not the name, is the trust root (Verify the token proxy image).
Set $version once, to the number of the latest release without the v, and read its notes. The first line is a placeholder: with it unchanged, the download fails and nothing runs.
$version = 'X.Y.Z' $base = "https://github.com/CircleCI-Labs/scalable-machine-runner/releases/download/v$version" $zip = "machine-runner-swarm-$version.zip" Then paste this block. It stops at the first failing check, and only a bundle that passes all three checks (the signature, the ref in the certificate, and the checksum) is unpacked.
& { $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop' foreach ($f in $zip, 'SHA256SUMS', 'SHA256SUMS.sigstore.json') { Invoke-WebRequest -UseBasicParsing -Uri "$base/$f" -OutFile $f } # 1. the signature: the CircleCI project and pipeline definition of this repository signed SHA256SUMS cosign verify-blob SHA256SUMS --bundle SHA256SUMS.sigstore.json ` --certificate-identity 'https://circleci.com/api/v2/projects/7bbdbb66-6ba8-4f6c-982e-d4fb401ec257/pipeline-definitions/8b2a66db-3f28-5c80-88e4-03f4694b5b60' ` --certificate-oidc-issuer 'https://oidc.circleci.com' if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'the signature does not verify: stop' } # 2. the ref: a job of any branch can sign with that identity, so the certificate must also say that the job ran for refs/heads/main # (the long string is the OID 1.3.6.1.4.1.57264.1.14 followed by the value refs/heads/main) $material = (Get-Content -Raw -LiteralPath SHA256SUMS.sigstore.json | ConvertFrom-Json).verificationMaterial if ($material.certificate) { $cert = $material.certificate.rawBytes } else { $cert = $material.x509CertificateChain.certificates[0].rawBytes } $hex = -join ([Convert]::FromBase64String($cert) | ForEach-Object { $_.ToString('x2') }) if ($hex -notmatch '^([0-9a-f]{2})*2b0601040183bf30010e0411(0c|13)0f726566732f68656164732f6d61696e') { throw 'NOT signed for refs/heads/main: stop' } # 3. the file: its checksum is in the signed list $want = ((Get-Content SHA256SUMS | Where-Object { $_ -match "\s$([regex]::Escape($zip))$" }) -split '\s+')[0] if ((Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 -LiteralPath $zip).Hash.ToLower() -ne $want) { throw "the checksum of $zip is not the signed one: stop" } # only a verified bundle is unpacked Expand-Archive -LiteralPath $zip -DestinationPath . 'RELEASE VERIFIED' } Continue only when the last line is RELEASE VERIFIED. Anything else, an error message or no output at all, means that the release is not verified: delete the downloaded files and start again, or ask in an issue. The ref check exists because the signing identity is the same for every branch, so the block looks in the certificate for the extension 1.3.6.1.4.1.57264.1.14 (the OID in the long string) with the value refs/heads/main, and fails when a job of another branch signed the file. Verify a release explains it, and How the signature works has the details.
Change into the unpacked bundle. The paths below are relative to it.
cd "machine-runner-swarm-$version" Pull the base image before you create the Swarm, because the network of the host drops for a few seconds after docker swarm init. A Server 2025 host runs this ltsc2022 image too.
docker pull mcr.microsoft.com/windows/servercore:ltsc2022 Copy the stack directory. For a first run, change nothing in it. You review it later, and from here on you deploy your copy and never the shipped files. The directory holds the stack files and the script that runners.yaml ships as a Swarm config, which the file names next to itself. A new release changes the shipped files, so an upgrade is a merge of your copy with the new files: Upgrade says how.
Copy-Item -Recurse windows\stack deploy Run the helper. It creates the Swarm, labels the node with the image tags it can run (the node is a manager, where the token proxy runs by default, so it needs no other label), asks for the token with hidden input, creates the secrets windows-default-token (the token proxy holds it) and runner-placeholder-token (what the runners read), and deploys your copy. Use the IPv4 address of the host. This is the whole install: the service runner-distributor-windows downloads and verifies the runner that the stack pins (the newest version that CI tests) and the pinned portable Git on its own, and Swarm pulls the token proxy image of this release by its digest.
.\windows\Setup.ps1 -InitSwarm -AdvertiseAddr <host IPv4 address> -Class windows-default -StackFile .\deploy\runners.yaml -Deploy Check that the runners are up and connected, and then run a job. docker stack deploy does not wait, so the replicas need a few minutes to start: the first download of the distributor takes a while, the first runner tasks fail until it is done and are started again every 10 seconds, and the first task also pulls the image if you skipped step 4. docker service logs runners_runner-distributor-windows shows the install.
docker stack services runners circleci runner instance list --org <org> --resource-class <namespace>/windows-default The runners are healthy when REPLICAS shows 2/2 (or fewer for Pending replicas) and the CLI lists an instance with the status online. The same list is in the web app under Runners. Then save the following as .circleci/config.yml in a project of your organization, replace my-namespace, commit, and push. Run the workflow twice.
version: 2.1 jobs: hello: machine: true resource_class: my-namespace/windows-default steps: - run: echo "computer $COMPUTERNAME, instance $MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_INSTANCE_ID" workflows: hello: jobs: - hello The two runs print different values, because Swarm starts a new container for each job. The file examples/windows-job.yml has more steps.
data.two-things-that-differ-from-linux#Two th: A job on Windows runs as an administrator. In a single-task class such as windows-default, the runner container holds only a placeholder, and the class token is in the service token-proxy-windows. A job can read the placeholder, and it may be able to send packets with a forged source address, because a Windows container cannot drop NET_RAW the way a Linux one can. This is not tested on Windows, and Security says what it could gain. The windows-persistent class is the exception: its container holds the real token, and a job can read it. Treat each class as a trust boundary. Refer to Token model on each OS. A stop of a busy container from outside, such as an update, a scale-down, or a node drain, kills its job after about 5 seconds. A job that finishes ends its container cleanly. Change a Windows class while it is idle. Refer to Stop a busy Windows container.
data.what-you-did-not-do#What you did not do: The helper starts Swarm. It does not install Docker or the runner, create classes or tokens, edit the stack file, label nodes for the optional classes, or build images. Optional: use the setup helper lists each option.

data: Linux: Deploy CircleCI machine runner 3 as a Docker Swarm stack on Ubuntu or RHEL, with one clean container for every job. Windows Server: Deploy CircleCI machine runner 3 as a Docker Swarm stack on Windows Server 2022 or 2025, with one clean container for every job. Multi-node clusters: Join Linux, Windows, and Arm nodes to one Docker Swarm, place resource classes with labels and constraints, and open the ports that the nodes need.

This page describes how to deploy CircleCI machine runner 3 as a Docker Swarm stack on Linux. The steps cover a single node, and Multi-Node Clusters extends them to several nodes.
Note If you can run Kubernetes, CircleCI recommends container runner for containerized jobs. CircleCI documents a plain machine runner 3 on Docker setup too. This page is a sibling of those pages for teams that run Docker Swarm and want a clean container for every job.
Status. This is a CircleCI Labs project, 0.x, and CircleCI support does not cover it. It is tested against CircleCI cloud only, and What is tested says how. Replicas are fixed: the stack does not add or remove nodes, and it does not scale to the queue.
The manual steps come first and use ordinary docker commands. Nothing is installed on a node by hand: the stack has a service that installs the runner on every node, and docker stack deploy is the whole install. The optional setup helper runs the same steps. For a first run, Quickstart on Linux is shorter.
data.1-create-the-resource-classes#1. Create:
Create a namespace if your organization has none. Each organization can have one namespace, and orbs use the same one.
$ circleci namespace create --org Create one resource class for each service in the stack file. The class name must equal the service name. The shipped file linux/stack/runners.yaml has one service, linux-default. For a first run, keep this name. To rename it, edit your copy of the file first (step 5), and then create the class and the secret under the new name. More classes come later, one resource class each, from the add-on stack files of step 5 or from Resource Classes.
$ circleci runner resource-class create /linux-default --org --generate-token Each command prints a token once. Store each token in your secret manager. If you lose a token, create a new one with circleci runner token create / --nickname .
data.2-prepare-each-node#2. Prepare each node: Run these steps on every node that runs services.
data.3-start-swarm#3. Start Swarm:
On a single node, start Swarm so that it listens on the loopback address only. Nothing is exposed to the network.
$ docker swarm init --advertise-addr 127.0.0.1 --listen-addr 127.0.0.1:2377 $ docker swarm update --task-history-limit 2 The second command keeps fewer stopped containers on the node (setup.sh --swarm-init does both). The node is a manager, and the token proxy runs on a manager by default, with no label. In a cluster, label the node that runs the proxy with machine-runner-swarm.proxy=true (docker node update --label-add machine-runner-swarm.proxy=true ): runner services never run on a node with that label, so a job never shares a node with the proxy. On a single node, do not set it. With several managers, pin the proxy to one: refer to Where the proxy runs, and when it moves. Each finished job leaves a stopped container until Swarm prunes its task, and every stopped container keeps its writable layer on disk.
A node that listens on the loopback address cannot accept other nodes. For several nodes, initialize Swarm with a routable address instead. Refer to Multi-Node Clusters. A node that joins needs nothing else, because the distributor service starts on it by itself.
data.4-create-the-secrets#4. Create the secre:
Create one secret for each service in the stack file. The secret is a runner config file and holds only the token:
api: auth_token: The token proxy mounts these secrets at /run/secrets/-token, owned by uid 65534 with mode 0400, and the runners never see them. The runners read one more secret, runner-placeholder-token, with a made-up token: create it once, with any value, in the same format. The stack mounts it at /run/secrets/circleci_runner_config.yaml, owned by the runner user (uid 2000) with mode 0400, and the runner reads it with --config. Only the persistent class mounts its own token in the runner. Every other setting is a CIRCLECI_RUNNER_* environment variable in the stack file.
Create the secrets with a hidden prompt, so that the token does not reach your shell history or the process list. This loop uses only POSIX features, so it works in bash, zsh, and dash. Do not replace it with read -rsp: that form is bash only, and zsh reads -p as a coprocess and fails, which leaves TOKEN empty and creates a secret without a token. The loop stops at an empty token.
for class in linux-default; do # one class; add the names of the other classes you deploy printf 'Token for %s (hidden): ' "$class" stty -echo; IFS= read -r TOKEN; stty echo; echo [ -n "$TOKEN" ] || { echo "no token entered for $class" >&2; break; } printf 'api:\n auth_token: %s\n' "$TOKEN" | docker secret create "$class-token" - done unset TOKEN printf 'api:\n auth_token: machine-runner-swarm-placeholder\n' | docker secret create runner-placeholder-token - Run every docker command in these steps with sudo, or as a user in the docker group. Without either, docker cannot reach the daemon. The setup helper below does the same in one command: sudo linux/setup.sh --secret linux-default, and then printf %s machine-runner-swarm-placeholder | sudo linux/setup.sh --secret runner-placeholder for the placeholder.
The secret name is the service name plus -token. docker stack deploy fails with secret not found when a service references a secret that does not exist. Create every secret that the file references, or delete the services you do not need from your copy of the file. Each optional class in step 5 needs its own secret.
docker stack config prints the mode 0400 as 256, its decimal value.
data.5-review-the-stack-file#5. Review the st:
Copy the directory linux/stack to a directory of your own, deploy/, and keep it under version control. From here on you check and deploy your copy and never the shipped files, so an edit never touches the shipped files. For a first run, change nothing: the copy works as it is, and you review it later.
$ cp -r linux/stack deploy The directory holds the stack files and the two scripts that they ship as Swarm configs, circleci-runner-entrypoint and runner-distributor.sh. The stack files name the scripts relative to themselves (file: circleci-runner-entrypoint), so keep the scripts in the same directory as the stack files. If you delete the add-on stack files that you do not use, keep runners.yaml and the two scripts.
Keep the service runner-distributor and the top-level configs: and volumes: in your copy: every class needs them. A Swarm config cannot change, so its name carries the first 12 hex digits of the SHA-256 of its file. If you edit the entrypoint or the distributor script, rename its config the same way: sha256sum | cut -c1-12. Review these settings first. Refer to Resource Classes for the details.
Setting Default Change it to Service name linux-default Your resource class name image cimg/base:2026.10 Your image, pinned by digest. Refer to Images deploy.replicas 2 The number of concurrent jobs you need deploy.resources 2 CPUs and 4 GB The size of one runner. Limits and reservations are equal placement.constraints node.platform.os == linux Add architecture or zone constraints x-distributor-env An exact runner version (an exact pin: 3.1.13 in this release) with the SHA-256 values of its tarballs, major version 3, a check every 24 hours Nothing for a first run. A newer pin or a floating version, or a mirror, are variables of docker stack deploy and need no edit. Refer to Upgrade the runner on Linux Check that the file parses. This needs no running Swarm.
$ docker stack config -c deploy/runners.yaml > /dev/null The optional classes are separate add-on stack files. Add each with another -c flag, and pass the same list of files on every deploy (how the files merge). Each add-on stack file needs its own resource class and its own secret -token.
File Service Purpose linux/stack/classes-extra.yaml (in deploy/ after the copy) linux-java, linux-hardened An image swap (cimg/openjdk) and a hardened class without sudo. They show how to add a class. Reserves 6 more CPUs and 12 GB. Refer to Resource Classes linux/stack/docker-build.yaml (in deploy/ after the copy) linux-docker-build Builds images with the host Docker engine. Needs a labeled worker node. Refer to Docker Builds linux/stack/microvm.yaml (in deploy/ after the copy) linux-microvm, linux-microvm-docker, and the DNS forwarder microvm-dns Runs each job in a Kata Containers microVM. Needs KVM and a node setup. Refer to MicroVM jobs linux/stack/persistent.yaml (in deploy/ after the copy) linux-persistent A long-lived runner with a named volume. Needs the node name edited in the file. Refer to Persistent mode linux/stack/ssh-rerun.yaml (in deploy/ after the copy) linux-default-ssh A class that supports Rerun job with SSH. Publishes port 54782 on the node. Refer to Rerun job with SSH An add-on stack file repeats the common service settings of runners.yaml, because YAML anchors do not cross files. That includes the four keys that a class needs for the runner: user: "0", the entrypoint, the config entrypoint, and the volume runner-bin mounted read-only. It repeats the top-level configs: and volumes: too, so it also loads alone. When you change a common setting, such as stop_grace_period or the logging options, change it in every file that you use.
data.6-deploy-the-stack#6. Deploy the stack:
Deploy your copy of the file from step 5. The command returns before the replicas run, because docker stack deploy does not wait.
$ docker stack deploy -c deploy/runners.yaml runners To add the optional classes, pass your copies of their files with more -c flags, and pass the same list on every later deploy:
$ docker stack deploy -c deploy/runners.yaml -c deploy/persistent.yaml runners This command is the whole install. The service runner-distributor starts on every Linux node, also on a node that joins later (not on a microVM node: its classes download their own runner). It downloads the runner of CircleCI (the exact version that the stack file pins, the newest that CI tests), checks its SHA-256 against the values that the stack file carries for that version, and puts it in the volume runner-bin of the node. The service token-proxy pulls its image from Docker Hub. A runner container that starts first waits up to 120 seconds for it. To deploy with other distributor settings, for example a floating version such as 3.1 (the distributor ignores the default SHA-256 list of the pin and trusts the manifest, which is weaker), set them as variables of this command. A host with sudo drops the environment, so write sudo env MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_VERSION=3.1 docker stack deploy ..., or run the command as a user in the docker group. Refer to Upgrade the runner on Linux.
data.additional-resources#Additional resource: Concepts Resource Classes Security Operations Machine runner 3 configuration reference
data.get-the-files#Get the files:
Use a release, or clone the repository at a release tag. The paths on this page are relative to the root of the repository or of the extracted release bundle.
git clone --branch https://github.com/CircleCI-Labs/scalable-machine-runner.git cd scalable-machine-runner Each GitHub release carries these files, where is the release number without the v:
File Content machine-runner-swarm-.tar.gz The bundle for Linux: the stack files, the entrypoint, the runner-distributor script, the setup scripts, the documentation, and the examples, without the tests machine-runner-swarm-.zip The same bundle for Windows SHA256SUMS The SHA-256 checksum of both bundles SHA256SUMS.sigstore.json A keyless cosign signature of SHA256SUMS The bundle has a top-level VERSION file with the release number and a CHANGELOG.md with the notes of every release.
A release is the recommended source, because its stack files name the token proxy image of that release by tag and digest. A git clone of a tag or of the default branch, or a “Download ZIP”, works too: the stack files there name the image tag latest, which only a release moves and which is not a pin. Refer to The token proxy image.
data.optional-use-the-setup-helper#Optional::
linux/setup.sh performs the steps above with checks. It never prints the token, and every step is idempotent. It needs bash 4.4 or later. It installs nothing on a node: the service runner-distributor of the stack installs the runner.
Step Effect --check Preflight: Linux on amd64, arm64, ppc64le or s390x, Docker running and 24 or later, Swarm state, NTP --swarm-init Runs docker swarm init on the loopback address unless Swarm is active, and sets the task history limit to 2. The node is a manager, which is where the token proxy runs --secret Creates the secret -token from a token read on stdin --deploy Runs docker stack deploy with each --stack-file. Without one it deploys the shipped linux/stack/runners.yaml, so pass your copy from step 5. It warns when MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_IMAGE is not pinned by digest With no step, it runs --check. The steps always run in the order of the table, whatever order you type them, and the hint after every run starts with Next: and names only the steps that are still to do (the Swarm, the secrets linux-default-token and runner-placeholder-token, the stack), read from Docker. When nothing is left it starts with Check: and names the commands that show the runners start. Options are --stack-file (repeatable) and --stack-name.
sudo linux/setup.sh --check --swarm-init sudo linux/setup.sh --secret linux-default # a hidden prompt asks for the token sudo linux/setup.sh --deploy --stack-file deploy/runners.yaml Create one secret for every service of the stack files you deploy. --deploy fails with secret not found when one is missing. Every command needs sudo or membership of the docker group, because each one talks to the Docker daemon. The helper is a bash script with a #!/usr/bin/env bash line, so it runs from any shell, including zsh. To script one secret, pipe the token: printf %s "$TOKEN" | sudo linux/setup.sh --secret linux-default. Several --secret values need a terminal, because stdin carries one token.
The distributor reads its settings from the environment of --deploy: MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_VERSION, MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_MAJOR, MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_CHECK_INTERVAL, MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_DOWNLOAD_BASE_URL, and MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_SHA256, and for the token proxy the variables MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_*. A host with sudo drops the environment, so to deploy with these variables, run sudo env MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_VERSION=3.1 linux/setup.sh --deploy, or run docker stack deploy as a user in the docker group. Refer to Upgrade the runner on Linux.
The helper accepts a token that has only letters, digits, ., _, and -, and it keeps an existing secret unchanged. To replace a token, refer to Rotate a runner token. The preflight warns when the clock is not NTP-synchronized. The helper does not label nodes. For a docker-build class, run docker node update --label-add machine-runner-swarm.docker-build=true yourself.
data.prerequisites#Prerequisites:
A CircleCI cloud organization and a user who is an organization admin. CircleCI server is not tested: CircleCI server says what is known.
The CircleCI CLI 1.4.0 or later, signed in. The commands on this page use its syntax (circleci --version prints the version). Pass --org , the organization slug such as gh/my-org or its UUID: without it the CLI takes the organization of the git remote of the current directory, which in a clone of this repository is not yours.
One or more Linux nodes with a supported operating system:
Operating system Architecture Status in this repository Ubuntu LTS amd64, arm64 Tested in CI on Ubuntu 26.04. On arm64, every pipeline checks that the stack installs the runner and starts, and probe jobs run on a real arm64 runner on main and smr-swarm/* branches RHEL 8 and later, and compatible distributions amd64, arm64 Steps documented, not tested in CI Any of the above ppc64le, s390x CircleCI lists these architectures. CI only starts the distributor and the token proxy image under emulation: no job has run on them Docker Engine 24 or later, running, with Swarm mode available. Podman cannot run Swarm.
Root access, or membership of the docker group. Docker and a Swarm join are all that a node needs: no runner, entrypoint, or tool is installed on a node.
A node clock that is synchronized with NTP. TLS to CircleCI fails silently when the clock drifts.
Outbound HTTPS access from each node to the hosts in Egress hosts, which include the release bucket of CircleCI (the runner download) and the registries that serve the stock image alpine (the distributor) and the token proxy image (Docker Hub). What needs internet lists everything. No inbound access is required. This release is not tested without internet access: Run the downloads from a mirror describes what a mirror replaces.
Enough CPU and memory for the services. The shipped file reserves 4 CPUs and 8 GB of memory in total, and replicas that do not fit stay pending. Size the limits has the numbers of every class.
Enough runner concurrency in your CircleCI plan for the replicas that you run. It limits how many jobs run at once, whatever the replicas: Capacity and concurrency describes the limits.
Membership of the docker group is equivalent to root on the node. Limit it to administrators.
data.rhel#RHEL:
Install Docker Engine from Docker’s repository by following Install Docker Engine on RHEL. The Podman packages that RHEL ships cannot run Swarm.
Enable the service, and confirm the engine and the clock.
$ sudo systemctl enable --now docker $ docker version $ timedatectl show -p NTPSynchronized --value Keep SELinux enforcing. The runner is in a Docker volume and not in a host directory, so no directory needs a label for it.
Note CI does not run on RHEL, so these steps follow Docker’s documentation and have not been exercised in this repository.
data.self-hosted-runner-terms-agreement#Self-: If you install self-hosted runners through the web app, an organization admin must agree to the CircleCI Runner Terms first. If you install and use self-hosted runners through the CLI, you agree to them by doing so. CircleCI documents this in Self-hosted runner terms agreement. The page that the terms link opens may carry another title, such as “Self-Hosted Applications Terms”. Whether running the token proxy between your runners and CircleCI is covered by these terms is a question for your own review: this project does not give legal advice.
data.the-token-proxy-image#The token proxy im:
The token proxy is the one container that holds your class tokens (The token proxy). It is a published image, ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy on Docker Hub, and the stack file pulls it when you deploy. ccilabs is the Docker Hub organization of CircleCI Labs. The name is not the trust root: the signature check of Verify the token proxy image is. You install nothing for it. It is a static Go binary in a minimal base, runs as a non-root user with a read-only root file system, and one tag covers linux/amd64, linux/arm64, linux/ppc64le and linux/s390x, so the node that runs it can have any of them. Windows nodes get the Windows image from the same tag (Windows).
Tag What it is X.Y.Z The image of a release. It never changes: pin this one X.Y, X The newest release of that minor or major line latest The newest release. It is the default of the stack files in a checkout, and only a release moves it edge The newest commit of the main branch that passed the end-to-end tests. Use it to test main, not to run jobs that matter sha-<12 characters> The image of one commit of the main branch, published before its tests have run The stack file reads the image from MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_IMAGE. A release bundle has the default ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy:@sha256: (the tag, and the digest that Docker pulls), a checkout has ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy:latest. linux/setup.sh --deploy prints a warning when the variable is not pinned by digest, which is the case in a checkout. To use another image, set the variable in the environment of docker stack deploy: a digest for a pin, a registry of your own for an air gap, or a local build for development.
# development: build the image from the checkout, and name it docker build -t machine-runner-swarm-proxy:dev proxy/ sudo env MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_IMAGE=machine-runner-swarm-proxy:dev docker stack deploy -c deploy/runners.yaml runners The image must be on the node that runs the proxy (a manager by default, or the node that you pin it to). A local build exists only on the node where you built it: build it there, or copy it with docker save machine-runner-swarm-proxy:dev | ssh docker load. Docker pulls a published image by itself. Verify the token proxy image shows how to check its signature, and Upgrade the token proxy how to change its tag.
data.troubleshooting#Troubleshooting: Refer to Troubleshooting. The most common problems on a first install are a missing secret, a node whose distributor cannot download the runner, and a task that stays pending because no node matches its constraints.
data.ubuntu#Ubuntu:
Install Docker Engine from Docker’s repository by following Install Docker Engine on Ubuntu.
Confirm the engine runs.
$ sudo systemctl enable --now docker $ docker version Confirm the clock is synchronized. The command prints yes.
$ timedatectl show -p NTPSynchronized --value A single node needs no firewall change. Multi-node clusters open the ports in Inter-node ports.
data.upgrade#Upgrade:
With the default settings, the nodes run the exact runner version that the stack file pins, and a new release of the runner changes nothing until you change the pin or deploy a release of this repository that carries a newer one. Upgrade the runner and images covers the runner version, the images, and a roll back.
A new release of this repository changes the shipped stack files, and your copy deploy/ is not updated by itself. To merge:
Read the notes of the release and the changelog: entries marked [BREAKING] say what to change. This is a 0.x project, so a minor release can change the files.
Verify and unpack the new release beside the old one (Verify a release). The old release directory is the base of the merge. If you cloned a tag, use git worktree or a second clone for the old tag.
See what changed between the two releases:
diff -ru "machine-runner-swarm-${old}/linux/stack" "machine-runner-swarm-${new}/linux/stack" Merge each file that differs into your copy. A three-way merge takes your changes and the changes of the release, and reports a conflict where both changed the same lines. Keep deploy/ under version control, so that you can see and revert the result.
git merge-file deploy/runners.yaml \ "machine-runner-swarm-${old}/linux/stack/runners.yaml" \ "machine-runner-swarm-${new}/linux/stack/runners.yaml" The command edits deploy/runners.yaml in place and exits with the number of conflicts, which it marks with <<<<<<< lines. Do the same for the other files that you copied. Take the entrypoint and the distributor script of the new release as they are unless you edited them, and rename their Swarm configs as Upgrade to a new release of this repository says.
The keys that you are likely to have changed are deploy.replicas, image, deploy.placement.constraints, and deploy.resources. Check each one after the merge, and check the pin of the runner version and its SHA-256 values, which a release changes together, and the token proxy image, which a release names by digest.
Check the result, and deploy with the same list of -c files as before:
$ docker stack config -c deploy/runners.yaml > /dev/null $ docker stack deploy -c deploy/runners.yaml runners Swarm replaces the token proxy and updates the runner services one replica at a time. While the proxy is replaced, no new job is claimed, and every runner that had already claimed stays refused (Restart the proxy). To roll back, deploy the previous copy.
data.verify-a-release#Verify a release:
CircleCI signs SHA256SUMS with the OIDC token of the CircleCI job that makes the release. No signing key is stored anywhere. The signature proves that a job of this CircleCI project made the file, and the checksums prove that your download is the file the job made. You need cosign 3.1.3 or a later 3.x (CI signs and verifies with 3.1.3, and earlier versions are not tested), curl, jq, and GNU coreutils, in a bash shell. On Windows, refer to Verify a release.
The release is the latest release of the releases page: set version once to its number without the v, and read its notes. The first line is a placeholder, and the download fails while it is unchanged.
version=X.Y.Z Then paste this block. It runs in a subshell and stops at the first failing check. Only a bundle that passes the signature, the ref, and the checksum is unpacked.
