( set -euo pipefail base="https://github.com/CircleCI-Labs/scalable-machine-runner/releases/download/v${version}" curl -fsSLO "${base}/machine-runner-swarm-${version}.tar.gz" \ -O "${base}/SHA256SUMS" \ -O "${base}/SHA256SUMS.sigstore.json" # 1. the signature: the CircleCI project and pipeline definition of this repository signed SHA256SUMS cosign verify-blob SHA256SUMS --bundle SHA256SUMS.sigstore.json \ --certificate-identity "https://circleci.com/api/v2/projects/7bbdbb66-6ba8-4f6c-982e-d4fb401ec257/pipeline-definitions/8b2a66db-3f28-5c80-88e4-03f4694b5b60" \ --certificate-oidc-issuer "https://oidc.circleci.com" # 2. the ref: a job of any branch can sign with that identity, so the certificate must also say that the job ran for refs/heads/main # (the long string is the OID 1.3.6.1.4.1.57264.1.14 followed by the value refs/heads/main) hex=$(jq -r '.verificationMaterial | (.certificate // .x509CertificateChain.certificates[0]).rawBytes' SHA256SUMS.sigstore.json \ | base64 -d | od -An -v -tx1 | tr -d ' \n') grep -Eq '^([0-9a-f]{2})*2b0601040183bf30010e0411(0c|13)0f726566732f68656164732f6d61696e' <<< "${hex}" \ && echo "signed for refs/heads/main" || { echo "NOT signed for refs/heads/main: stop"; exit 1; } # 3. the file: its checksum is in the signed list sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS --ignore-missing # only a verified bundle is unpacked tar -xzf "machine-runner-swarm-${version}.tar.gz" echo "RELEASE VERIFIED" ) Continue only when the last line is RELEASE VERIFIED. Anything else, an error message or no output at all, means that the release is not verified: delete the downloaded files, and start again or ask in an issue. The ref check exists because the signing identity is the same for every branch, so the block reads the certificate extension 1.3.6.1.4.1.57264.1.14 (the OID in the long string) and fails unless its value is refs/heads/main. The pattern starts on a byte boundary, and ASN.1 tag 0c or 13 is the string type of the value.
Then change into the bundle:
cd "machine-runner-swarm-${version}" What the three checks establish is limited. A valid signature and refs/heads/main mean that a job of this CircleCI project ran for the main branch of the repository and made these files. Whether anyone can change main without a review is a setting of the organization that owns the repository, and this page cannot check it. A ruleset for main describes what the project asks for.
The identity is the CircleCI project (7bbdbb66-...) and the pipeline definition (8b2a66db-...) that run this repository’s pipeline. The issuer https://oidc.circleci.com is the CircleCI OIDC issuer. Sigstore records every signature in a public transparency log.
To see the ref of a certificate, print it. The last line of the output ends with the ref, and a release comes from refs/heads/main.
jq -r '.verificationMaterial.certificate.rawBytes' SHA256SUMS.sigstore.json | base64 -d \ | openssl x509 -inform DER -noout -text | grep -A1 '1.3.6.1.4.1.57264.1.14:' If the project or its pipeline definition is ever re-created, the definition ID changes, and this page gives the new value.
data.verify-the-deployment#Verify the deploym:
List the services. Each shows the running and desired replicas.
$ docker stack services runners ID NAME MODE REPLICAS IMAGE ... runners_linux-default replicated 2/2 cimg/base:2026.10 ... runners_runner-distributor global 1/1 alpine:3 ... runners_token-proxy replicated 1/1 ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy:... The distributor shows one task for each Linux node (a microVM node has none), so 1/1 on a single node and 3/3 on three.
Check the tasks of a service. A task in the Running state is a runner that polls CircleCI.
$ docker service ps runners_linux-default Check that the distributor installed the runner. Its log has a line such as runner-distributor: [ ok ] current -> versions/3.1.13: circleci-runner 3.1.13 linux/amd64 for each node. Refer to See what runs.
$ docker service logs --tail 20 runners_runner-distributor Check that the runners connected. circleci runner instance list --org --resource-class /linux-default lists each replica with the status online, and the web app shows the same under Runners. A replica has a name of the form --, for example node1-linux-default-1.
Run a job. Use examples/linux-hello.yml: it is a complete config, and the quickstart shows it. Run the workflow twice. After each job, Swarm shows a new task for the slot. The file examples/linux-jobs.yml has a job named clean-check that fails if anything from an earlier job is still present.

data:
This page describes how to deploy CircleCI machine runner 3 as a Docker Swarm stack on Windows Server. Every job runs in a new Windows Server Core container, and Swarm replaces the container after the job.
Note If you can run Kubernetes, CircleCI recommends container runner for containerized jobs. This page is for teams that run Docker Swarm and need a clean Windows container for every job.
Status. This is a CircleCI Labs project, 0.x, and CircleCI support does not cover it. It is tested against CircleCI cloud only, and What is tested says how. Replicas are fixed: the stack does not add or remove nodes, and it does not scale to the queue.
The manual steps are short: start or join a swarm, label the node, create the secrets, deploy. The optional setup helper runs most of them. For a first run, Quickstart on Windows Server is shorter.
Important The services run the stock Server Core image, and no image is built. Stopping a busy container from outside kills its job after about 5 seconds, so change a Windows class while it is idle. Refer to Stop a busy Windows container.
data.1-create-the-resource-classes#1. Create:
Create a namespace if your organization has none.
$ circleci namespace create --org Create one resource class for each service in the stack files. The class name must equal the service name. The shipped file windows\stack\runners.yaml has the service windows-default and deploys on its own. The optional add-on stack files in the same directory add windows-custom (custom-image.yaml), windows-persistent (persistent.yaml), windows-docker-build (docker-build.yaml), and windows-default-ssh (ssh-rerun.yaml, untested). Create the classes you plan to use.
$ circleci runner resource-class create /windows-default --org --generate-token The command prints the token once. Store it in your secret manager.
data.2-prepare-each-host#2. Prepare each host:
Run these steps in an elevated PowerShell on every host. Do them before you start Swarm. The network of the host drops for a few seconds after docker swarm init, and the pull needs it.
Confirm that Docker runs Windows containers. The command prints windows.
docker info --format '{{.OSType}}' Pull the base image of the shipped services once, so the first task does not wait for it. A Server 2025 host runs ltsc2022 images too, so this is the image for both hosts. Pull ltsc2025 as well only for a service that you put on that image.
docker pull mcr.microsoft.com/windows/servercore:ltsc2022 On the host that runs the token proxy (a manager, by default), pull its image too: docker pull ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy:latest, or the image that you build (The token proxy image).
data.3-start-swarm-and-label-the-node#3. Star:
On the first host, start Swarm. Always pass --advertise-addr with the IPv4 address of the host. A plain docker swarm init fails on some hosts with could not find the system's IP address, and a host with several network adapters needs the address to pick the right one.
docker swarm init --advertise-addr <host IPv4 address> The network of the host drops for a few seconds after this command, so pull the images first (step 2). For more than one node, refer to Multi-Node Clusters: a node that joins needs nothing else on the host, because the stack installs the runner on it.
Label the node with the image tags it can run. A Server 2022 node gets one label, and a Server 2025 node gets both.
docker node update --label-add machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2022=true <node name> docker node update --label-add machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2025=true <node name> # Server 2025 only On a single node, the token proxy needs no label: it runs on the manager, which keeps its state, and the jobs run there too. In a cluster, give the proxy a node of its own. Label the node that runs it (a manager) with machine-runner-swarm.proxy=true: runner services never run on a node with that label, so a job never shares a node with the proxy. Do not set the label on the only node of a swarm, because no runner would be placed. In a swarm whose managers are Linux hosts, or one with several managers, also pin the proxy to a Windows node of your choice by deploying with the placement in the environment of docker stack deploy:
docker node update --label-add machine-runner-swarm.proxy=true <node name> $env:MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_PLACEMENT = 'node.labels.machine-runner-swarm.proxy == true' Without a matching node the proxy stays pending and no runner can claim. Refer to Where the proxy runs, and when it moves.
The optional classes need one more label each. Add it to the nodes that run them:
Class Label windows-docker-build machine-runner-swarm.docker-build=true windows-persistent machine-runner-swarm.class.windows-persistent=true
data.4-create-the-secrets#4. Create the secre:
Create one secret for each service you deploy, including each optional class, the persistent one too (windows-persistent-token: persistent.yaml declares it as external, so the deploy fails without it). The secret is a runner config file and holds only the token. The token proxy mounts the secrets of the proxied classes, and those runners never see them. The persistent class is the exception (The persistent class). Every secret has this format:
api: auth_token: The runners read one more secret, runner-placeholder-token, with a made-up token: create it once, with any value, in the same format (the setup helper does it). Swarm mounts it at C:\ProgramData\Docker\secrets\circleci_runner_config.yaml, and the runner reads it with --config. Only the persistent class mounts its own token there. Every other setting is a CIRCLECI_RUNNER_* environment variable in the stack file.
The following commands ask for the token with hidden input and pass the config to docker secret create on stdin, as windows\Setup.ps1 does, so that no file with the token is written on the host.
$class = 'windows-default' $secure = Read-Host -Prompt "Runner token for $class" -AsSecureString $bstr = [Runtime.InteropServices.Marshal]::SecureStringToBSTR($secure) try { $token = [Runtime.InteropServices.Marshal]::PtrToStringBSTR($bstr) } finally { [Runtime.InteropServices.Marshal]::ZeroFreeBSTR($bstr) } if (-not $token) { throw "no token entered for $class" } "api:`n auth_token: $token`n" | docker secret create "$class-token" - Remove-Variable token "api:`n auth_token: machine-runner-swarm-placeholder`n" | docker secret create runner-placeholder-token - Repeat the first block for each class, with its name in $class. The placeholder is created once.
Windows does not support the uid, gid, and mode options of secrets. Only administrators and SYSTEM can read the file inside the container, and jobs run as an administrator. Swarm also writes the secret in clear text to the disk of the container until the container stops, which is a Swarm limitation on Windows. Linux keeps the secret in memory. Enable BitLocker on the Docker volume. Refer to Token model on each OS.
data.5-review-the-stack-files#5. Review the s:
Copy the directory windows\stack into a directory of your own, deploy\, and keep it under version control. From here on, you check and deploy your copies and never the files under windows\stack, so an edit never touches the shipped files. For a first run, change nothing: the copy of runners.yaml works as it is, and you review it later.
Copy-Item -Recurse windows\stack deploy The directory holds the stack files and runner-distributor.ps1, the script that runners.yaml ships as a Swarm config (file: runner-distributor.ps1). The stack files name it relative to themselves, so keep the script next to runners.yaml. Review these settings first. Refer to Resource Classes for the details.
Service File Purpose runner-distributor-windows runners.yaml Installs and upgrades the runner and Git on every Windows node. Keep it in your copy windows-default runners.yaml Stock Server Core image, two replicas windows-custom custom-image.yaml Your own image on top of stock Server Core. Refer to Images windows-persistent persistent.yaml A long-lived runner with a named volume. Refer to Persistent mode windows-docker-build docker-build.yaml Builds Windows images with the host engine. Refer to Docker Builds windows-default-ssh ssh-rerun.yaml Supports Rerun job with SSH and publishes port 54782. Untested on Windows. Refer to Rerun job with SSH runners.yaml needs the secrets windows-default-token and runner-placeholder-token. Each add-on stack file needs its own -token secret, and custom-image.yaml has a placeholder image that you replace with yours. The distributor settings are variables of docker stack deploy and need no edit: the runner version (an exact pin by default, with the SHA-256 values of its tarballs, or 3.1, 3 or current, which follow CircleCI’s manifest and are checked every 24 hours), a mirror and an explicit SHA-256 list for an exact pin. Refer to Upgrade the runner on Windows. A Server 2025 node runs the shipped ltsc2022 services. For a class on the ltsc2025 image, copy a service under a new name and resource class, use the ltsc2025 image tag, and set the constraint node.labels.machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2025 == true. The optional classes are add-on stack files. Add each with another -c flag, and pass the same list of files on every deploy (how the files merge). Each add-on stack file repeats the anchors of runners.yaml, because an anchor does not reach into another file, and declares the volume runner-bin too, so that it also loads alone. When you change a common setting, change it in every file that you use.
Check that your copies parse. This needs no running Swarm.
docker stack config -c deploy\runners.yaml | Out-Null With the optional files, pass them all, in the same order as you deploy them:
docker stack config -c deploy\runners.yaml -c deploy\custom-image.yaml -c deploy\persistent.yaml -c deploy\docker-build.yaml | Out-Null For the keys that Windows honours and the keys that it ignores, refer to Stack keys on Windows.
data.6-deploy-the-stack#6. Deploy the stack:
Deploy your copy of the file from step 5:
docker stack deploy -c deploy\runners.yaml runners To add the optional classes, pass your copies of their files after runners.yaml with more -c flags, for example your own image on top of stock Server Core:
docker stack deploy -c deploy\runners.yaml -c deploy\custom-image.yaml runners This is the whole install: nothing is staged on the host. The service runner-distributor-windows starts on every Windows node, downloads the runner version that the stack file pins (the newest that CI tests) and the pinned portable Git (about 60 MB, 406 MB unpacked), verifies their SHA-256 checksums (the runner against the values that the stack file carries for that version, not against CircleCI’s manifest), installs them into the per-node volume runner-bin, and flips two links. The runner services mount the volume read-only, twice: the link current at C:\machine-runner-swarm, and the link git\current at C:\Program Files\Git, the path where the task agent expects tar.exe. The stock Server Core image therefore needs no changes, and no entrypoint script exists on Windows, because circleci-runner.exe is the main process of the container.
On a new node the first runner tasks fail with cannot access path ... \current until the distributor has flipped the link, which takes a few minutes for the first download. Swarm starts the next task after the restart delay of 10 seconds, so nothing needs to be done. Watch the distributor:
docker service logs runners_runner-distributor-windows
data.additional-resources#Additional resource: Concepts Resource Classes Security Operations Machine runner 3 on Windows
data.get-the-files#Get the files:
Clone the repository at a release tag, or extract a release bundle. Paths on this page are relative to the root of either. The GitHub release has the machine-runner-swarm-.zip bundle for Windows, and the Linux page lists every file of a release.
git clone --branch <release-tag> https://github.com/CircleCI-Labs/scalable-machine-runner.git cd scalable-machine-runner
data.image-tags-and-host-builds#Image tags an:
With process isolation, the image build must be the host build or an older one. Label every node with the image tags it can run, and the stack places each service on a node that carries the label of the service’s image tag.
Host Images it can run Node labels Windows Server 2022 ltsc2022 only machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2022=true Windows Server 2025 ltsc2025 and ltsc2022 machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2022=true and machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2025=true A service requires the label that names its image tag. The shipped services use ltsc2022 images, so they run on 2022 and 2025 nodes alike. A service on an ltsc2025 image requires machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2025 == true, so it runs on 2025 nodes only. A mismatch that the labels do not catch fails with the error 0xc0370101. Server 2019 is untested and has no label.
data.install-cosign#Install cosign:
cosign 3.1.3 or a later 3.x verifies the release (CI signs and verifies with 3.1.3, and earlier versions are not tested). On Windows, download the executable and the checksum list of the cosign release, compare the checksum, and put the file in a directory on your PATH:
$cosign = '3.1.3' $u = "https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/releases/download/v$cosign" Invoke-WebRequest -UseBasicParsing -Uri "$u/cosign-windows-amd64.exe" -OutFile cosign.exe Invoke-WebRequest -UseBasicParsing -Uri "$u/cosign_checksums.txt" -OutFile cosign_checksums.txt $want = ((Get-Content cosign_checksums.txt | Where-Object { $_ -match '\scosign-windows-amd64\.exe$' }) -split '\s+')[0] if ((Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 -LiteralPath cosign.exe).Hash.ToLower() -ne $want) { throw 'the checksum of cosign.exe does not match: stop' } .\cosign.exe version This checks the file against a list from the same place, so it catches a damaged download and not a compromised release page. Your own package manager is another source.
data.optional-use-the-setup-helper#Optional::
windows\Setup.ps1 checks the host, starts Swarm on request, labels the node, creates the secrets, and deploys, with checks. It does not install the runner: the distributor service of the stack does that on every node. It runs in an elevated Windows PowerShell 5.1 session and is safe to run again. It prints CHECK PASS or FAIL for each preflight check: administrator, Windows Server build, Windows-container mode, Docker 28.0 or later, and Swarm manager. After every run it prints Next: with the steps that are still to do (Swarm, secrets, deploy, read from Docker), or Check: with the commands to watch the start when nothing is left.
The helper does not add the labels of the optional classes.
Parameter Effect -InitSwarm -AdvertiseAddr Creates a Swarm when none exists, and waits until the node is a manager. The address is needed only then: on a Swarm that is active, -InitSwarm needs no address and changes nothing -Class , Asks for each token with hidden input and creates the secret -token. An existing secret stays unchanged (placeholder) With -Class or -Deploy it also creates the secret runner-placeholder-token with a made-up token, which every runner reads. -InitSwarm creates a manager, which is where the token proxy runs -Deploy Runs docker stack deploy with -StackFile (one or more files, runners.yaml first) and -StackName (default runners). Without -StackFile it deploys the shipped windows\stack\runners.yaml as it is, which suits a first run. Once you keep copies as in step 5, pass them. The helper prints the files that it deploys The helper labels the node from the host build: machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2022=true on Server 2022, and both windows-ltsc2022=true and windows-ltsc2025=true on Server 2025. It supports Server 2022 and 2025 only. Server 2019 is untested and gets no label. The distributor reads its settings from the environment of -Deploy.
The first example is a first run: it deploys the shipped runners.yaml unchanged. The second deploys your copy from step 5, with its optional file.
.\windows\Setup.ps1 -InitSwarm -AdvertiseAddr 10.0.0.5 -Class windows-default -Deploy .\windows\Setup.ps1 -Class windows-default,windows-custom -StackFile .\deploy\runners.yaml,.\deploy\custom-image.yaml -Deploy
data.prerequisites#Prerequisites:
A CircleCI cloud organization and a user who is an organization admin. CircleCI server is not tested: CircleCI server says what is known.
The CircleCI CLI 1.4.0 or later, signed in. It can run on your workstation. The commands on this page use its syntax (circleci --version prints the version). Pass --org , the organization slug such as gh/my-org or its UUID: without it the CLI takes the organization of the git remote of the current directory, which in a clone of this repository is not yours.
One or more Windows Server hosts. Machine runner 3 supports these versions:
Windows Server Machine runner 3 Status in this repository 2025 Compatible Tested in CI, image tag ltsc2025 2022 Compatible Tested in CI, image tag ltsc2022 2019 Compatible Untested here: the stack files have no label or placement for it, so this page does not cover it 2016 and older Not compatible Not supported The host cannot be a domain controller.
Docker Engine 28.0 or later (the CLI and the engine), in Windows-container mode, with the Windows Containers feature (enabling it needs a restart of the host). The stack files mount a subpath of a volume (current and git\current). The Docker release notes say that Swarm passes volume.subpath to the engine from 26.1.0 (26.0 dropped it from the task), and that docker stack deploy stopped ignoring volume.subpath in the CLI with 28.0.0 (before that the whole volume was mounted at the runner path, and the runner did not start). The CI of this repository runs Docker 29.4.0 on Windows. windows\Setup.ps1 checks the version. The Install-DockerCE script in the helpful_tools directory of the Microsoft Windows Containers repository installs both.
An elevated Windows PowerShell 5.1 session.
A host clock that is synchronized with NTP. TLS to CircleCI fails silently when the clock drifts.
Outbound HTTPS access from each host to the hosts in Egress hosts. The distributor needs circleci-binary-releases.s3.amazonaws.com for the runner and its manifest, and github.com and release-assets.githubusercontent.com for Git and 7-Zip. The host needs mcr.microsoft.com for the base image, and Docker Hub for the token proxy image. What needs internet lists everything. This release is not tested without internet access: Upgrade the runner on Windows describes what a mirror replaces.
Disk space for the base image. The servercore image is about 2.2 GB compressed. Each container shows 20 GB free on C: by default. Add "storage-opts": ["size=60GB"] to C:\ProgramData\docker\config\daemon.json to raise the limit. Every finished container keeps its layer until Swarm prunes it, and the disk use of a job is not measured here.
Enough CPU and memory for the services, and enough runner concurrency in your CircleCI plan for the replicas that you run. Size the limits has the numbers of every class.
data.self-hosted-runner-terms-agreement#Self-: If you install self-hosted runners through the web app, an organization admin must agree to the CircleCI Runner Terms first. If you install and use self-hosted runners through the CLI, you agree to them by doing so. CircleCI documents this in Self-hosted runner terms agreement. The page that the terms link opens may carry another title, such as “Self-Hosted Applications Terms”. Whether running the token proxy between your runners and CircleCI is covered by these terms is a question for your own review: this project does not give legal advice.
data.stop-and-uninstall#Stop and uninstall: Refer to Uninstall. Every stop of a busy service kills its job after about 5 seconds. Refer to Stop a busy Windows container.
data.the-token-proxy-image#The token proxy im:
The token proxy holds your class tokens (The token proxy). On Windows it is the image ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy of Docker Hub (ccilabs is the Docker Hub organization of CircleCI Labs, and the signature check, not the name, is the trust root), which the stack file token-proxy-windows pulls when you deploy: a static binary on Nano Server, for windows/amd64. The same tag also holds the Linux images, and a manifest list holds one Windows image for Windows Server 2022 and one for Windows Server 2025, so Docker picks the one of the host. Tags, pinning and the signature are the same as on Linux: refer to The token proxy image and Verify the token proxy image.
The image runs as ContainerAdministrator, as the stock Server Core image does: Windows maps no user to a named volume, and ContainerUser of Nano Server cannot write to the volume that keeps the state of the proxy.
There is no windows/arm64 image, because CI has no Windows on Arm host to build and test one on. In a cluster with Windows on Arm nodes, pin the proxy to a windows/amd64 node with MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_PLACEMENT (Multi-Node Clusters). A cluster of Windows on Arm nodes only needs an image of your own: build the proxy with GOARCH=arm64, build proxy\Dockerfile.windows on an arm64 host with an arm64 Nano Server image as --build-arg BASE=, and name the result with MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_IMAGE.
To use another image, for development or an air gap, set MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_IMAGE in the environment of docker stack deploy. A checkout builds it from the source: build the binary on any host with Go, put it in an empty directory, and build on the Windows host whose build matches the base image.
$env:GOOS = 'windows'; $env:GOARCH = 'amd64'; $env:CGO_ENABLED = '0' New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path build | Out-Null Push-Location proxy; go build -trimpath -o ..\build\machine-runner-swarm-proxy.exe .\cmd\machine-runner-swarm-proxy; Pop-Location docker build -f proxy\Dockerfile.windows -t machine-runner-swarm-proxy:dev build $env:MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_IMAGE = 'machine-runner-swarm-proxy:dev' The image must be on the node that runs the proxy. A local build exists only where you built it.
data.troubleshooting#Troubleshooting: Refer to Troubleshooting. The most common problems are an image tag that does not match the host build, a distributor that has not installed the runner yet, and a job that ends about 5 seconds after a stop. A task also stays pending when no node carries the machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2022 label (or windows-ltsc2025, for a service on an ltsc2025 image).
data.upgrade#Upgrade:
By default the distributor pins the exact runner version that this release of the repository tests, with the SHA-256 values of its tarballs, and the nodes keep it until you change it. 3.1, 3 or current (weaker: they trust the hash of the manifest) make it follow CircleCI’s manifest and check every 24 hours. A pin of your own is two variables of docker stack deploy: the version and its SHA-256 values (or manifest for an exact version without a list). Running jobs keep the version they started with, and the runner services never restart. Refer to Upgrade the runner on Windows.
A new release of this repository changes the shipped stack files, and your copy deploy\ is not updated by itself. To merge, with git from Git for Windows or another diff and merge tool:
Read the notes of the release and the changelog: entries marked [BREAKING] say what to change. This is a 0.x project, so a minor release can change the files.
Verify and unpack the new release beside the old one (Verify a release). The old release directory is the base of the merge.
See what changed between the two releases, and merge each file that differs into your copy. Keep deploy\ under version control, so that you can see and revert the result.
git diff --no-index "machine-runner-swarm-$old\windows\stack" "machine-runner-swarm-$new\windows\stack" git merge-file deploy\runners.yaml "machine-runner-swarm-$old\windows\stack\runners.yaml" "machine-runner-swarm-$new\windows\stack\runners.yaml" git merge-file edits deploy\runners.yaml in place and exits with the number of conflicts, which it marks with <<<<<<< lines. Do the same for the other files that you copied, and take runner-distributor.ps1 of the new release as it is unless you edited it (Upgrade to a new release of this repository explains the names of the Swarm configs).
The keys that you are likely to have changed are deploy.replicas, image, deploy.placement.constraints, and deploy.resources. Check each one after the merge, and check the pin of the runner version and its SHA-256 values, which a release changes together, and the token proxy image, which a release names by digest.
Check the result, and deploy during a time when the classes are idle (Stop a busy Windows container), with the same list of -c files as before:
docker stack config -c deploy\runners.yaml | Out-Null docker stack deploy -c deploy\runners.yaml runners To roll back, deploy the previous copy.
data.verify-a-release#Verify a release:
CircleCI signs the file SHA256SUMS of each release with the OIDC token of the job that makes the release. The signature proves that a job of this CircleCI project made the file, and the checksum proves that your download is the file that the job made. The Linux page explains what the signature proves, and what it does not.
Set $version once, to the number of the latest release without the v, and read its notes. The first line is a placeholder: with it unchanged, the download fails and nothing runs.
$version = 'X.Y.Z' $base = "https://github.com/CircleCI-Labs/scalable-machine-runner/releases/download/v$version" $zip = "machine-runner-swarm-$version.zip" Then paste this block. It stops at the first failing check. The variables are set outside it, because & runs the block in a scope of its own. Only a bundle that passes the signature, the ref, and the checksum is unpacked.
& { $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop' foreach ($f in $zip, 'SHA256SUMS', 'SHA256SUMS.sigstore.json') { Invoke-WebRequest -UseBasicParsing -Uri "$base/$f" -OutFile $f } # 1. the signature: the CircleCI project and pipeline definition of this repository signed SHA256SUMS cosign verify-blob SHA256SUMS --bundle SHA256SUMS.sigstore.json ` --certificate-identity 'https://circleci.com/api/v2/projects/7bbdbb66-6ba8-4f6c-982e-d4fb401ec257/pipeline-definitions/8b2a66db-3f28-5c80-88e4-03f4694b5b60' ` --certificate-oidc-issuer 'https://oidc.circleci.com' if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'the signature does not verify: stop' } # 2. the ref: a job of any branch can sign with that identity, so the certificate must also say that the job ran for refs/heads/main # (the long string is the OID 1.3.6.1.4.1.57264.1.14 followed by the value refs/heads/main) $material = (Get-Content -Raw -LiteralPath SHA256SUMS.sigstore.json | ConvertFrom-Json).verificationMaterial if ($material.certificate) { $cert = $material.certificate.rawBytes } else { $cert = $material.x509CertificateChain.certificates[0].rawBytes } $hex = -join ([Convert]::FromBase64String($cert) | ForEach-Object { $_.ToString('x2') }) if ($hex -notmatch '^([0-9a-f]{2})*2b0601040183bf30010e0411(0c|13)0f726566732f68656164732f6d61696e') { throw 'NOT signed for refs/heads/main: stop' } # 3. the file: its checksum is in the signed list $want = ((Get-Content SHA256SUMS | Where-Object { $_ -match "\s$([regex]::Escape($zip))$" }) -split '\s+')[0] if ((Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 -LiteralPath $zip).Hash.ToLower() -ne $want) { throw "the checksum of $zip is not the signed one: stop" } # only a verified bundle is unpacked Expand-Archive -LiteralPath $zip -DestinationPath . 'RELEASE VERIFIED' } Continue only when the last line is RELEASE VERIFIED. Anything else, an error message or no output at all, means that the release is not verified: delete the downloaded files, and start again or ask in an issue. The ref check exists because the signing identity is the same for every branch, so the block reads the certificate extension 1.3.6.1.4.1.57264.1.14 (the OID in the long string) and fails unless its value is refs/heads/main. The pattern starts on a byte boundary, and ASN.1 tag 0c or 13 is the string type of the value.
Then change into the bundle:
cd "machine-runner-swarm-$version"
data.verify-the-deployment#Verify the deploym:
List the services and tasks.
docker stack services runners docker stack ps runners --no-trunc The service runners_runner-distributor-windows shows one replica for each Windows node.
Check that the runners connected. circleci runner instance list --org --resource-class /windows-default lists each replica with the status online, and the web app shows the same under Runners. A replica has a name of the form --.
Run a job. The quickstart has a complete config, and examples/windows-job.yml has more steps. Run the workflow twice. The two runs print different values for $MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_INSTANCE_ID, because each job runs in a new container.
data.what-jobs-can-use#What jobs can use: The default shell is Git Bash (bash -eo pipefail). Set shell: powershell.exe -ExecutionPolicy Bypass for Windows PowerShell 5.1, or shell: cmd.exe, per job or step. The working directory is C:\cci\w, and the task agent lives in C:\cci\agent. The PATH of the service reaches every step, because the runner passes its environment to the task agent and the task agent passes it to the steps. checkout, caches, test results, and artifacts need Git and outbound access. Workspaces use the tar and gzip from the mounted Git. Caches and test results use built-in code. OpenID Connect tokens need a writable %TEMP%. The stack enables Git long paths through the environment. The Windows registry value LongPathsEnabled is not set. A job that needs long paths for other tools sets the value itself, or sets it in its own image. Not supported: desktop or UI automation, Docker commands in jobs (except the opt-in docker-build class), and service containers. Not tested: add_ssh_keys, Hyper-V isolation, group managed service accounts, and proxies. The variables MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO and MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_USER of the Linux entrypoint do not exist on Windows, and Windows ignores them. There is no step-down.

data:
This page describes how to run the stack on a cluster of nodes: Linux amd64, Linux arm64, and Windows. One Swarm schedules every replica, and labels decide which node may run which resource class.
Start with the single-node steps on Install on Linux with Docker Swarm or Install on Windows Server with Docker Swarm, then use this page to add nodes.
flowchart LR subgraph nodes["Nodes and their labels"] A["linux-alinux, x86_64machine-runner-swarm.zone=build"] B["linux-blinux, aarch64machine-runner-swarm.zone=build"] C["linux-clinux, x86_64machine-runner-swarm.zone=deploy"] D["linux-d (worker)linux, x86_64machine-runner-swarm.docker-build=true"] W["win-awindowsmachine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2022=true"] end subgraph services["Services and their constraints"] S1["linux-buildos == linuxzone == build"] S2["linux-arm64arch == aarch64"] S3["linux-deployzone == deploy"] S4["linux-docker-buildrole == workerdocker-build == true"] S5["windows-defaultos == windowsmachine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2022 == true"] end S1 -.-> A S1 -.-> B S2 -.-> B S3 -.-> C S4 -.-> D S5 -.-> WA dotted line means that the node satisfies every constraint of the service, so Swarm may place a replica of it there. A service stays pending when no node matches.
data.additional-resources#Additional resource: Resource Classes Operations, including how to drain a node for patching Security
data.arm-nodes#Arm nodes:
The runner-distributor service reads the architecture of the node and installs the arm64 runner build on an Arm node. Swarm reports the architecture of Arm nodes as aarch64 and that of Intel and AMD nodes as x86_64.
Give each architecture its own resource class, for example linux-arm64, and constrain it with node.platform.arch == aarch64. A class that spans both architectures places replicas unpredictably, and a job cannot pick one. Use an image that publishes an arm64 variant. For example, check with docker buildx imagetools inspect .
data.built-in-node-properties#Built-in node p: Property Values node.platform.os linux, windows node.platform.arch x86_64, aarch64 node.hostname The hostname of the node node.role manager, worker
data.create-the-swarm#Create the swarm:
Initialize Swarm on the first manager with an address that the other nodes can reach. The loopback address that the single-node install uses cannot accept other nodes.
$ docker swarm init --advertise-addr \ --task-history-limit 2 \ --default-addr-pool 10.20.0.0/16 --default-addr-pool-mask-length 24 Two options matter for this stack, and neither is the default:
--task-history-limit 2. Every finished job ends a task, and Swarm keeps the last 5 tasks of each slot, with their containers and their disk, unless you lower it. The single-node install sets 2, and a swarm that you create here does not. Refer to Free disk space. Change it later with docker swarm update --task-history-limit 2. --default-addr-pool. Each Linux class gets its own overlay network, a /24 from the default pool of Swarm, which is 10.0.0.0/8. Choose a pool that does not overlap your own networks, because an overlap makes tasks unreachable in ways that are hard to see. A /16 split into /24 networks gives 256 of them, which is enough for the classes of one stack and for the networks of your own services. You can set the pool only when you create the swarm. If you started with the loopback address, remove the stack with docker stack rm runners, run docker swarm leave --force, initialize again, and recreate the secrets.
Get the join command for each node type on a manager:
$ docker swarm join-token worker $ docker swarm join-token manager Run the printed command on the node. It has the form docker swarm join --token :2377. A join token grants cluster membership, so keep it secret. Rotate it with docker swarm join-token --rotate worker when it leaks.
Confirm the nodes from a manager:
$ docker node ls
data.encrypted-class-networks#Encrypted class:
The Linux stack files create the class networks as encrypted overlays: driver: overlay with driver_opts: {encrypted: "true"}. The runners reach the token proxy over http://token-proxy:8080, and that traffic carries task tokens, the job configuration with the secrets of its contexts, and step output. Between nodes it would cross the network in clear text, and anyone on that network could also inject packets into the overlay, which the source-address guarantee of the proxy depends on. Swarm encrypts the VXLAN traffic between the nodes with IPsec instead, and a node that cannot reach another over ESP drops that traffic: tasks on different nodes then cannot reach each other, which looks like a runner that cannot find token-proxy. If a runner cannot reach the proxy from another node, check ESP first, with the ports above.
What you pay. IPsec costs CPU on every node and some throughput, which a class of long jobs with little network traffic never notices. A single-node Swarm sends nothing between nodes, so it needs nothing open. Opt out. If the network between your nodes is yours (a private network, or a link that you encrypt another way), delete the line driver_opts: {encrypted: "true"} from every class network of your copy of the Linux stack files (runners.yaml and the add-on files you use), remove the stack, and deploy again. A Swarm network cannot change after it exists, so a plain docker stack deploy leaves an existing network as it is: run docker stack rm runners, wait until the networks are gone (docker network ls), and deploy again. Without the option, ESP is not needed. Windows. Docker does not support encrypted overlay networks for Windows containers, so the Windows stack files set no driver_opts, and their overlay carries the traffic of the Windows classes and token-proxy-windows in clear text between nodes. Keep the Windows nodes on a network that you trust, or encrypt the link between them at the host (for example with Windows Firewall connection security rules for IPsec). The Windows stack files also create no network of their own for each class, so all of their classes share the default overlay of the stack. Windows Server:
New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName 'Swarm TCP' -Direction Inbound -Action Allow -Protocol TCP -LocalPort 2377,7946 -RemoteAddress <cluster subnet> New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName 'Swarm UDP' -Direction Inbound -Action Allow -Protocol UDP -LocalPort 7946,4789 -RemoteAddress <cluster subnet> On a Windows host with a single network adapter, an existing transparent network can block the creation of the overlay networks. Refer to the Microsoft documentation on Windows container networking if overlay creation fails.
data.inter-node-ports#Inter-node ports:
Swarm needs these ports between all nodes of the cluster. Open them only for the addresses of cluster nodes.
Port Protocol Purpose Nodes 2377 TCP Cluster management Managers only receive it 7946 TCP and UDP Node discovery All nodes 4789 UDP Overlay network (VXLAN) All nodes IP protocol 50 (ESP) IPsec Encrypted overlay networks (the Linux class networks). It is a protocol, not a port All nodes with Linux services The runner containers need no inbound ports, and the stack publishes none. Outbound HTTPS from each node is the only other requirement. A Linux node reaches the release bucket of CircleCI for the runner download of the distributor, or your mirror. Refer to Egress hosts.
Ubuntu with ufw:
$ sudo ufw allow from to any port 2377 proto tcp $ sudo ufw allow from to any port 7946 $ sudo ufw allow from to any port 4789 proto udp $ sudo ufw allow from proto esp RHEL with firewalld:
$ sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --new-zone=swarm $ sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=swarm --add-source= $ sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=swarm --add-port=2377/tcp --add-port=7946/tcp --add-port=7946/udp --add-port=4789/udp $ sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=swarm --add-protocol=esp $ sudo firewall-cmd --reload In a cloud, add the protocol to the security group of the nodes: a rule for the protocol number 50 (ESP), with the security group of the nodes as the source. Most consoles list it as “Custom protocol 50” or “ESP”.
data.keep-the-docker-build-node-to-itself#Kee: A job on a docker-build class controls the whole Docker engine of its node, so it can inspect and enter every other container there, and read the tokens of any class that runs on that node. The stack files keep the other classes off that node: every runner service except the docker-build ones carries the constraint node.labels.machine-runner-swarm.docker-build != true. The service runner-distributor has no such constraint, because the docker-build class needs the runner on its node too. A node without the label matches it, because Swarm treats a missing label as “not equal”. A node that gets the label stops running those services: Swarm shuts their tasks down and starts replacements on other nodes, or leaves them pending when no other node matches. Add the same constraint to every service you write yourself.
data.labels-and-constraints#Labels and constr:
A service constraint says where Swarm may place a replica. All constraints of a service must hold. Add them under deploy.placement.constraints in the stack file.
deploy: placement: constraints: - node.platform.os == linux - node.platform.arch == aarch64 - node.labels.machine-runner-swarm.zone == build preferences: - spread: node.id The spread: node.id preference spreads the replicas of a service evenly over the matching nodes. The shipped stack files set it.
data.labels-used-by-this-repository#Labels us:
Set a label with docker node update --label-add = . Remove it with --label-rm .
Label Value Used by machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2022 true Every shipped Windows service, which uses ltsc2022 images. Set on Server 2022 and on Server 2025 nodes machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2025 true Services on an ltsc2025 image. Set on Server 2025 nodes only machine-runner-swarm.zone The name of a network zone Services that must run in one zone. A commented example sits in the Linux placement block machine-runner-swarm.docker-build true The docker-build services (pattern A). Refer to Docker Builds machine-runner-swarm.proxy true The node that runs the token proxy, in a cluster. Label it, and deploy with MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_PLACEMENT='node.labels.machine-runner-swarm.proxy == true': the proxy then runs only there, and no runner service ever runs on a node with this label, so jobs never share a node with the class tokens and the proxy state proxy-state. On a single node, with no label, nothing changes. Refer to Where the proxy runs, and when it moves machine-runner-swarm.microvm true The microVM services, on nodes whose Docker daemon runs every container in a Kata microVM. Every other service stays off these nodes. Refer to MicroVM jobs machine-runner-swarm.class. true Pins a service to the labeled nodes. windows-persistent uses machine-runner-swarm.class.windows-persistent. linux-persistent pins itself with node.hostname instead Constraints on labels use the form node.labels. == . For example, node.labels.machine-runner-swarm.docker-build == true.
data.linux-nodes#Linux nodes:
On each node:
Install Docker Engine and confirm that the clock is synchronized. Refer to Prepare each node. Open the ports in Inter-node ports. Run the join command. Nothing else is installed on the node. The runner-distributor service is global, so Swarm starts it on the new node by itself, and it installs the runner into the volume runner-bin of that node (it skips a node with the label machine-runner-swarm.microvm=true: the microVM classes download their own runner, MicroVM jobs). A runner container that Swarm starts there first waits up to 120 seconds for it.
data.managers-and-quorum#Managers and quorum:
Managers keep the cluster state in a Raft log, including every Swarm secret. Swarm encrypts the log at rest and in transit, and each manager holds a copy.
Use one manager for a small installation without availability needs. Use three managers to survive the loss of one, or five to survive the loss of two. Use an odd number, because quorum is a majority and an even number adds no tolerance. Keep the managers on reliable, low-latency links. Quorum matters more for this stack than for a typical Swarm. Every job ends with a runner exit, and only a manager with quorum can create the replacement task. Without quorum, running jobs finish, but the runners are not replaced, so the capacity drops to zero.
Keep jobs off managers when you can. A container breakout on a manager exposes the tokens of every class. In a cluster, label the node that runs the token proxy (a manager), and tell the deploy about it. The runner services never run on a node with that label, so no job shares a node with the class tokens, and that node needs no drain:
$ docker node update --label-add machine-runner-swarm.proxy=true $ sudo env MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_PLACEMENT='node.labels.machine-runner-swarm.proxy == true' docker stack deploy -c deploy/runners.yaml runners Keep the variable with your other deploy variables (Keep the deploy variables in version control), because a deploy without it puts the proxy back on any manager. Drain the other managers (a node drain) so that they run no tasks:
$ docker node update --availability drain Warning The token proxy needs a node that is not drained. token-proxy runs on a manager by default (node.role == manager), and with the label above it runs on the labelled node. A drained node takes no task. If you drain every manager, or the labelled node, the proxy stays Pending (no suitable node) and no runner can claim a job, with no other error: the runners only log 502 or a refused connection to token-proxy. The same happens when the managers are Linux hosts and the proxy is the Windows one (token-proxy-windows also defaults to a manager, and a Windows task cannot run on a Linux manager), and when a Windows-only swarm has no Windows manager. Label a Windows node for it, a worker included, and in a mixed cluster label one Linux and one Windows node, because each proxy also keeps to its own operating system. Never drain the labelled node without the steps in The node of the proxy. A proxy on a worker still holds every class token, so choose a node that runs no jobs: the label keeps the runner services away from it.
On a single-node Swarm the only node is a manager and runs the replicas, and with it the proxy: there is no label, and nothing changes. Never use the Docker socket classes (pattern A) there. Refer to Docker Builds.
data.mixed-architectures#Mixed architectures:
One cluster can have x86_64 and aarch64 nodes. Nothing else is needed on the nodes.
Which build a node gets. Each runner-distributor task reads the architecture of its own node (x86_64 is amd64, aarch64 is arm64), downloads circleci-runner_linux_.tar.gz of that architecture, and checks its SHA-256 against the entry of that architecture in the manifest. If you set MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_SHA256, list the hash of every architecture in the cluster. One pinned version, or current, gives each node the build for its own architecture. A tarball that does not match its entry installs nothing on that node, and the other nodes still install. Placement. A class without an architecture constraint can run on both kinds of node. Add node.platform.arch == aarch64 or node.platform.arch == x86_64 to the deploy.placement.constraints of the classes that need one. The constraint is added to the shared ones of runners.yaml. When the nodes of that architecture are drained or gone, the class stays Pending with no suitable node. It never moves to the other architecture. What is tested. linux/tests/mixed-arch.sh (the optional CI job linux-mixed-arch, see CI) runs the shipped stack file on a Swarm of an amd64 manager and an arm64 worker. It checks that each node installs the runner of its own architecture (the ELF header of the binary, and the tarball SHA-256 of that architecture), that a release whose arm64 tarball does not match its manifest entry installs on the amd64 node and not on the arm64 node, that the real arm64 runner prints its version in a stock cimg/base, and that classes constrained by node.platform.arch run only on their architecture, also when the other node is drained. What is emulated, and what is real. The arm64 worker of that test is a docker:dind container under QEMU user-mode emulation on an x86_64 host, not Arm hardware. QEMU cannot run runc or program iptables itself, so the emulated engine uses native copies of those helpers, and IPVS (the virtual IP of a service) and IPsec on overlays do not work there. The test therefore proves the install, the verification and the placement logic, and not the speed or the system call behavior of an Arm node. It deploys the plain-overlay copy of the stack files, the opt-out of Encrypted class networks, because IPsec cannot run under emulation. The test placement.sh runs the shipped, encrypted files on two nodes and checks that a replica reaches its peer on the other node. A real arm64 node is tested by the single-node jobs linux-arm64 (the distributor and the shipped stack) and e2e-linux-arm64 (a real runner on an Arm VM).
data.network-zones#Network zones:
Use the label machine-runner-swarm.zone when your nodes sit in different network zones, for example a build network and a deploy network with different firewall rules or egress addresses.
Label each node with its zone:
$ docker node update --label-add machine-runner-swarm.zone=build linux-a $ docker node update --label-add machine-runner-swarm.zone=deploy linux-c Copy a service for each zone, give each copy its own resource class, secret, and name, and add the constraint:
linux-deploy: # ... deploy: placement: constraints: - node.platform.os == linux - node.labels.machine-runner-swarm.zone == deploy A job picks the zone by picking the resource class. Do not use zones to balance capacity. Use replicas and spread for that.
data.plan-the-cluster#Plan the cluster: Node type Role Needs Manager Holds the cluster state and every secret. Schedules tasks Docker Engine. Linux managers can manage Windows workers Linux worker Runs Linux services Docker Engine. The runner-distributor service installs the runner for the architecture of the node Windows worker Runs Windows services Docker Engine in Windows-container mode, the ltsc2022 base image, the machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc* labels. Nothing else: the distributor installs the runner and Git
data.registry-needs#Registry needs:
Swarm does not share images between nodes. Each node pulls the image of a task from a registry the first time the task lands there.
Every node must reach the registry of every image that a service on that node uses. Refer to Egress hosts. For a private registry, run docker login on the manager and deploy with docker stack deploy --with-registry-auth. Swarm then passes the credentials to the nodes that run the tasks. Pin images by digest, for example cimg/base:2026.10@sha256:, so that every node runs the same content. Tags such as 21.0 move. Pull large images ahead of time. A Windows servercore image is about 2.2 GB compressed. Public registries apply pull rate limits. A mirror or an authenticated pull avoids failed pulls on a busy cluster. The service runner-distributor runs the stock alpine:3 image on every Linux node, so every Linux node must be able to pull it. Mirror it in your registry and change image in your copy of the stack file, if the nodes cannot reach Docker Hub. Copy it with its digest (docker buildx imagetools create keeps it), so that the pin still holds. The token proxy runs from ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy. Mirror it with its signature (cosign copy), pin the digest in MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_IMAGE, and keep that in your deploy file (Upgrade the token proxy). A manager that cannot reach the registry cannot resolve a tag to a digest when you deploy. Deploy with docker stack deploy --resolve-image never, or use images that you pinned by digest and mirrored. Images are not the whole list. A site with no route to the internet also needs the runner download and the task agent: refer to CircleCI server, proxies, and hosts without internet. Your own image must be in a registry that all nodes of its OS can reach. Refer to Images.
data.verify-the-placement#Verify the placemen: $ docker node ls $ docker node inspect --format '{{ .Spec.Labels }}' $ docker service ps runners_linux-default The NODE column of docker service ps shows where each replica runs. A task that stays in Pending shows the reason in the ERROR column, for example no suitable node (scheduling constraints not satisfied on 2 nodes). Refer to Troubleshooting.
data.windows-nodes#Windows nodes:
On each node:
Install Docker Engine in Windows-container mode and the Windows Containers feature. Pull the images. Refer to Prepare each host. Do this before the join. The runner and Git are not staged: the service runner-distributor-windows installs them on the node after the join. Open the ports in Inter-node ports. Run the join command. Label the node from a manager with the image tags it can run: docker node update --label-add machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2022=true . On Server 2025, add machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2025=true as well, because a 2025 node runs ltsc2022 images too. The labels are required, because the image build must be the host build or an older one. Refer to Image tags and host builds.
Deploy the Linux and Windows files into the same stack name. The service names differ, so they do not collide. Do not use docker stack deploy --prune there, because it removes the services of the other file.
Mixed Linux and Windows clusters are tested by hand, not in CI. The Linux and the Windows stack files are made to be deployed into one Swarm: the constraints on node.platform.os keep each service on its own operating system, and the service names differ. A mixed cluster of a Linux manager and a Windows Server 2022 worker ran real CircleCI jobs on both operating systems, with both runner distributors and an overlay network between Linux and Windows containers. CI tests each operating system on its own Swarm, because the Linux and the Windows VMs of CI cannot reach each other. A mixed cluster needs the ports 2377, 7946 and 4789 open between its nodes (refer to Inter-node ports), and a Linux manager that both stack files are deployed from.

data: Operations: Status and logs, monitoring, capacity, backups, runner upgrades, token rotation, node drain, and uninstall for the Swarm runner stack. Troubleshooting: Symptoms, causes, and fixes for the Docker Swarm runner stack on Linux and Windows, with the error text to search for.

This page describes the day-to-day tasks for a running stack: checking status, running the cluster, upgrading, rotating tokens, patching nodes, and uninstalling. The commands use the stack name runners and the service names of the shipped files. Run them on a manager node.
data.a-claim-whose-outcome-is-unknown#A claim:
A claim can reach CircleCI while its answer is lost: the connection resets, or CircleCI sends no response headers within 60 seconds. The proxy cannot tell whether CircleCI handed a task to that runner. It treats the claim like one that did: it latches the runner, as for a claim that returned a task, and so it fails closed. The runner gets an error and no task, and every later claim of that container is refused (403) until Swarm replaces the container. The cost is one idle runner that is replaced. If CircleCI had allocated a task to that runner, the task never runs, and the job waits for CircleCI to give up on it: rerun the job if it does not. A claim that never reached CircleCI (the proxy cannot connect, for example) is not latched.
The proxy runs from its image, so a restart does not change its version: the same tag or digest as before, unless the tag has moved since (latest moves with a release, edge with a merge to the main branch that passed the end-to-end tests). Upgrade the token proxy says how to change the image on purpose.
data.a-windows-node#A Windows node:
A drain kills a busy Windows container, and no setting changes that. Use pause, which keeps new tasks away and stops nothing:
$ docker node update --availability pause $ docker node ps --filter desired-state=running A running job keeps its container. Each replica that finishes its job exits, and Swarm starts its replacement on another node, so the node empties by itself. An idle replica exits only at its idle timeout (1 hour in the shipped files), and it can still claim a job until then. So the upper bound is the idle timeout plus the longest job. Wait until the second command prints nothing, then drain the node (no job is left to kill), patch it, and set it active.
data.back-up-the-managers-and-recover#Back up:
The state of the cluster is the directory /var/lib/docker/swarm of each manager. It holds the Raft log with every Swarm secret, so the backup holds every runner token. Keep it as you keep a password vault, and delete old copies.
The method needs a second manager: Docker stops on the manager that you copy, and the other managers must keep the quorum. A cluster with one manager has no safe way to take this copy while it runs. Keep your stack files and your deploy variables in version control (Keep the deploy variables in version control) and rely on the redeploy below.
If the managers use autolock, save the unlock key first: docker swarm unlock-key.
Choose a manager that is not the leader (docker node ls, the column MANAGER STATUS), and that does not run token-proxy (docker service ps runners_token-proxy). Stopping Docker on the node of the proxy stops the proxy for the length of the copy, and a move of the proxy to another node loses its state (Where the proxy runs, and when it moves). Use three managers, so that the quorum stands while one is stopped.
If the manager runs jobs, drain it first and wait until its tasks are gone, because stopping Docker ends every container on the node (Swarm mode does not support live restore). A manager that carries the proxy label runs no jobs. Refer to Drain a node for patching.
Stop Docker, copy the whole directory, start Docker again, and set the node active again:
$ sudo systemctl stop docker $ sudo tar -czf swarm-backup-$(date +%F).tar.gz -C /var/lib/docker swarm $ sudo systemctl start docker $ docker node update --availability active For this stack, disaster recovery means redeploying and issuing new tokens, because the stack files hold the whole desired state and the tokens are the only secrets:
Create a new Swarm on a new manager, and join the nodes. Refer to Create the swarm. Label the node of the proxy again (Where the proxy runs, and when it moves). Create a new token for each class, delete the old tokens, and create the secrets. Refer to Rotate a runner token. Create the secret runner-placeholder-token as well, which every runner reads in place of a token, or the deploy fails with secret not found: printf %s machine-runner-swarm-placeholder | linux/setup.sh --secret runner-placeholder on Linux, and the placeholder step of windows/Setup.ps1 on Windows. Refer to The token proxy. Deploy the same stack files with your deploy variables, the same list of -c files, and the same pins. The volumes are not recovered: the proxy starts with no state and asks CircleCI, and a persistent class starts with an empty volume. Restore the backup only to keep the node membership, or after a loss of quorum. Stop Docker on the target manager, replace the contents of /var/lib/docker/swarm with the backup, start Docker, and run docker swarm init --force-new-cluster --advertise-addr . This makes the manager a single-manager cluster with the old state. Unlock it if the swarm uses autolock, check docker node ls and docker service ls, and then add managers and workers again. Back up again afterwards.
data.capacity-and-concurrency#Capacity and co:
The replicas of a class are the jobs it runs at the same time, and the sum over all classes is the capacity of the cluster. A job with parallelism: n is n tasks, so it needs n replicas at once.
Two limits sit above the replicas, and both are set on the CircleCI side:
The runner concurrency of your plan, which all self-hosted runner jobs of the organization share. maxConcurrentTasks of the resource class, which is 20 by default and which CircleCI support raises. A class with more than 20 replicas leaves the extra replicas idle until it is raised. Queued tasks count against concurrency, and the runner inventory shows running tasks only, so runners can look idle while jobs wait. A job for a class that has no runner queues indefinitely and holds concurrency. Check unclaimed_task_count, and cancel the tasks of a class that no longer has runners. Refer to Jobs wait while the runners are idle.
On the Swarm side, the reservations of the replicas on a node must fit in the node. Refer to Size the limits.
The replicas are fixed, and the nodes are yours. The stack does not scale by itself. It has no autoscaling and no integration with a cloud provider: a class runs the number of replicas that its stack file says, on the nodes that you joined to the swarm, and a node that dies is not replaced. Raise the replicas with docker service scale or in the stack file (a change of the file is the durable one), and add nodes yourself. Plan for one node less than you have: the replicas of a class must still fit when any one node is gone, and the node of the token proxy, when it is labelled, carries none of them (Where the proxy runs, and when it moves).
One proxy for the fleet. There is one token-proxy replica for all classes of an OS, by design: a second replica would not share the list of the runners that have claimed. All idle runners poll through it, about one claim every 5 seconds for each, so 100 idle runners are 20 claims a second. The calls of the runners and task agents of the running jobs go through it as well. It limits itself (Monitor the token proxy): 50 requests a second for each client IP, and 512 requests at once. The shipped limits of its container are 0.5 CPU and 128 MB on Linux, and 1 CPU and 512 MB on Windows.
This project has not load-tested the proxy and states no tested fleet size. The CI runs fleets of a few replicas. Before you run a fleet of more than a few dozen replicas, test it with your own load and watch the proxy:
docker stats --no-stream on its node: CPU near its limit, or memory near the limit (a kill for memory restarts the task on the same node, with its state). 503 answers with Retry-After in the log of the runners, which say that the limit of 512 requests at once is reached. A rising count of claims in the summary line, with idle runners. Raise the limits of token-proxy in your copy of the stack file if the proxy is the bottleneck. If one proxy is not enough, the project has no tested way to scale it. A second stack, with another name, its own proxy, and its own classes and tokens, is the structure to try, and it is not tested.
data.check-status-and-logs#Check status and l:
List the services and the replicas that run:
$ docker stack services runners List the tasks, including the finished ones that Swarm keeps for a short time. The ERROR column shows why a task failed or stays pending.
$ docker stack ps runners --no-trunc $ docker service ps --no-trunc runners_linux-default Read the runner output of a service. On Linux, the entrypoint prints one line that starts with circleci-runner-entrypoint:.
$ docker service logs --tail 100 --follow runners_linux-default On Linux, the lines of the runner-distributor service start with runner-distributor:. They say which version the node installs and when the link current moves.
$ docker service logs --tail 50 runners_runner-distributor Healthy single-task replicas show a steady stream of tasks that end in Complete, because every finished job ends a task. A task that ends in Failed with task: non-zero exit needs attention. Alert on these signals:
Tasks that end with a non-zero exit code, including 80 and 1. Code 143 is the exception: a replica that gets SIGTERM while it still retries to reach CircleCI at start-up exits with 143, and needs no action. Log lines that start with circleci-runner: error or circleci-runner-entrypoint: error, and lines that contain 401. In the log of the distributor, alert on cannot download, SHA-256 mismatch, and error. Tasks that stay Pending. Many tasks of one node that end within seconds, one after another. A node can stay Ready and still fail every job it claims. Refer to Many jobs fail within seconds on one node. In the web app, select Runners to see the replicas of each class in the inventory. A name that you do not recognize means that someone else holds a token of that class.
data.circleci-server-proxies-and-hosts-withou: Two setups are not tested yet: CircleCI server, and an installation with no route to the internet. This section says what that means, what works today, and what each part needs from the network. Nothing here promises that a server or an air-gapped installation works.
data.compatibility-with-circleci#Compatibilit: The token proxy sits between the runner and CircleCI, so it depends on the runner API more closely than a plain runner install does. This section lists what it relies on, what the CI tests, and what fails when one of them changes.
data.drain-a-node-for-patching#Drain a node f:
A node drain (docker node update --availability drain) stops the tasks of a node and keeps new tasks away. On Linux, Swarm sends SIGTERM and waits for the grace period, so a running job finishes. On Windows, a drain kills a running job after about 5 seconds, so use the procedure for a Windows node below. Refer to Stop a busy Windows container. Restarting the Docker daemon stops every running container, because live restore does not work in Swarm mode, so always empty the node before you patch Docker or reboot.
$ docker node update --availability drain $ docker node ps Wait until docker node ps shows no running tasks. Swarm starts the replacement tasks on other nodes at once. If the other nodes lack capacity, the replacements stay Pending until the drained tasks exit. Patch and reboot the node, and then return it to service:
$ docker node update --availability active Tasks do not move back to the node by themselves. Single-task replicas restart after every job, so new tasks spread over the nodes again within a short time. Patch managers one at a time, so the cluster keeps its quorum. Refer to Managers and quorum.
data.free-disk-space#Free disk space: A full disk is the most common way a node stops running jobs, and a full manager disk can break Swarm itself. This section says where the space goes, how to keep it from filling, and what to do when it is full.
data.freeze-the-nodes-now#Freeze the nodes no:
To stop all change at once, pin the version that the nodes run now. That version is installed, so the pin needs no network. Read it first, as in See what runs, and then update the distributor. The list of SHA-256 values belongs to the default pin, so name the hash policy together with the version (manifest makes no request for a version that is installed):
$ docker service update --env-add MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_VERSION=3.1.12 --env-add MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_SHA256=manifest runners_runner-distributor A freeze is an emergency step, so the command is quick and changes nothing in your files. Put the same two values in deploy/deploy.env straight away: a deploy without them sets the default pin and its list from the stack file again, which undoes the freeze.
data.how-this-compares-with-machine-runner-3-:
CircleCI’s own runners leave the version to the operator as well, and differ in what they offer to float on:
How the version is chosen Floating Machine runner 3 on a host The operating system package (apt, yum, Homebrew) or a manual install. The runner has no auto-update, so you update the package yourself The package manager’s latest, when you run it Container runner The tag of the image in the Helm values. You set it, and the Helm chart is pinned to a major version tag The image has a floating tag for each major and minor version (kubernetes-3, kubernetes-3.0), and a fixed tag for each patch release Machine runner orchestrator The Helm chart, and the container disk image of the pool The default image tag floats to the latest published image, and each release has a dated tag that pins it This repository MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_VERSION of the distributor service 3.1, 3 and current float. The default is an exact pin This is the model of container runner: an exact pin for production, a floating tag when you want the newest patch release of a line. The default here is the exact pin, so a deploy of the same files always gives the same runner. Choose 3.1 to take patch releases of the line that you have tested, and current only for a class that may run whatever CircleCI releases.
data.if-a-token-leaked#If a token leaked:
Do not swap first. Until the old token is deleted in CircleCI, it stays valid for anyone who holds it. For a class that holds its token in its runners (a persistent class, or Windows), the swap above can take up to N times 5 hours and 5 minutes for N replicas, because it replaces one replica at a time and each busy replica finishes its job first. For a single-task class on Linux the swap is in the proxy and takes seconds, but the leak itself means that someone reached the proxy’s node or the secret, so read the end of this section. Delete the token as soon as its replacement exists:
Create the new token, and the secret with the new token. Use the steps 1 and 2 above. Nothing uses the new secret yet.
Delete the old token at once.
$ circleci runner token list --resource-class /linux-default $ circleci runner token delete CircleCI stops accepting the old token for new claims, so nobody can start a runner on the class with it. Jobs that already run continue until they end. A proxy that still holds the old secret, or idle runners of a persistent class or Windows that still hold it, fail with 401 until the swap, so the class claims no new jobs until step 3 completes.
Swap the secrets. For a single-task class on Linux, swap it in the proxy with the command of step 3 above, and replace the idle runners (docker service update --force --update-parallelism 0 runners_; on Windows, as in Replace refused runners on Windows). For the other classes, replace every replica at once so that the class recovers soon:
$ docker service update --update-parallelism 0 \ --secret-rm linux-default-token \ --secret-add source=linux-default-token-v2,target=circleci_runner_config.yaml,uid=2000,gid=2000,mode=0400 \ runners_linux-default Each replica still finishes the job that it runs before Swarm replaces it. On Windows, drop uid, gid, and mode, and expect the update to end a running job after about 5 seconds: rerun those jobs. Refer to Stop a busy Windows container.
Do steps 4 and 5 above (wait for the update, record the new name in your stack file), and remove the old secret with docker secret rm linux-default-token. Then look for what the leaked token did: the runner inventory in CircleCI for names you do not know, and the jobs that ran on the class.
A leaked token of a single-task class on Linux did not come from a job in a runner container, because those hold no token. Look at who can read Swarm secrets (the docker group on a manager), at the node that runs the proxy, and at the backups of the managers. Rotate the tokens of every class whose secret that path reached, because the proxy holds all of them.
data.keep-the-deploy-variables-in-version-con:
The variables of docker stack deploy are the only record of your choices that the stack files do not hold: the runner pin and its SHA-256 values, the token proxy image, and the proxy placement. A deploy that leaves them out sets the defaults again, with no message: the pin of the shipped file, the tag latest of the proxy image, and the placement node.role == manager. The last one can move the proxy to a node without its state (Where the proxy runs, and when it moves). A change that you made with docker service update is lost in the same way, because the next deploy returns the stack to its files.
So keep the variables in a file in your own repository, next to your stack files, and never deploy by hand. linux/setup.sh --deploy prints a warning when MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_IMAGE is not pinned by digest.
deploy/deploy.env (no secrets in it, only pins and placement):
MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_VERSION=3.1.13 MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_SHA256= MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_IMAGE=ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy@sha256: MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_PLACEMENT='node.labels.machine-runner-swarm.proxy == true' deploy/deploy.sh, which is the only way to deploy (on Linux):
#!/bin/sh set -eu cd "$(dirname "$0")" set -a . ./deploy.env set +a exec docker stack deploy -c runners.yaml runners Add the -c files of your add-on stack files to the last line. Run it with sudo ./deploy/deploy.sh: the script reads the file itself, so sudo does not need to keep the environment. Before the first deploy, and after every edit of the file, check that the values reach the stack:
$ (set -a; . deploy/deploy.env; set +a; docker stack config -c deploy/runners.yaml) | grep -E 'machine-runner-swarm.proxy ==|image: ccilabs' On Windows, load the file into the environment of the session, and deploy from the same session:
Get-Content deploy\deploy.env | ForEach-Object { if ($_ -match '^\s*([^#=\s]+)\s*=\s*(.*)$') { Set-Item -Path "env:$($Matches[1])" -Value $Matches[2].Trim("'") } } docker stack deploy -c deploy\runners.yaml runners Change a pin or the proxy image in the file, review the change like code, and run the script. Upgrade the runner and Upgrade the token proxy show the values.
data.monitor-the-cluster#Monitor the cluster:
Watch the Swarm and CircleCI. The Swarm commands run on a manager, and they need nothing but Docker.
$ docker service ls $ docker node ls $ docker stack ps runners --filter desired-state=running --format '{{.Name}} {{.Node}} {{.CurrentState}}' | grep -v Running The next command counts, for each node, the tasks that ended within the last minute or so. Every finished job ends a task, so a node with many Complete or Failed tasks that ended seconds ago either fails its jobs, or has more work than the others. Compare the nodes. Refer to Many jobs fail within seconds on one node.
$ docker stack ps runners --format '{{.Node}} {{.CurrentState}}' | grep -E ' (Complete|Failed) [0-9]+ seconds? ago' | cut -d' ' -f1 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn The runner API shows what CircleCI sees. It needs a personal API token. Refer to the runner API reference. Set the host of the runner API first: runner.circleci.com for CircleCI cloud, and the runner API URL of your installation for CircleCI server (refer to CircleCI server, proxies, and hosts without internet).
$ RUNNER_API=https://runner.circleci.com $ curl -s -H "Circle-Token: $CIRCLECI_API_TOKEN" \ "$RUNNER_API/api/v3/runner?resource-class=/linux-default" \ | jq -r '.items[] | "\(.name) \(.last_connected)"' $ curl -s -H "Circle-Token: $CIRCLECI_API_TOKEN" \ "$RUNNER_API/api/v3/runner/tasks?resource-class=/linux-default" $ curl -s -H "Circle-Token: $CIRCLECI_API_TOKEN" \ "$RUNNER_API/api/v3/runner/tasks/running?resource-class=/linux-default" Signal Where Alert when Replicas running against desired docker service ls, the REPLICAS column Fewer than desired for more than 10 minutes. Refer to A task stays pending Node state docker node ls A node is not Ready, a manager is Unreachable, or no manager is Leader Runners connected /api/v3/runner, items and last_connected Fewer items than replicas, or a last_connected older than 2 minutes, which is when the CLI stops calling an instance online Jobs that wait /api/v3/runner/tasks, unclaimed_task_count Above 0 for several minutes. With every replica busy, add replicas. With idle replicas, check concurrency Jobs that run /api/v3/runner/tasks/running, running_runner_tasks Equal to the replicas of the class for a long time: the class is full Task exits docker service ps Exit code 80, or a restart loop. Refer to The container restarts every 10 seconds Runner distributor docker service ps runners_runner-distributor, and its log Fewer running tasks than Linux nodes, or log lines with cannot download or SHA-256 mismatch. A line with not adopting it says that current is not a version that the distributor follows Disk df -h /var/lib/docker on every node, and docker system df Above 80 percent on a worker, above 70 percent on a manager. Refer to Free disk space A node that fails jobs The tasks that ended within seconds, for each node (the command above) One node far above the others, or a node with tasks that end in Failed over and over. Refer to Many jobs fail within seconds on one node Token proxy docker service ps runners_token-proxy, docker stats --no-stream on its node, and the summary line of its log Restarts, CPU near the limit, or a rising count of refused claims. Refer to Monitor the token proxy A job that starts A canary job for each class (below) The canary fails, or does not start within a few minutes A canary job. Every signal above is a part.
