The job ends with a message that points at an issue with your infrastructure, and its log stops without an error of its own.
Cause. The runner stopped while it ran the job, or its connection to CircleCI broke. Typical causes are a node that died or rebooted, a stop from outside (an update, a scale-down, or a node drain) that outlasted the grace period or, on Windows, killed the job after about 5 seconds, or an out-of-memory kill.
Fix. Find the container that ran the job with docker service ps --no-trunc runners_: a task that ended with non-zero exit or on a node that is Down names the cause. Self-hosted runners do not retry a job, so rerun it. Refer to Node death and Stop a busy Windows container.
data.a-node-cannot-join-the-swarm#A node cann:
docker swarm join times out or fails with a connection error.
Cause. The manager is not reachable on the advertised address and port 2377, or the manager listens on the loopback address only.
Fix. Open the ports in Inter-node ports, and check that the swarm was initialized with a routable --advertise-addr.
data.a-service-shows-no-logs#A service shows:
docker service logs runners_ prints nothing, or prints less than you expect.
Cause. Swarm prunes the old tasks of a slot, and their logs go with them, because every finished job ends a task and the history limit is 2. The command also works only for the local, json-file, and journald drivers, so a service that you moved to a shipping driver has no logs to read back.
Fix. Read docker service ps --no-trunc runners_ for the reason a task ended, and docker logs on the node for a task that still has its container. To keep logs, ship them. Refer to Ship the logs.
data.a-service-update-is-paused-or-rolled-bac:
docker service update or docker stack deploy stops partway, and docker service inspect --format '{{.UpdateStatus.State}}' runners_ prints paused, rollback_started, or rollback_completed. The Message field says which task failed.
Cause. A new task failed to start, for example with exit code 80 after a wrong setting or a missing secret. The stack files set no failure_action, so Swarm pauses the update at the first failure, and the replicas that it did not reach keep the old version.
Fix. Read why the task failed with docker service ps --no-trunc runners_, correct the cause in your stack file, and deploy again with the same list of files. To go back at once, run docker service update --rollback runners_. Refer to Update the images.
data.a-task-is-rejected-because-the-image-can:
docker service ps shows rejected with No such image or an authentication error.
Cause. The node cannot pull the image: the registry is not reachable, the image is private, or the registry rate limit applies.
Fix. Check egress to the registry, deploy with docker stack deploy --with-registry-auth for a private registry, and use a mirror or authenticated pulls. Refer to Registry needs, and, for a site without a route to the registries, What needs the internet.
data.a-task-stays-pending#A task stays pendin:
The ERROR column of docker service ps --no-trunc runners_ shows no suitable node, and the task stays in the Pending state.
Cause. No node satisfies the task.
scheduling constraints not satisfied on N nodes: no node matches the constraints. A label is missing, the OS or architecture differs, or the service needs a worker and the label sits on a manager. insufficient resources on N nodes: the reservations of the replicas exceed what the matching nodes have free. Reservations equal the limits, so extra replicas wait on purpose. An error that mentions max replicas per node: the SSH add-on runs one replica on each node, because a node has one host-mode port 54782. Add nodes, or lower replicas. Fix. Compare the constraints of the service with the labels of the nodes.
$ docker service inspect --format '{{ json .Spec.TaskTemplate.Placement }}' runners_ $ docker node inspect --format '{{ .Description.Hostname }} {{ .Spec.Labels }}' $(docker node ls -q) Add the missing label with docker node update --label-add, lower replicas, or lower the reservations. Refer to Labels and constraints.
data.cannot-connect-to-the-docker-daemon-in-a:
docker build fails with Cannot connect to the Docker daemon.
Cause. The class does not mount a Docker engine, by design.
Fix. Use the opt-in class, or a daemonless builder. Refer to Docker Builds.
data.collect-information-for-a-bug-report#Col:
Gather the output of these commands. Remove tokens before you share it.
$ docker version $ docker node ls $ docker stack ps runners --no-trunc $ docker service logs --tail 200 runners_ $ docker service logs --tail 200 runners_token-proxy On Linux, include the runner version and the log of the distributor: docker run --rm -v runners_runner-bin:/v:ro alpine cat /v/current/VERSION on the node, and docker service logs --tail 100 runners_runner-distributor. On Windows, include the log of runner-distributor-windows: docker service logs --tail 100 runners_runner-distributor-windows. Then open an issue.
data.downloads-fail-right-after-docker-swarm-:
Outbound connections fail with Unable to connect to the remote server or no such host for a few seconds after you create the swarm.
Fix. Pull the images first, and run docker swarm init last. The distributor retries its downloads.
data.error-0xc0370101#Error: 0xc0370101:
A task is rejected with The container operating system does not match the host operating system.
Cause. The image build is newer than the host build. A Server 2022 host runs only ltsc2022 images, and a Server 2025 host runs ltsc2025 and ltsc2022 images. The placement labels normally keep a service off a node that cannot run its image, so look for a node that carries a label it should not.
Fix. Use an image tag that the host can run, and label the node with the matching machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2022 and windows-ltsc2025 capabilities. Refer to Image tags and host builds.
data.error-could-not-find-the-systems-ip-addr:
docker swarm init fails with could not find the system's IP address - specify one with --advertise-addr.
Fix. Always pass the IPv4 address of the host: docker swarm init --advertise-addr . A host with several network adapters needs it too, and Setup.ps1 -InitSwarm requires -AdvertiseAddr.
data.error-does-not-match-its-sha-256-record#:
The container exits with code 80 and a message such as /opt/machine-runner-swarm/versions/3.1.13/bin/circleci-runner does not match its SHA-256 record ...: refusing to start.
Cause. The binary in the volume is not the one that the distributor recorded. The install is incomplete, the volume was changed, or the disk is damaged. The entrypoint checks the binary at every start and never runs one that differs. Refer to Runner binary integrity on Linux.
Fix. The distributor compares the active binary with its record at every check, and installs the version again when it differs. To do it now, force an update of the distributor. It downloads the version again on every node, and the next containers start:
$ docker service update --force runners_runner-distributor If the binary changes again, find out what writes to the volume: a privileged container on the node, or a person with access to it.
data.error-failed-to-remove-working-directory:
Every task fails. The runner log shows failed to remove working directory before starting task or failed to remove working directory while cleaning up task, each with permission denied. A could not clean up task line with the same error has the same cause.
Cause. This happens only if someone sets CIRCLECI_RUNNER_CLEANUP_WORK_DIR to true on a Linux service: the entrypoint and the stack files default it to false. The runner removes its working directory itself, as the runner user (uid 2000), but the job user owns that directory and its files. The removal fails even for the first task, because the parent directory belongs to the job user too. The stack files and the entrypoint set the variable to false for this reason.
Fix. Set CIRCLECI_RUNNER_CLEANUP_WORK_DIR: "false", or remove the variable so that the entrypoint default applies, and deploy again. A single-task container is discarded after the job, so nothing is lost. In a persistent class, start every job with a step that removes what an earlier job left. Refer to Working directory cleanup.
data.error-hcssystemstart-context-deadline-ex:
A Windows container does not start, and docker service ps --no-trunc shows hcs::System::Start: context deadline exceeded.
Cause. One cause is an image build that replaced a registry key. New-Item -Force on an existing key deletes its values and subkeys. On HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\cexecsvc, it removes the definition of the container exec service, and the container cannot start.
Fix. Rebuild the image, and set registry values with reg add or Set-ItemProperty, which only set a value. Never use New-Item -Force on an existing registry key.
data.error-jobs-cannot-be-stepped-down-in-thi:
The container exits with code 80 and the message jobs cannot be stepped down in this image: it needs sudo or util-linux setpriv.
Cause. The image has neither sudo nor util-linux setpriv, or it has no setpriv and no su to start the runner.
A hardened class (MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO=false) exits with code 80 and the message needs util-linux setpriv with --no-new-privs when the image has no util-linux setpriv, even if it has sudo. The hardened class never steps jobs down with sudo, because a setuid binary could then lift a job to root.
Fix. Add the packages in a derived image. Refer to What an image needs.
data.error-must-be-owned-by-root-and-not-grou:
The container exits with code 80 and a message such as /opt/machine-runner-swarm/versions/3.1.13/bin/circleci-runner must be owned by root and not group/world writable.
Cause. The entrypoint refuses to run a runner that the job user or the runner user can replace. The distributor makes the files of the volume owned by root with the mode 0755, so something changed them.
Fix. On the node, set the owner and the mode again:
$ docker run --rm -v runners_runner-bin:/v alpine sh -c 'chown -R 0:0 /v && chmod -R go-w /v'
data.error-secret-not-found#Error: secret not:
docker stack deploy fails with secret not found: linux-default-token.
Cause. A service references an external secret that does not exist. Every service in the file needs its -token secret, and on Linux every runner service also needs runner-placeholder-token.
Fix. Create the secret, or delete the service from your copy of the stack file together with its entries under secrets: and networks:. On Windows, runners.yaml needs only windows-default-token, and each add-on stack file (custom-image.yaml, persistent.yaml, docker-build.yaml, ssh-rerun.yaml) needs its own -token secret when you deploy it.
data.error-swarm-is-encrypted-and-needs-to-be:
A Swarm command fails with Swarm is encrypted and needs to be unlocked before it can be used.
Cause. The managers use autolock, and this manager restarted. It stays out of the cluster until someone unlocks it.
Fix. Run docker swarm unlock on the manager and enter the unlock key. Get the key from a manager that is unlocked with docker swarm unlock-key. Refer to Unlock a locked swarm.
data.error-the-swarm-does-not-have-a-leader#E:
A Swarm command fails with The swarm does not have a leader. It's possible that too few managers are online.
Cause. The managers lost their quorum. A majority of them must be online: two of three, or three of five. Without it, running jobs finish, but no replacement task starts, so the capacity of the cluster drops to zero.
Fix. Bring the managers back, starting with the ones that were stopped last, and check docker node ls on a reachable manager. A manager that is locked needs docker swarm unlock. If the managers are lost for good, recover the cluster from one surviving manager with docker swarm init --force-new-cluster --advertise-addr . Refer to Back up the managers, and recover and Managers and quorum.
data.error-this-node-is-not-a-swarm-manager#E:
Swarm commands such as docker stack deploy fail on a worker.
Fix. Run them on a manager. Use docker node ls on a manager to list the managers.
data.jobs-in-the-hardened-class-cannot-instal:
apt-get install fails with Permission denied, or sudo reports that the user may not run sudo.
Cause. The hardened class steps jobs down with setpriv --no-new-privs, so sudo cannot raise the job user, by design.
Fix. Build the tools into the image. Refer to Bring your own image.
data.jobs-queue-but-no-runner-claims-them#Job:
Cause. The resource_class in the config does not match a class that has running replicas, or the replicas cannot reach CircleCI.
Fix.
Check that / in the job config equals the namespace and the service name. Check the inventory under Runners in the web app. If the replicas are missing, check that the tasks run and that the egress rules allow the hosts in Egress hosts. Check that jobs are not in a class that has replicas: 0.
data.jobs-wait-while-the-runners-are-idle#Job:
The runner inventory shows idle runners, and jobs stay queued.
Cause. The inventory shows running tasks only. Queued tasks are invisible there, and they count against concurrency. A class can sit at the maxConcurrentTasks limit of the resource class (20 by default) or at the runner concurrency of your plan, and jobs for a class that has no runner queue forever and hold concurrency.
Fix. Ask the runner API how many tasks wait, and compare it with the replicas:
$ RUNNER_API=https://runner.circleci.com # the runner API of your installation, for CircleCI server $ curl -s -H "Circle-Token: $CIRCLECI_API_TOKEN" \ "$RUNNER_API/api/v3/runner/tasks?resource-class=/" A count above 0 with idle replicas points at a limit or at a class name that no service serves. Cancel the tasks of a class that no longer has runners, and ask CircleCI support to raise maxConcurrentTasks. Refer to Capacity and concurrency.
data.many-jobs-fail-within-seconds-on-one-nod:
Jobs of a class fail within seconds, or end with no work done, and docker stack ps runners lists many tasks of one node that ended seconds after they started. The node is Ready, and the other nodes are fine.
Cause. A node that is Ready can still fail every job it claims: a full disk, a runner volume whose link current is wrong, a Docker engine in a bad state, a clock that is far off, or a broken route to the registry or to CircleCI after the claim. A failed task is replaced at once, and the replacement claims again, so the broken node takes a large share of the jobs of the class and fails them one after another. Swarm does not see it, because the node answers its heartbeats.
Fix.
Count the tasks that ended in the last minute for each node. A node far above the others is the one:
$ docker stack ps runners --format '{{.Node}} {{.CurrentState}}' | grep -E ' (Complete|Failed) [0-9]+ seconds? ago' | cut -d' ' -f1 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn $ docker stack ps runners --no-trunc --format '{{.Node}} {{.Name}} {{.CurrentState}} {{.Error}}' | grep '' | head -20 Stop it from taking jobs. On Linux, drain it. On Windows, pause it: jobs that fail in seconds free the node quickly, and a drain would kill a good job after about 5 seconds (A Windows node).
$ docker node update --availability drain Find the cause on the node:
$ df -h /var/lib/docker $ docker run --rm alpine true $ docker run --rm -v runners_runner-bin:/v:ro alpine ls -l /v/current $ docker ps -a --filter 'name=runners_' --format '{{.Names}} {{.Status}}' | head $ timedatectl show -p NTPSynchronized --value Read the log of the newest failed container (docker logs ) and, on Linux, journalctl -u docker -n 100. A full disk is in Free disk space. A missing current means that the distributor has not installed a runner on this node: read its log (The runner waits for the distributor, and then exits with code 80).
Fix the cause and set the node active. If the cause is not clear, take the node out for good: run docker swarm leave on it, then docker node rm on a manager, and rebuild it.
Rerun the jobs that failed. Self-hosted runners do not retry a job by themselves.
To see it early, alert on the count in step 1 and keep a canary job for each class.
data.overlay-network-creation-fails#Overlay n:
Cause. On a host with one network adapter, an existing transparent network can block the creation of overlay networks.
Fix. Refer to the Microsoft documentation on Windows container networking, and move the transparent network to a second adapter or remove it.
data.permission-denied-on-optmachine-runner-s:
On RHEL, a replica reports Permission denied for files under /opt/machine-runner-swarm while SELinux is enforcing.
Cause. Untested: this repository’s CI does not run on RHEL. The runner is in a named volume, and Docker labels the files of a volume for containers in the usual case. A setup where it does not leaves the files with a type that containers may not read. A Swarm service mount has no :z option to relabel them.
Fix. Confirm the denial with sudo ausearch -m avc -ts recent, then label the volume on the node. The files that the distributor writes later inherit the label.
$ sudo chcon -R -t container_file_t /var/lib/docker/volumes/runners_runner-bin/_data Keep SELinux enforcing. Do not disable it to work around the error, and open an issue with the avc line if you needed this.
data.permission-denied-on-the-docker-socket-i:
A job on a docker-build class fails with permission denied while trying to connect to the Docker daemon socket at unix:///var/run/docker.sock.
Cause. The entrypoint adds the job user to the group of the mounted socket so that the job can use it, but it skips a socket whose group id is 0, because group 0 is root’s group and giving the job user that group would be wrong. A host whose socket is owned by root:root therefore leaves the job user without access.
Fix. Give the socket on the host a group that is not root, normally docker. With systemd, the socket unit of Docker sets it with SocketGroup=docker. Check with stat -c '%U:%G %g' /var/run/docker.sock, which must show a group id above 0, and deploy again so that the new containers pick it up. Refer to Docker Builds.
data.setupps1-reports-check-windows-server-fa:
Cause. The helper supports Windows Server 2022 (build 20348) and 2025 (build 26100), and the host is another version or a client edition.
Fix. Use a Server 2022 or 2025 host. Server 2019 is untested: the stack files have no label or placement for it, so a 2019 node needs your own image tag, label, and constraint.
data.tar-fails-with-cannot-stat-when-you-test:
You run C:\Program Files\Git\usr\bin\tar.exe in a container with a backslash path, and it fails with Cannot stat.
Cause. The task agent starts this tar.exe from the root of the drive, with --force-local, and with forward-slash operands that are relative to the root. For C:\cci\w\ws, it passes cci/w/ws. It never passes a backslash operand, which this tar does not accept.
Fix. Use the same form in your test. A workspace step that fails in a job is more likely a missing tar or gzip on the PATH, as in the previous entry.
data.the-container-restarts-every-10-seconds#:
docker service ps lists many tasks of one slot, each with task: non-zero exit (80) or (1), started about 10 seconds apart.
Cause. The runner or the entrypoint exits at start-up because of a configuration error. Swarm restarts the container after the restart delay. It never gives up and never backs off, so the loop runs until you fix the cause. The log line names the problem:
Log text Cause api.auth_token must be set The secret has an empty token, or the wrong structure runner.name must be set CIRCLECI_RUNNER_NAME is missing runner.name must contain only letters, numbers, .()_-, and spaces The name has other characters, or exceeds 64 characters because of a long hostname or class name --runner.mode must be one of "continuous","single-task" CIRCLECI_RUNNER_MODE has another value error parsing config file, or a missing file (exit code 1) The secret is not valid YAML, or it is not attached with the target circleci_runner_config.yaml circleci-runner-entrypoint: error: ... The entrypoint found a missing prerequisite, or no runner. Refer to the Linux entries below Fix. Correct the stack file or the secret, and deploy again. To stop the loop meanwhile, run docker service scale runners_=0.
The restart delay is a pause between starts, not a back-off. Swarm creates the replacement task at once and starts its container after the delay, so the containers start 10 to 12 seconds apart. A max_attempts value in restart_policy would end the loop, but then the runner never recovers by itself after you fix the cause, so the stack does not set it. Alert on exit code 80 instead.
data.the-disk-fills-up#The disk fills up:
A task fails with no space left on device, Docker commands on the node fail, or the node stops taking jobs.
Cause. Each finished job leaves a stopped container, and Swarm keeps the last five tasks of every slot by default. Images, build cache, and logs add to it.
Fix. Stop the node from taking jobs, free the space, and set the history limit. The steps, and the schedule that keeps it from happening again, are in Free disk space. A node that fails jobs because its disk is full can also look like Many jobs fail within seconds on one node.
data.the-distributor-log-shows-cannot-downloa:
A line of docker service logs runners_runner-distributor reads runner-distributor: cannot download , for the file manifest.json or for a tarball such as /circleci-runner_linux_amd64.tar.gz. The distributor keeps the runner that it has and tries again in 5 minutes. Without a runner, the runner containers of the node end in the entry above.
Cause. The node cannot reach circleci-binary-releases.s3.amazonaws.com or your mirror: an egress rule, a proxy, DNS, or the clock. Or the file is not on the mirror, for example the version that you pinned. An https mirror needs a certificate from a public certificate authority, because the distributor uses the CA bundle of the stock Alpine image. A proxy rarely helps: the wget of the distributor reads only the lowercase http_proxy, sends an https:// URL to the proxy as a plain GET and not as a CONNECT, and ignores no_proxy.
Fix. Download the same file from the node with the same tool:
$ docker run --rm alpine wget -q -O /dev/null https://circleci-binary-releases.s3.amazonaws.com/circleci-runner/manifest.json && echo reachable Open the host in Egress hosts, or fix the mirror. A mirror that the node reaches without a proxy is the dependable setup. Refer to Run the downloads from a mirror and Proxies and certificate authorities, component by component.
data.the-distributor-log-shows-not-adopting-i:
The log has runner-distributor: current is (major ), not 3: not adopting it (MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_MAJOR), or current has SHA-256 , which no versioned release of the manifest has: not adopting it.
Cause. The first line says that current of CircleCI moved to another major version. The distributor keeps the version that it has, so nothing breaks, and the nodes stay where they are. The second line says that the manifest names no version for current, which happens with a mirror that has an old or edited manifest.json.
Fix. For a new major version, read the changelog of the runner, try it, and then set MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_MAJOR or pin the version. Refer to Pin a version. For the second line, copy manifest.json to the mirror again, with the tarball of the version that current names.
data.the-distributor-log-shows-sha-256-mismat:
A line reads runner-distributor: SHA-256 mismatch for circleci-runner_linux_amd64.tar.gz : got , wanted : refusing to install. The distributor installs nothing and tries again later.
Cause. The tarball does not have the SHA-256 that the manifest, or your list in MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_SHA256, names. The usual causes are a list that lacks the value of one architecture (a fleet with amd64 and arm64 nodes needs both), a mirror whose tarball and manifest do not belong together, and a proxy that changes the download.
Fix. Compare wanted with the SHA-256 of the file that you expect, from the checksums.txt of the release or from the manifest. Correct the list, the mirror, or the proxy. Never copy the got value into the list without checking where the file came from.
data.the-distributor-of-windows-keeps-a-versi:
The log says circleci-runner is in use: removing it at a later check.
Cause. Windows cannot remove files that a running container uses. A job on that version is still running.
Fix. None needed: the distributor removes the version at a later check, when the job has ended.
data.the-first-task-on-a-host-takes-a-long-ti:
Cause. The node pulls the Server Core image, which is about 2.2 GB compressed, when the first task lands there.
Fix. Run docker pull for the image on each node before you deploy.
data.the-runner-log-shows-401#The runner log:
The log contains 401 (Unauthorized), and the runner never claims a job.
Cause. CircleCI rejected the token. The token was deleted, or the secret holds a token of another class or a mistyped one. A 401 is not a clock problem: a clock that drifted fails the TLS handshake before any request, which gives the error in the next entry.
Fix.
Check that the secret -token holds the token of the resource class with the same name as the service. A swapped token does not fail loudly. The runner serves the class of its token, so jobs of the intended class stay queued. On Linux, the token is in the proxy, so look in the log of runners_token-proxy for upstream status 401, and check that its variable for the class names the right secret. Create a new token and rotate it. Refer to Rotate a runner token.
data.the-runner-log-shows-403-and-the-proxy-l:
The runner log contains 403 (Forbidden) for the claim, and the log of runners_token-proxy says claim from refused.
Cause. The proxy answers a claim only from an address that Swarm DNS lists now for tasks. of a class that it serves, and only once for each container. The reason is in the log line.
Fix.
not a runner of any class: the class is not in the proxy (a new class needs its secret -token and, on Linux, its network under token-proxy; refer to Define a class), the proxy is not on the network of the class, or the claim comes from a container that is not a runner. this runner has already claimed a task: the proxy restarted while the runner was idle, the proxy moved to another node and started with a lost state, or a claim of this runner had an unknown outcome and the proxy latched the runner to fail closed. The runner retries every 5 seconds until it is replaced, at its idle timeout. On Linux, replace the idle runners now with docker service update --force --update-parallelism 0 runners_. On Windows, do not: it kills the busy jobs. Remove only the refused containers instead. Refer to Replace refused runners on Windows, A claim whose outcome is unknown, Restart the proxy and Where the proxy runs, and when it moves. too many claims (429), or a 503 with Retry-After: the proxy limits each client IP, and serves at most 512 requests at once. A runner stays far below the limits, so look for a client that polls in a loop, or for a proxy that is overloaded. Refer to Monitor the token proxy and Capacity and concurrency.
data.the-runner-log-shows-x509-certificate-er:
The log contains x509: certificate has expired or is not yet valid, or x509: certificate signed by unknown authority, and the runner never connects.
Cause. The clock of the node drifted, so TLS to CircleCI fails silently as far as the job is concerned. Or an inspecting proxy re-signs the traffic with a CA that the container does not trust.
Fix. Check the clock with timedatectl show -p NTPSynchronized --value, which must print yes, and fix NTP on the node. For the CA of an inspecting proxy or of your CircleCI server, add the CA to your image for the runner and the jobs. The token proxy and the distributors read other stores, so they need their own step. Refer to Proxies and certificate authorities, component by component, Private certificate authorities, and Do proxies and custom certificate authorities work?.
data.the-runner-never-claims-a-job#The runner:
The container runs and logs the start-up lines, but the runner never claims a job and logs no clear error.
Cause. The runner creates a symbolic link when it installs the task agent. Without the SeCreateSymbolicLinkPrivilege, it retries the download forever. This happens when the container runs as a user other than ContainerAdministrator.
Fix. Never set user: in a Windows service, and never change USER in a derived image.
data.the-runner-waits-for-the-distributor-and:
The log of a runner container shows circleci-runner-entrypoint: waiting for the runner-distributor of this node to install the runner. After the wait, which is 120 seconds by default, the container exits with code 80 and the message /opt/machine-runner-swarm/current is 'missing': the runner-distributor of this node has not installed the runner. Swarm starts a new container after 10 seconds, and the loop repeats.
Cause. The volume runner-bin of the node has no runner yet. The runner-distributor task of the node is not running, or it cannot download the runner, or it refuses the download. A first deploy and a node that just joined are normal: the wait covers a download of a few seconds, and the next container starts as soon as current exists.
Fix. Check that the distributor runs on that node, and read its log. Each line starts with the task and the node.
$ docker service ps --no-trunc runners_runner-distributor $ docker service logs --tail 50 runners_runner-distributor A node that has no task is Down, drained, or not a Linux node. Otherwise the log names the problem: refer to The distributor log shows cannot download and The distributor log shows SHA-256 mismatch. To wait longer, set MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_WAIT in the environment of the runner services.
data.the-token-proxy-service-does-not-start-t:
docker service ps runners_token-proxy --no-trunc (Windows: runners_token-proxy-windows) shows No such image, manifest unknown, pull access denied, or no matching manifest for , and the runners get connection errors for token-proxy. The distributor and the runner are unaffected.
Cause. The image is ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy (or what MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_IMAGE names). The usual causes are a node that cannot reach Docker Hub (a proxy or an allow list), a tag that does not exist (a typo, or edge before the first publication of the main branch), a local image name such as machine-runner-swarm-proxy:dev that exists on another node and not on the node that runs the proxy, and a platform that the tag lacks (Windows on Arm).
Fix. Check the name with docker service inspect runners_token-proxy --format '{{.Spec.TaskTemplate.ContainerSpec.Image}}' and pull it on the node: docker pull . Behind an allow list, add Docker Hub (Egress hosts), or mirror the image and set MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_IMAGE (Upgrade the token proxy). A local build must be on the node that the proxy runs on: build it there, or docker save | ssh docker load. Swarm tries again by itself.
data.the-windows-runner-fails-to-start-cannot:
docker service ps --no-trunc runners_windows-default shows tasks that fail with cannot access path ...\runner-bin\_data\current (or ...\git\current) or with invalid mount config, and Swarm starts the next task after 10 seconds.
Cause. The service runner-distributor-windows has not flipped the links current and git\current of the volume on this node yet. This is normal on a new node, because the first download of the runner and of portable Git takes a few minutes. It lasts when the distributor cannot install.
Fix. Read the log of the distributor: docker service logs runners_runner-distributor-windows. A SHA-256 mismatch, a cannot download line, or not adopting it names the cause. The service must run on the node: docker service ps runners_runner-distributor-windows needs a task there, so the node must carry the label machine-runner-swarm.windows-ltsc2022=true, and the base image must be pulled. On a host behind a proxy, set HTTPS_PROXY on the distributor service (it reads HTTPS_PROXY only, and no NO_PROXY). For a site without internet access, refer to Upgrade the runner on Windows.
data.warning-sudo-unable-to-send-audit-messag:
Every sudo call in a job prints unable to send audit message.
Cause. The AUDIT_WRITE capability is dropped.
Fix. Keep AUDIT_WRITE out of cap_drop. A hardened class keeps it in cap_add.
data.windows-container-exits-with-code-322122:
A job ends about 5 seconds after a rolling update, a scale down, a node drain, or docker stop. docker service ps --no-trunc shows task: non-zero exit (3221225786), which is 0xC000013A.
Cause. The container was stopped from outside while it ran a job, and Windows gives a stock Server Core container about 5 seconds, whatever stop_grace_period says. A job that finishes by itself does not end this way.
Fix. Rerun the interrupted jobs, and change a service only while its class runs no job. Refer to Stop a busy Windows container.
data.workspaces-fail-because-tar-or-gzip-is-m:
persist_to_workspace or attach_workspace reports a missing tar or gzip.
Cause. The Git mount is missing, or the PATH of the service does not include C:\Program Files\Git\usr\bin. The PATH of a service replaces the one of the image.
Fix. Keep both mounts and the full PATH from the shipped file.

data: Changelog: Release notes are on GitHub Releases. Read every release between yours and the one you install before you upgrade. Migrate from Docker Compose: Move from the old docker-compose.yml setup to the Docker Swarm stack, and map each Compose setting to its Swarm equivalent.

The release notes are on GitHub Releases. Read the notes of every release between yours and the one that you install before you upgrade: the project follows Semantic Versioning and starts at 0.x, so a minor release can contain breaking changes, which the notes list first.
A CircleCI job writes the notes of each release from the Conventional Commits on main, with the rules in cliff.toml. Nobody edits this file by hand, and the release job never commits to main. Each release bundle contains a CHANGELOG.md with the notes of every release, and you can create the same text with git cliff. Refer to Releasing for how versions and notes are made, and to Contributing for the commit types and for how to mark a breaking change.

Warning This repository no longer ships the Docker Compose setup. The files docker-compose.yml, base-image/, convenience-image/, and machine-image/ were removed in the Swarm rewrite, and the change is marked [BREAKING] in the changelog. Find the old files in the Git history with git log -- docker-compose.yml.
The old setup ran the runner in single-task mode with restart: unless-stopped and replicas. A restart reuses the same container, so the old setup did not give a clean environment for every job. The Swarm stack creates a new container for every job. Refer to Why not plain Docker Compose?
This page describes how to move an existing setup. It covers Linux hosts, which the old setup supported.
data.behavior-to-expect#Behavior to expect: Runner updates. With the default settings, the runner is an exact pin: the newest version that this repository’s CI tests, which each release of this repository bumps, so the nodes keep a version until you change it. Set 3.1, 3 or current to let it follow CircleCI’s manifest. Refer to Upgrade the runner on Linux. Sudo. The default classes keep passwordless sudo, as the old images did. The hardened class removes it. Refer to Concepts. Fixed replicas. The stack does not scale by itself. A class runs the replicas that its stack file says, on the nodes that you joined to the swarm, and a node that dies is not replaced. Refer to Capacity and concurrency. Startup time. A new container starts for every job, so a job waits about 10 seconds longer than before for the next claim, plus the task agent download. Add replicas for busy classes. Swarm on one host. Swarm mode is required even on a single host. The shipped helper and the install page start it on the loopback address, so nothing is exposed. Working directory. The runner no longer removes the working directory on Linux, because it runs as another user than the jobs and cannot delete their files. The container is new for every job, so nothing stays. The old machine service becomes a persistent class, which keeps files between jobs, so start its jobs with a cleanup step. Refer to Working directory cleanup.
data.migrate#Migrate: Decide how to name the classes. A Swarm service must have the name of its resource class. To keep your resource classes and tokens, name each service after the class that it replaces, for example base. To start with new classes, create them as described in Create the resource classes. Prepare the host. Docker Engine is already there. Start Swarm, and install nothing else: the runner-distributor service of the stack installs the runner on every node. Refer to Start Swarm. Create the secrets. Use the token of each class. It is the value of CIRCLECI_RUNNER_API_AUTH_TOKEN in your old .env file. Create one secret for each service, as in Create the secrets. Choose the images. The old convenience service maps to cimg/base, or to another cimg image. The old base service maps to a stock image that has the tools you need. If your Dockerfiles installed extra tools, move them into an image that you derive. Refer to Linux: bring your own image. Edit the stack file. Rename or copy the services, set the replica counts you used before, and keep only the services you need. The old machine service becomes linux/stack/persistent.yaml. Refer to Resource Classes. Deploy next to the old setup. Both can run at the same time, because the new runner names are different. Check that the new runners show up in the inventory. If a new service keeps a class whose old runners are busy, the token proxy sees running tasks at its first start and cannot tell whose they are, so it refuses the runners that are present. Those runners claim nothing until their idle timeout, or until you run docker service update --force --update-parallelism 0 runners_ once the old runners are idle. New classes avoid this. Refer to Restart the proxy. Stop the old setup. When the old runners are idle, run docker compose down in the old directory. A running job is stopped after the Compose grace period, so wait for a quiet period first. Clean up. Delete the old .env files, which hold tokens in clear text. If you created new classes, delete the old tokens and classes in CircleCI.
data.what-changed#What changed: Old setup Swarm stack Services base, convenience, and machine in docker-compose.yml One service for each resource class in linux/stack/runners.yaml. The continuous runner is linux/stack/persistent.yaml restart: unless-stopped, which restarts the same container restart_policy: condition: any, which creates a new container deploy.replicas deploy.replicas, with placement, reservations, and limits Token in a .env file as CIRCLECI_RUNNER_API_AUTH_TOKEN, visible in docker inspect Swarm secret -token, which holds a runner config file The same CIRCLECI_RUNNER_NAME for every replica {{.Node.Hostname}}--{{.Task.Slot}}, unique for each replica Dockerfiles that build the runner into an Ubuntu, cimg, or runner-agent image A stock image, with the runner mounted from the volume runner-bin, which the runner-distributor service fills. Refer to Images Runner logs written to a mounted file in the machine service Logs on stdout, read with docker service logs CIRCLECI_RUNNER_MODE and CIRCLECI_RUNNER_CLEANUP_WORK_DIR in the service environment The same variables, in the stack file. Cleanup is "false" on Linux Jobs with resource_class: / No change Your job configs do not change. Your resource classes and tokens can stay.

data:
This page describes what the stack protects, what it does not protect, and which controls you must apply on the CircleCI side. Read it before you give a class to a team.
Important Untrusted jobs on a self-hosted runner pose significant risks to your machines and your network. Never use self-hosted runners for public projects that build forked pull requests.
Status. This is a CircleCI Labs project at version 0.x. It has not been independently reviewed or penetration-tested. The documentation site follows the main branch, so it can describe a control that your release does not have: the copy of this page in your release bundle is the one for that release. What is tested says how each claim is checked, and which claims are not.
data.bitlocker-on-windows-hosts#BitLocker on:
Docker keeps a Swarm secret in clear text on the container root disk until the container stops. Encrypt the volume that holds the Docker root directory, which is C:\ProgramData\docker by default, with BitLocker. Confirm the protection status:
Get-BitLockerVolume The status of the volume must show that protection is on. BitLocker protects the token when someone steals the disk, or a snapshot or backup of it. It does not protect against a job, or an administrator who is logged in to the live host, because both read the decrypted file. Limit the local administrators of the host, use one token for each class and host, and rotate tokens. Refer to the Microsoft documentation for BitLocker on Windows Server for the setup steps, including the recovery key.
data.circleci-server#CircleCI server: CircleCI documents machine runner 3 for server 4.4 and later, and says that an install on server sets the API URL of the runner (CIRCLECI_RUNNER_API_URL, or api.url in the config file). This repository is tested against CircleCI cloud only. In this stack the runners send their calls to the token proxy, so the URL of your server goes to the -upstream argument of the token-proxy service (its command in the stack file), and the runners keep CIRCLECI_RUNNER_API_URL: http://token-proxy:8080. Whether the proxy and the runner download work against your server version is not known, and no job of this project has run against one. Config policies, which the CircleCI-side controls above use, need the Scale plan on cloud or server 4.2 or later.
data.circleci-side-controls#CircleCI-side con:
The stack cannot decide which projects may use a class. Apply these controls in your organization.
One class and one token for each service. Give each token a nickname that names its host or purpose, so you can revoke it alone. Only organization admins create and delete resource classes. Delete the tokens of a class before you delete the class.
Config policies. Restrict each class to named projects with the resource_class_by_project helper. Config policies need the Scale plan on cloud, or server version 4.2 or later. A class that is not in the mapping stays available to every project.
package org import data.circleci.config policy_name["runner_policies"] enable_hard["resource_class_check"] resource_class_check = config.resource_class_by_project({ "/linux-hardened": {""}, "/linux-docker-build": {"", ""} }) Enable evaluation and push the policy. Refer to Config policies for self-hosted runner.
$ circleci policy settings set --org --enabled $ circleci policy push ./config-policies --org Context restrictions. Project restrictions, security groups, and expression restrictions combine with logical AND. Restrict every context that jobs on a runner class use. For deploy contexts, add an expression such as pipeline.git.branch == "main" and not job.ssh.enabled.
No fork builds on public projects. CircleCI does not make self-hosted runners available to public projects that have Build forked pull requests enabled.
SSH rerun stays off unless a class needs it. The shipped classes leave CIRCLECI_RUNNER_SSH_ADVERTISE_ADDR unset and publish no ports, so they cannot serve SSH. If you deploy the SSH add-on stack file, keep its class for named projects and restrict inbound port 54782 with the DOCKER-USER chain or a cloud security group, not with ufw or firewalld, which a published port bypasses. Refer to Rerun job with SSH.
Monitoring. Watch the runner inventory for names you do not know, and the logs for 401 and for exit code 80. In the log of the token proxy, a claim that is refused comes from a container that is not a runner of a class, or from a runner that tries to claim twice. Refer to Monitor the token proxy.
Runner classes are usable only by jobs of the organization that owns them.
data.cloud-nodes-block-the-metadata-address#C:
A job runs in a container on your node, and nothing in this stack or in Docker stops it from sending traffic to the instance-metadata service that cloud providers serve at the link-local address 169.254.169.254. On a cloud virtual machine, that service can hand out the credentials of the role that is attached to the node and, on some clouds, the user data of the instance. A job that reads them acts as the node. This is true of every self-hosted runner on a cloud VM, and it is not specific to Swarm. The recipes below are the usual ones. They are not tested in this repository’s CI: check them on your own nodes with a job that runs curl -m 3 http://169.254.169.254/ and must fail.
Give the node role the fewest permissions that the node needs, which is often none. Do not leave the Swarm join token readable in the user data or the startup script of an instance, because any job that reaches the metadata service reads it, and with it joins a node to your Swarm.
Block the address for containers on Linux. Add a rule to the DOCKER-USER chain, which Docker evaluates before its own rules for container traffic:
sudo iptables -I DOCKER-USER -d 169.254.169.254 -j DROP Docker creates the chain when it starts, so the rule must be added after Docker is up, and again after a reboot: put it in a systemd unit that starts after docker.service. The unit adds the rule only when it is missing.
[Unit] Description=Block the instance metadata address for containers After=docker.service Requires=docker.service [Service] Type=oneshot RemainAfterExit=yes ExecStart=/bin/sh -c 'iptables -C DOCKER-USER -d 169.254.169.254 -j DROP 2>/dev/null || iptables -I DOCKER-USER -d 169.254.169.254 -j DROP' [Install] WantedBy=multi-user.target The rule does not cover a container on the host network, which the docker-build class can use, and it does not cover the host itself. Check it with sudo iptables -S DOCKER-USER after a reboot and after a restart of Docker. If your Docker uses another firewall backend, use its equivalent of the rule.
On AWS, require IMDSv2 and a hop limit of 1. This disables IMDSv1 and stops the session-token response from reaching a container behind Docker’s bridge or NAT, because the extra hop exceeds the limit:
aws ec2 modify-instance-metadata-options --instance-id --http-tokens required --http-put-response-hop-limit 1 --http-endpoint enabled It does not cover containers on the host network. It also breaks every job that uses the node role through the metadata service: give such jobs their credentials another way, for example through a context or OIDC.
On other clouds, apply the same two ideas. Allow the metadata service from the host only (the rule above), use the provider’s session or header requirement for it if it has one, and attach a role with minimal permissions. Refer to the documentation of your provider for the setting, because this page does not cover each cloud.
On Windows, this page has no rule that is tested. The role, user data and cloud-side settings above apply to a Windows node too, but have not been tried with Windows containers.
data.compared-with-the-official-runner-instal:
This table puts the Linux classes of this repository next to the installs that CircleCI documents. The first three columns are our reading of the public CircleCI documentation as of 17 October 2026: they are not statements by CircleCI, the pages change, and the sources below are the reference. The last two columns come from the tests of this repository. Where the public documentation says nothing, the cell says so.
Machine runner 3 package Container runner Machine runner orchestrator This repository, default class This repository, hardened class Can a job read the resource class token? According to the documentation, a job gains the privileges of the task agent, and with the packages the runner runs as the same user (circleci) Not stated in the public documentation. The agent holds the tokens in a Kubernetes secret Documented as no: a sidecar keeps the token out of the VM, and the documentation ties grantSudo to it No, even with sudo: the token is in the token proxy, and the container holds a placeholder. A job on the node of the proxy could read it, after a container escape No, for the same reason. The persistent class is the exception, refer to The persistent class Can jobs use sudo? Whatever you grant the circleci user Set by the job image and the pod securityContext that you configure No by default (grantSudo: false), and jobs run as the unprivileged circleci user. Optional with grantSudo: true Yes, passwordless, as in the Docker executor No. A setuid binary cannot lift a job to root, because the step-down uses setpriv --no-new-privs The boundary between jobs None: each job runs on the machine where the runner is installed An ephemeral pod, which Kubernetes tears down after the job. Pods share the node kernel A virtual machine for each job, provisioned on demand and shut down after the job A new container for each job, on a kernel that all containers on the node share The same: a new container for each job, with a shared kernel Sources: Self-hosted runner concepts, Self-hosted runner overview, Container runner reference, and the Machine runner orchestrator reference, including its sidecar and grantSudo.
Read the table this way:
A clean container is not a virtual machine. The orchestrator is the only column with a hardware-level boundary between jobs. If jobs must not share a kernel, use the orchestrator, or dedicate nodes to one trust group. Refer to Why Swarm and not container runner or another runner? The token. According to its documentation, in the orchestrator the token never reaches the VM, so even a root job cannot read it. The single-task classes of this repository work the same way: the token proxy adds the token to the claim, as the sidecar does, and the container holds a placeholder, so even a root job cannot read it. What differs is that a job that escapes its container onto the node of the proxy reaches the tokens, where in the orchestrator the sidecar is next to a virtual machine. The persistent class and Windows are weaker: there the token is a file in the container, readable by a job that uses sudo (persistent) or by every job (Windows). The runner binary. The table does not compare how the installs verify the runner. In this repository the distributor installs it with a SHA-256 check, and the entrypoint checks it at every container start. Refer to Runner binary integrity on Linux. Windows. A single-task class holds only the placeholder, and the proxy holds the token, so the job cannot read the token from its own container. No test asserts that on Windows, and it is not a boundary against a hostile job on the same host as the proxy (refer to Windows). The persistent class is at parity with the official Windows runner: the job can read the token. The Windows classes have no hardened variant. Treat each Windows class as a trust boundary.
data.egress-hosts#Egress hosts:
Runners need outbound HTTPS only, and no inbound access. Allow these hosts by name, because their addresses change.
Host Port Used for runner.circleci.com 443 The runner API: claiming tasks. With the token proxy, only the node of the proxy calls it for the single-task Linux classes, because the runners and their task agents reach the API through the proxy circleci-binary-releases.s3.amazonaws.com 443 The task agent, which every new container downloads, and the runner download: on Linux by the runner-distributor service (the manifest and the tarball), or by each container of a microVM class, and on Windows by the runner-distributor-windows service circleci-tasks-prod.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com 443 Caches, workspaces, artifacts, and test results internal.circleci.com 443 Named in earlier versions of this page for checkout. It is not on CircleCI’s list of hosts for self-hosted runners (the two hosts above, the cache host, and your VCS host), so allow it only if a job log shows that a step needs it Your VCS host, for example github.com 443, and 22 for SSH checkouts Checkout. For Bitbucket Cloud over SSH, CircleCI’s changelog says the agent uses ssh.bitbucket.org from 12 November 2026 Your image registries, for example Docker Hub and mcr.microsoft.com 443 Pulling the service images, on Linux also the alpine image of the runner-distributor service. The token proxy image comes from Docker Hub (registry-1.docker.io, auth.docker.io and its content delivery network), from a mirror of it that you name with MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_IMAGE github.com and release-assets.githubusercontent.com 443 On Windows, Git for Windows and 7-Zip, which the runner-distributor-windows service downloads (not in an air-gapped setup with a mirror). The first host redirects the downloads to the second If your VCS organization uses an IP allow list, add the egress addresses of your nodes. The list applies to every checkout method. If you use an explicit proxy, test a checkout through it before you roll out a class. Jobs inherit HTTPS_PROXY and NO_PROXY from the service environment in the stack file.
data.isolation-between-runners#Isolation betw:
Replicas of one class share an overlay network and can reach each other. Swarm cannot prevent this: enable_icc=false is ignored on swarm-scoped networks, overlay networks have no such option, and a stack cannot use a node-local bridge network. On Windows, the overlay is the only network option for services, and Windows has no equivalent control for it. All Windows classes share one overlay network of the stack, and it is not encrypted, so Windows classes can reach each other, and their traffic is in clear text between nodes (Encrypted class networks).
On Linux, each class gets its own overlay network, so classes cannot reach each other. Containers can still reach the host network and the internet through default egress. To reduce the exposure:
Run sensitive classes on dedicated nodes. Refer to Multi-Node Clusters. Treat the proxy as part of every class network: any container on a class network can reach it, and the proxy answers only claims from the runners of the class. Filter egress on the host, for example in the DOCKER-USER chain on Linux. Docker bypasses ufw and firewalld rules for published ports and for container traffic, so a rule in either of those does not filter it. Rely on single-use containers. A compromised replica disappears with its job.
data.linux#Linux:
Single-task classes: the token proxy. The class secret -token is mounted into the token-proxy service and nowhere else. The runners read a made-up placeholder config, and the proxy adds the class token to their claims. A job cannot read what the container does not hold, so the sudo setting no longer decides whether a job can reach the class token. Refer to The token proxy. Storage. A class secret is a minimal runner config file that holds only api.auth_token. Swarm mounts it as a read-only file in memory, in the proxy container at /run/secrets/-token (uid 65534, mode 0400), or, in a persistent class, in the runner container at /run/secrets/circleci_runner_config.yaml, owned by the runner user circleci-runner (uid 2000) with mode 0400. The runners of the other classes mount the placeholder secret runner-placeholder-token at the same path. The runner reads it with --config. The token is in no environment variable, no command line, and no stack file, and docker inspect does not show it. Users. The runner runs as circleci-runner, which has no sudo rights and cannot write to /opt/machine-runner-swarm. Jobs run as the job user, stepped down with command_prefix. Default class. The job user keeps passwordless sudo. A job that uses sudo is root in its container. It can read the placeholder, the files of the runner, and become the runner user, but the container holds no class token. What a job still gets is the task token of its own job, which the task agent already has. Hardened class. MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO: "false" steps every job down with setpriv --no-new-privs, even when the image has sudo, and the container does not start when the image has no util-linux setpriv. The entrypoint edits no file: Swarm ignores no-new-privileges, so this per-job flag, inherited by everything the job starts, is what stops a setuid binary (sudo with its rules intact, su, or one with a local-root bug) from lifting a job to root. The job also gets none of the CIRCLECI_RUNNER_* and MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_* variables of the container. The job user cannot read the file or the process of the runner, and cannot become another user. A kernel or container-runtime bug can still lift a job to root, because the containers share the host kernel. Tools must be in the image. Use this for shared or regulated classes, and for the persistent class when its jobs can do without sudo. The test linux/tests/token.sh measures the probes below against the real runner binary, with the sentinel token in the runner’s config file as the persistent class has it. The test linux/tests/proxy.sh shows that, with the proxy, no class token is in a runner container: it scans the files, /proc/*/environ, and /proc/*/cmdline of the runners as root.

data.runner-binary-integrity-on-linux#Runner: The runner executes the jobs of your classes, so it must be the binary that CircleCI published. The runner-distributor service installs it, and the entrypoint checks it before every start. Refer to The runner distributor on Linux for how the parts fit.
data.runner-binary-integrity-on-windows#Runne:
The trust is the one of Linux: the service runner-distributor-windows downloads the tarball over HTTPS from the release bucket of CircleCI, compares its SHA-256 with the two values (amd64 and arm64) that the stack file carries for the pinned version (a floating value ignores that list and uses the manifest.json of CircleCI, which is weaker, as on Linux; a mirror must be https:// unless a usable list is set for an exact pin, or MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_ALLOW_HTTP=true when there is no list), checks that the binary reports the version, and records the SHA-256 of the binary in versions\\SHA256. Portable Git and 7zr.exe are pinned by SHA-256 in the script, so a new Git version is a new script and a new release of this repository.
Two things differ. The runner is the main process of the container and there is no entrypoint, so nothing checks the binary when a container starts. The distributor compares the active binary with its record at every check interval (24 hours by default) and installs it again when it changed. And a job runs as an administrator, but in its own container: the volume is mounted read-only through two links, so a job cannot change the runner or Git. A container with write access to the volume, for example one of the docker-build class (it controls the engine and is root-equivalent on its node), can still change them. Refer to Docker Builds.
data.swarm#Swarm: Swarm stores secrets encrypted in the Raft log of the managers, and sends a secret only to nodes that run a task that uses it. Optionally lock the managers with docker swarm update --autolock=true. It protects the secrets at rest, but each manager then needs docker swarm unlock after every Docker daemon restart. Keep join tokens private, and rotate them with docker swarm join-token --rotate. A user in the docker group on a manager can read every token. Limit administrator access to the managers.
data.the-checks#The checks: When Who What Download Distributor The SHA-256 of the tarball must equal a value of the list (the pinned version’s by default), or, with manifest, the manifest value. Otherwise it installs nothing Install Distributor The binary must report exactly the version that it installs (a pin of 3.1.1 does not accept 3.1.13). The distributor records the SHA-256 of the binary in versions//SHA256, the files are owned by root and not writable by others, and the copy in place and the link current are checked again after the install and the flip Every check interval (24 hours by default) Distributor It compares the active binary with its record, and installs the version again when the binary changed Every container start Entrypoint It resolves current once and runs sha256sum -c against the record. A missing record or a different binary ends in exit code 80 and the log line does not match its SHA-256 record. Refer to Error: does not match its SHA-256 record. The entrypoint is a Swarm config, which is immutable and read-only
data.the-persistent-class#The persistent clas:
A persistent class (persistent.yaml) does not use the proxy. A continuous runner claims a task after every job, and the proxy allows one claim for each container, so the runner keeps its token in a file in its own container. This class is weaker than the proxied classes:
The shipped file sets MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO: "false", so the token file is unreadable to the job user, and the tools that jobs need must be in the image. If you set "true" (the opt-in), a job that uses sudo reads the class token, and it can then run a runner of its own on that class. State from one job is visible to the next, because the container lives on. Therefore give the persistent class a resource class of its own, restrict it to trusted projects with a config policy, keep production contexts away from it, and rotate its token on a schedule. Refer to Persistent mode.
data.the-token-proxy#The token proxy:
The service token-proxy in runners.yaml keeps the class tokens of the Linux single-task classes away from the runner containers and from the jobs that run in them. One proxy serves every class of the stack, and docker-build.yaml and ssh-rerun.yaml add their classes to it. Refer to Concepts for how the pieces fit.
What it does:
The claim is the only call that gets the class token. The runners send every API call to the proxy and hold a made-up token. The proxy replaces the Authorization header of the task-claim call (POST /api/v3/runner/claim) with the class token and passes every other call on unchanged. The runner and its task agent use the task token from the claim response for the rest, and the token is scoped to one task. The class is decided by the network, not by the caller. The proxy finds its classes in its own secrets directory: every secret -token is the class , whose runners are tasks.. The made-up secret runner-placeholder-token is never a class, and no runner token is mounted into the proxy. A claim is allowed only from an IP address that Swarm DNS lists now for tasks. of a class, and it gets the token of that class. Any other address, such as a container that you started on the class network, gets 403 and nothing reaches CircleCI. An address that two classes list is refused too. The 403 says only claim refused: the reason, with what DNS lists, is in the log of the proxy and nowhere a job can read it. One claim per container. After a claim that returns a task, that address cannot claim again until DNS has not listed it for 30 seconds in a row, which means the container is gone. One missing answer, even a no such host for the whole class, is one poll of the 30 and never a release. A job that runs in a container cannot use the proxy to claim again for itself or to start more tasks of its class. The source address cannot be forged by a job. The proxy attaches to each class overlay network with endpoint_mode: dnsrr, so it sees the address of the container that connects, not an address that the Swarm load balancer rewrote. The runner services drop NET_RAW, so even root in a container cannot send packets with another address. The encrypted class networks need Docker Engine 23.0.3 or later (or 20.10.24): earlier engines accepted unauthenticated VXLAN traffic on encrypted overlay networks (CVE-2023-28840), which would let a host on the node network inject packets into a class overlay. The setup helper requires Docker 24 or later. Keep cap_drop: [NET_RAW, MKNOD] or ALL on every class that uses the proxy. The one exception is linux-microvm-docker, which cannot drop it (BuildKit needs it): it runs in a VM with no NET_ADMIN, stays at one replica, and has an overlay of its own, so there is no other runner of its class to impersonate (MicroVM jobs). It knows who has claimed, also after a restart. The proxy writes the addresses that have claimed to the small volume proxy-state before the runner gets its task. If it cannot write them, the claim fails and the runner does not get the task, and the proxy removes the state file (and keeps its marker), so that its next start takes the fail-safe path below instead of reading a state that is behind. A restart with a state refuses every address in it, whether Swarm DNS lists that address yet or not, and only those, so a runner that started before the proxy, or waited through a restart, is never locked out. A start with no state (an empty proxy-state, a state that was lost, or a class that is new) does not guess: for each class the proxy asks CircleCI (GET /api/v3/runner/scale, with the token of that class) how many tasks run. With none running, no runner present can hold a job, and they may claim. With some running, or when the call fails, the proxy refuses every runner of that class present until Swarm replaces it, so a runner that holds a job cannot claim another after a failover. The state stays on the node, so if the proxy moves to another node, it starts empty there: refer to Where the proxy runs, and when it moves for what to do. The service runs on a manager by default, and you can pin it to the node that keeps the volume with the label machine-runner-swarm.proxy=true and the placement variable. A claim with an unknown outcome counts as a claim. When the request reached CircleCI but the answer was lost (a timeout, a broken connection), the proxy cannot know whether CircleCI handed the runner a task. It latches the runner as if the claim had succeeded, so that runner is refused until Swarm replaces it. This costs a runner, never a second task for one container. The proxy waits at most 60 seconds for the response headers of the upstream. It fails closed otherwise. The proxy does not start without a usable token file for every class, nor when it cannot write its state. It answers 503 when DNS fails, when a token file disappears or when it cannot write its state. A count of running tasks that CircleCI does not give as a whole number of 0 or more (data.attributes.running_task_count and unclaimed_task_count, exactly these names), or does not give in 25 seconds for all classes together, counts as running tasks. It logs addresses, class names, and status codes, never a token. It limits what a job can send it. A claim is accepted from one address at most twice a second, with bursts of 10 (a runner claims about every 5 seconds), and its body is at most 64 KiB. The server has timeouts for the request header, the whole request and an idle connection, and caps the size of the headers. A runner that has claimed, or has a claim in flight, is refused from memory with no DNS lookup, and the lookups of all other claims share one answer for a second, so a job that floods the proxy with claims cannot make claims of other classes fail. Besides the claim limit, every client address is limited to 50 requests a second, with bursts of 200, on all paths, and the proxy serves at most 512 requests at the same time: more get a 503 with a Retry-After header. The proxy logs one summary line a minute: the claims it forwarded, the claims it latched, and the claims it refused, by reason. These limits keep one runner from starving the rest, and they do not make the proxy proof against a hostile job: the 512 shared slots and the one replica can still be used up by a job that sends enough requests from the containers of its class, and the claims of every class then wait. Watch the log line and Monitor the token proxy. It is small and locked down. One static Go binary, in a published image on a minimal base (distroless static: CA certificates, no shell, no package manager), runs as uid 65534 with no capabilities, a read-only root filesystem and no published port. The image is signed, and a release pins it by digest: refer to The token proxy image. Its secrets are the class tokens and nothing else. What it does not do:
It sees the runner traffic of its classes. The runner and the task agent send their API calls through it, over plain HTTP on the overlay network: claims, task configuration, and step output. The class token is never on that path, but the task token is. Between nodes, the Linux class networks are encrypted by default (driver_opts: {encrypted: "true"}, IPsec between the nodes, which needs IP protocol 50 (ESP) open between them: refer to Encrypted class networks), so the task tokens and the step output do not cross the network of the nodes in clear text, and a host on that network cannot inject packets into a class overlay. Docker does not support encrypted overlay networks for Windows containers, so the Windows class traffic is plain between nodes: keep the Windows nodes on a network that you trust. It is one point of failure. One replica serves all classes, because a second replica would not share the record of who has claimed. While it is down, no runner can claim. A job that is running keeps its container and its calls wait for the proxy. Refer to Monitor the token proxy. The node of the proxy holds every class token. A job that escapes its container onto that node reads them. The proxy never runs on a Docker-build node. It runs on a manager by default. In a cluster, label the node that runs it with machine-runner-swarm.proxy=true: runner services never run on a node with that label, so a job never shares a node with the proxy. On a single node there is no such label, nothing changes, and the jobs run next to the proxy. With several managers, pin the proxy to one with the label and MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_PLACEMENT. It depends on the runner API. The proxy knows two runner API calls: POST /api/v3/runner/claim, and GET /api/v3/runner/scale with the fields running_task_count and unclaimed_task_count. They are tested against the runner version that this release pins. If CircleCI changes them, the proxy fails closed and jobs wait until a release of this project follows the change. Pin the runner version in production. This page makes no claim about how the Runner Terms apply to a proxy between your runners and CircleCI: that is for your own review. It does not cover the persistent classes. Refer to The persistent class. Windows has its own proxy. The Windows stack runs token-proxy-windows (the windows/amd64 image of the same tag) for the Windows classes, because a Windows node does not share its network with a Linux proxy. It works as described here, with the differences in Windows. There is no windows/arm64 image (Windows). It does not replace CircleCI-side controls. A stolen class token still lets its holder run a runner on that class. Rotate tokens and restrict classes to projects, as in CircleCI-side controls.
data.the-token-proxy-image#The token proxy im:
The token proxy is not installed by the distributor: it is the image ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy of Docker Hub, which Swarm pulls. Its integrity rests on the image digest, not on a volume. A release bundle names the image by tag and digest (ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy:@sha256:), so Docker pulls exactly the image that the release pipeline pushed, whatever happens to the tag later. A checkout names the tag latest, which only a release moves and which is not a digest: pin a digest for anything that matters (Upgrade the token proxy). linux/setup.sh --deploy prints a warning when MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_IMAGE is not pinned by digest. ccilabs is the Docker Hub organization of CircleCI Labs. The name is not what you trust: the signature below is, and an image of that name that does not verify is not this project’s.
Every digest that the pipeline pushes is signed, and the pipeline checks the signature of the image again before it gives the image its release tags. The Linux index (four platforms), each Windows image (Server 2022 and 2025) and the manifest list that joins them are signed separately, so you can verify the list that you name or the image of one platform. The image runs as the user 65534 (Windows: ContainerAdministrator, because a Windows volume has no user mapping), and the state of the proxy is the only thing it writes.
data.token-model-on-each-os#Token model on ea:
A resource class token only authorizes a runner to claim tasks for that class. A holder of the token can still run a runner of their own on that class, and claim jobs that were meant for yours. That gives them the code and secrets of those jobs, so treat the token as a secret and rotate it.

data.verify-the-token-proxy-image#Verify the:
The signature is a keyless cosign signature, made with the OIDC token of the CircleCI job that pushed the image, like the signature of a release (Verify a release). It proves that a job of this CircleCI project pushed that digest. Verify the digest that you run, before you run it. You need cosign 3.1.3 or a later 3.x (CI signs and verifies with 3.1.3, and earlier versions are not tested). A digest of the manifest list covers every platform; pass the tag, and cosign resolves it to the digest and prints it.
cosign verify ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy: \ --certificate-identity "https://circleci.com/api/v2/projects/7bbdbb66-6ba8-4f6c-982e-d4fb401ec257/pipeline-definitions/8b2a66db-3f28-5c80-88e4-03f4694b5b60" \ --certificate-oidc-issuer "https://oidc.circleci.com" The command prints the verified claims as JSON when the project and the pipeline definition above signed the image. This is only the signature check. It does not look at the ref, so a reader who stops here accepts an image that a job of any branch signed: the ref check below is a second, separate step. Compare the digest in its output with the one in your stack file. A tag from a commit that is not a release (edge, sha-<12 characters>) verifies the same way. The identity does not name a branch, and a job of any branch can sign with it, so also check the ref in the certificates: the extension 1.3.6.1.4.1.57264.1.14 must be refs/heads/main, for every signature of the digest. cosign has no flag for that extension, so the command reads it, with the same pattern as Verify a release (the OID, then the value refs/heads/main, from a byte boundary):
cosign download signature ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy: \ | jq -r '.verificationMaterial | (.certificate // .x509CertificateChain.certificates[0]).rawBytes' \ | while read -r cert; do printf '%s' "$cert" | base64 -d | od -An -v -tx1 | tr -d ' \n' \ | grep -Eq '^([0-9a-f]{2})*2b0601040183bf30010e0411(0c|13)0f726566732f68656164732f6d61696e' \ || { echo "NOT signed for refs/heads/main: do not use this image"; exit 1; }; done && echo "every signature is for refs/heads/main" The notes of every release name the image of that release.

data.what-remains#What remains:
Not verified by this stack:
The task agent, which every container downloads from the same bucket at start, with no pin and no check. It runs as the job user and holds the task token. The source of the pinned SHA-256 values: CircleCI’s manifest at the time of the bump. The gap between the hash check and the exec of one container start (the next point). Also:
A privileged sibling container with SYS_ADMIN on the same node could mount the volume read-write and change both the binary and its record. The microVM classes do not mount the volume for this reason: each VM downloads and verifies its own runner. Refer to MicroVM jobs. The check at the start of a container narrows the window and does not close it: a sibling that rewrites the file between the hash and the exec of one start is not detected. The docker-build class mounts the Docker socket of the host and is root-equivalent on its node, so it can change the volume too. Refer to Docker Builds. Whoever can update the runner-distributor service, for example a user in the docker group of a manager, chooses the version and the download address. A list in MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_SHA256 limits what can be installed to the tarballs on it.
