data.where-the-runner-comes-from#Where the ru:
The distributor downloads the tarball over HTTPS from the release bucket of CircleCI. By default it compares the SHA-256 of the tarball with the values that the stack file carries for the pinned version (MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_SHA256: amd64, arm64, ppc64le and s390x, taken from CircleCI’s manifest when the version was bumped, and reviewed with the release of this repository). The manifest is not asked, so a change of the bucket after the bump cannot change what the nodes install. Each release of this repository bumps the version and its values together. The values are copied from CircleCI’s manifest when the version is bumped, so this is trust on first use from the same bucket: CircleCI publishes no signature for the runner that this stack checks.
A floating value (3.1, 3, current) cannot have such a list, because the version is not known in advance. The distributor ignores the default list of the pin and compares the SHA-256 with the value in the manifest.json of CircleCI, which it also gets over HTTPS. This is weaker: the manifest comes from the same bucket as the tarball, so whoever can change one can change the other, and the check proves that the download is whole, not that CircleCI published it. It is the same trust as the runner’s own download of the task agent, which every container fetches from the same bucket. An exact version of your own needs its own list, from the checksums.txt of its release (the tarballs of every architecture of your nodes), or the word manifest. The distributor then installs only a tarball that matches.
MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_DOWNLOAD_BASE_URL, the address of a mirror, must be an https:// URL unless a usable SHA-256 list is set for an exact pin: over plain http the manifest could be changed on the way, and with it the hash that it names. A floating value has no list, so an http:// base is refused unless MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_ALLOW_HTTP=true. The microVM classes download the runner into every VM with the same rules.
data.who-can-attack#Who can attack: A job author whose code runs in your container, which is the normal case. The job can do anything its user can do. A dependency or script that a job downloads and runs. A forked pull request, when you allow fork builds on a public project. Do not allow it. Another job that ran earlier on the same node, or that runs next to it.
data.windows#Windows: Single-task classes: the token proxy. The class secret -token is mounted into the service token-proxy-windows and nowhere else. The runners read a made-up placeholder config, and the proxy adds the class token to their claims, as on Linux. Refer to The token proxy. Storage. A class secret is the same minimal runner config file. Swarm places it at C:\ProgramData\Docker\secrets\ (in the proxy container -token, in the runner container of the persistent class circleci_runner_config.yaml). Windows does not support uid, gid, or mode for secrets, and only administrators and SYSTEM can read the file. No step-down. The runner and the jobs run as ContainerAdministrator, because the runner needs its symbolic link privilege. A job can read the config file of its runner, which holds the placeholder (in a persistent class: the token). The token is not in the job environment. An administrator in a container has no dropped NET_RAW, so the guarantee of the proxy that a job cannot forge a source address does not hold on Windows the way it does on Linux. What a forged address gets the job is limited: the answer to a claim goes to the owner of the address, not to the sender, and a container that has claimed cannot claim again. Windows is not tested for this, so treat each class as a trust boundary all the same. Clear text on disk. The token is stored as plain text on the disk of the container of the proxy (and of the runner, in a persistent class). Swarm writes the secret to the root disk of the container, and keeps it there until the container stops. This is a limitation of Swarm on Windows. On Linux, the secret is a mount in memory (tmpfs) and never reaches the disk of the container. Anyone who can read the Docker root directory of the host can read a Windows token, so enable BitLocker on the volume that holds it. Refer to BitLocker on Windows hosts. What the proxy gives on Windows. The proxy keeps the class token out of the job environment and out of the file system that the job sees. It is not a boundary against a hostile job on the same host: a job runs as an administrator, with process isolation, next to the proxy when both run on one node. It becomes a boundary only when the proxy runs on a node that runs no jobs (in a cluster, label that node machine-runner-swarm.proxy=true: runner services never run on a node with that label), and untrusted classes run with Hyper-V isolation, which is not tested here. The end-to-end jobs on Windows run real jobs through the proxy, but they only record whether a job can read the token and assert nothing about it, and no test forges a source address, so treat these protections as untested. Process isolation. Microsoft does not treat process isolation as a security boundary. Use one trust group of classes for each host. Hyper-V isolation adds a kernel boundary, needs nested virtualization on a virtual machine, and is not tested here. Treat each Windows resource class as a trust boundary. Use one token for each class and host, restrict who can use the class, and rotate tokens.

data.working-directory-cleanup#Working direct:
The runner can remove its working directory before it starts a task and again after the task. On Linux, the stack files and the entrypoint turn this off with CIRCLECI_RUNNER_CLEANUP_WORK_DIR: "false".
The reason is file ownership. The runner runs as the runner user (uid 2000), and the working directory and the files in it belong to the job user. The runner cannot remove them, so with cleanup on every task fails before it starts. The log shows failed to remove working directory before starting task with permission denied, even for the first task, because the parent directory belongs to the job user too. Giving the runner user the ownership does not help, because the job user must then be able to create the directory again. Running jobs as the runner user would give every job the runner token and remove the step-down, so the stack does not do that.
What this means for each class:
Single-task classes. Nothing is lost. Swarm discards the container after the job, so no file survives. Persistent classes. Nothing removes what a job leaves in the working directory, and the next job can read it. Start every job with a step that removes what an earlier job left. Recycle the class on a schedule. Refer to Persistent mode. Do not set the variable to true on Linux. Refer to Error: failed to remove working directory. Windows jobs and the runner use the same account, so the Windows files keep cleanup on.
